Purpose and Scope of This Graph: This knowledge graph is a curated summary of the Sanskrit Mahabharata written for the Living Epic voyage; it is intended as the grounding the app uses when answering questions about the epic.
Every fact in this graph is a paraphrase and summary written for this app, not a quotation from any translation or edition of the Mahabharata.
The graph is organised in two levels: a top-level theme (for example 'Kuru Dynasty and Lineage') and descriptive subtopics, each holding short self-contained facts.
Where the Mahabharata's manuscript traditions disagree, this graph tries to say so explicitly with phrases such as 'in some versions', 'the Critical Edition omits' or 'popular retellings add'.
The graph describes what the epic narrates; it does not claim that the events, people or battles of the Mahabharata are historically verified.
Places are described 'as described in the epic'; modern locations are given only as traditional identifications, never as proven sites.
Interpretive and devotional readings (for example Krishna as an avatar of Vishnu) are reported as what the text or a tradition says, not as settled fact.
Provenance and Honesty Policy: Provenance: the content of this graph is a summary compiled from general scholarly knowledge of the Mahabharata, chiefly the narrative as preserved in the Pune Critical Edition, with differences in other recensions and popular retellings flagged where known.
No quotation in this graph is presented as a verbatim translation; short Sanskrit terms (such as dharma, niyoga, akshauhini) are used as vocabulary only.
Numbers in this graph are only those widely reported for the text; where a number differs between editions or recensions, the variants are stated rather than one figure being chosen silently.
When a widely known story (for example Ganesha writing down the epic) is absent from the Critical Edition, this graph labels it as a later or variant addition rather than omitting it.
Users should treat this graph as a guide, and consult a full translation (for example of the Critical Edition) for exact wording.
Recensions and Manuscript Traditions: The Mahabharata survives in many manuscripts that scholars group into two main recensions: a Northern recension and a Southern recension.
The Northern recension includes versions in the Sharada (Kashmiri), Nepali, Maithili, Bengali and Devanagari scripts.
The Southern recension includes versions in the Telugu, Grantha and Malayalam scripts and is generally fuller, with more added passages.

The 'vulgate' text familiar from older translations is essentially the Devanagari version transmitted with the late-17th-century commentary of Nilakantha Chaturdhara; vulgate-type texts were printed in 19th-century Calcutta and Bombay editions (the Bombay editions with Nilakantha's commentary).
The English translation by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (published 1883–1896) follows a vulgate-type Northern text, so it contains passages that the Critical Edition omits.
A Southern-recension edition was printed at Kumbakonam in the early 20th century and is larger than the Northern vulgate.
Because recensions add, omit and reorder passages, verse and chapter numbers differ between editions, and the same episode can have different details in different manuscripts.
Regional-language retellings (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Bengali, Odia, Javanese and others) are separate literary works that often add episodes not found in any Sanskrit manuscript.
The Critical Edition (BORI, Pune): The Critical Edition of the Mahabharata was produced by the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) in Pune, India.
Critical Edition timeline: work begun 1919 | critical text completed 1966 | Harivamsha critical edition published 1969–1971.

V. S. Sukthankar is usually named as the first general editor of the Critical Edition, serving until his death in 1943; S. K. Belvalkar succeeded him, and P. L. Vaidya later became general editor and also edited the Harivamsha volumes.
The Critical Edition editors collated well over 1,000 manuscripts (a figure of about 1,200 or more is commonly reported) to reconstruct the oldest text recoverable from the surviving manuscripts.
The Critical Edition keeps in its main text only passages supported across the manuscript traditions; passages found in only some manuscripts were moved to footnotes and appendices.
The Critical Edition does not claim to recover an 'original' authorial Mahabharata; its editors described it as the oldest form reachable from the manuscript evidence.

The Critical Edition's text of the 18 parvas is commonly described as filling 19 volumes, published together with a large critical apparatus; the Harivamsha was edited separately, and index volumes followed.
Several modern English translations follow the Critical Edition, including the unfinished University of Chicago translation begun by J. A. B. van Buitenen and Bibek Debroy's complete translation.
Dating and Composition (Scholarly View): Most scholars think the Mahabharata grew over several centuries, with a commonly cited composition range of roughly 400 BCE to 400 CE.
Many scholars think the text reached something close to its present form by around the Gupta period (c. 4th–5th century CE), though precise dates are debated.
Panini's Sanskrit grammar (usually dated c. 5th–4th century BCE) mentions devotees of Vasudeva and Arjuna, which is often cited as early evidence for the epic's heroes being known.
An early 6th-century CE copper-plate inscription refers to the Mahabharata as a collection of 100,000 verses, showing that the large form was established by then.
Vedic texts mention Kuru kings named Parikshit and Janamejaya, but whether these are the same figures as the epic's Parikshit and Janamejaya is debated.

Traditional Indian chronology places the Kurukshetra war just before the start of the Kali Yuga, conventionally reckoned as 3102 BCE; this is a traditional reckoning, not a historically established date.

Some 19th- and 20th-century scholars proposed that a short core poem called 'Jaya' grew into a 'Bharata' and then the 'Mahabharata'; this layered model is a hypothesis built partly on statements in the Adi Parva, not a documented history.
Dating ranges: commonly cited composition window c. 400 BCE – c. 400 CE | traditional war date c. 3102 BCE (Kali Yuga reckoning, not historical consensus).
Later Additions and Popular Variants to: Ganesha as scribe: the story that Ganesha wrote the epic as Vyasa dictated is absent from the Critical Edition and appears only in some manuscripts; it is treated as a later addition.

Draupadi's sari: the Critical Edition keeps the miracle of Draupadi's garment being endlessly replaced during the dice-hall assault, but her explicit prayer to Krishna and Krishna's direct intervention appear in other manuscripts and in popular retellings, not in the Critical Edition text.
Barbarika, the warrior who watches the whole war as a severed head, is not in the Sanskrit Mahabharata; his story comes from the Skanda Purana and regional folk traditions.

Karna's natural armour and earrings (kavacha and kundala) are part of the epic's core story, but many details about them, and Karna's curses, are elaborated differently in different versions and retellings.
The Jaimini Ashvamedha is a separate Sanskrit work attributed to Vyasa's disciple Jaimini that retells the horse sacrifice with many episodes not found in the Mahabharata.
Popular television and comic-book retellings often merge Puranic, regional and modern invented material with the Sanskrit epic; this graph flags such material where known.
Some versions say Gandhari's boon of a hundred sons came from Shiva; in the Critical Edition the boon is granted by Vyasa.

Accounts of Bhishma being bound by oath to serve the throne of Hastinapura itself are a popular (especially television) framing; in the epic his vows are to renounce the kingship and to remain celibate, and his loyalty to the throne is presented as duty rather than a sworn third vow.

Draupadi's taunt at the Maya Sabha that 'the son of a blind man is also blind' is a popular addition; the Critical Edition describes Bhima and others laughing at Duryodhana's mishaps in the hall but does not contain that taunt.

Popular retellings describe the svayamvara target as a revolving fish that Arjuna shoots while watching its reflection in water; the Critical Edition speaks of a target set high behind a mechanical device, and the fish-and-reflection details belong to other versions.
Retellings Beyond the Sanskrit Text: The Telugu Andhra Mahabharatam was composed by three poets (the Kavitraya): Nannaya (11th century), Tikkana (13th century) and Errana (14th century).
The Kannada poet Pampa composed the Vikramarjuna Vijaya (also called Pampa Bharata) in the 10th century, presenting Arjuna as its hero.
The Tamil Villi Bharatam of Villiputturar (c. 14th century) is a major Tamil retelling with its own episodes and emphases.
The Odia Mahabharata of Sarala Das (15th century) and the Bengali Mahabharata of Kashiram Das (usually dated to the late 16th or early 17th century) are major regional-language retellings.
The Mughal emperor Akbar commissioned a Persian translation called the Razmnama ('Book of War') in the 1580s.
Javanese and Balinese traditions, including wayang shadow puppetry, retell the Mahabharata with distinct characters such as the comic Punakawan servants not found in the Sanskrit text.
Key Terms and Spelling Conventions: Parva means 'book' or 'section'; the Mahabharata has 18 major parvas, traditionally subdivided into 100 sub-parvas (upaparvas).
Adhyaya means 'chapter'; shloka refers to a verse, especially the 32-syllable anushtubh verse that makes up most of the epic.
Itihasa ('thus indeed it was') is the traditional genre label of the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, usually rendered 'history' or 'traditional narrative'.
Names are spelled here in simplified English transliteration (for example Yudhishthira, Duhshasana or Dushasana, Draupadi); scholarly IAST spellings use diacritics such as Yudhiṣṭhira.
The Kauravas are, strictly, all descendants of Kuru, which includes the Pandavas; in common usage 'Kauravas' means the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra.
The Pandavas are the five sons of Pandu (legally), fathered by gods through Kunti and Madri.
Niyoga is the ancient custom described in the epic by which a widow or the wife of an incapable husband could bear a son by an appointed man so that the lineage continued.
How to Read Numbers in This Graph: Numeric facts use the compact form 'Label: A n | B m | ...' so that a chart model can read them directly.
Counts that differ between editions are given with each variant named, for example 'Verse count: Critical Edition n | vulgate m'.
Traditional figures (such as 100,000 verses or 100 sub-parvas) are labelled traditional; they are not exact counts of any surviving edition.
Chapter counts in this graph follow the Critical Edition unless stated otherwise.
Durations in the story (such as 13 years of exile or 18 days of war) are narrative durations stated by the epic, not historical measurements.
