The 18 Parvas in Order (Overview): The Mahabharata is divided into 18 major books called parvas.

Parva order: 1 Adi | 2 Sabha | 3 Vana (Aranyaka) | 4 Virata | 5 Udyoga | 6 Bhishma | 7 Drona | 8 Karna | 9 Shalya | 10 Sauptika | 11 Stri | 12 Shanti | 13 Anushasana | 14 Ashvamedhika | 15 Ashramavasika | 16 Mausala | 17 Mahaprasthanika | 18 Svargarohana.

Parva name meanings: Adi 'the beginning' | Sabha 'the assembly hall' | Vana or Aranyaka 'the forest' | Virata 'King Virata' | Udyoga 'the effort or preparation' | Bhishma, Drona, Karna, Shalya named after successive Kaurava commanders | Sauptika 'the sleepers' | Stri 'the women' | Shanti 'peace' | Anushasana 'instruction' | Ashvamedhika 'the horse sacrifice' | Ashramavasika 'the hermitage dwelling' | Mausala 'the clubs' | Mahaprasthanika 'the great departure' | Svargarohana 'ascent to heaven'.

Parvas by narrative phase: origins and youth (Adi) | rise, fall and exile (Sabha, Vana) | hidden year (Virata) | diplomacy (Udyoga) | war (Bhishma, Drona, Karna, Shalya, Sauptika) | grief and instruction (Stri, Shanti, Anushasana) | restoration and old age (Ashvamedhika, Ashramavasika) | endings (Mausala, Mahaprasthanika, Svargarohana).
Number of parvas per phase: Pre-war 5 | War 5 | Post-war 8 (the Sauptika, counted here among the war books, narrates the night attack after the 18th day of battle).
The Shanti Parva is the longest parva and the Mahaprasthanika Parva is the shortest in the Critical Edition.
The Harivamsha ('lineage of Hari', i.e. Krishna) is not counted among the 18 parvas; it is treated as a khila, a supplement or appendix to the Mahabharata.
Sub-parvas: The Traditional 100: Tradition divides the 18 parvas into 100 sub-parvas (upaparvas); the list of 100 is given in the Parvasamgraha, the second chapter of the Adi Parva.

The traditional list of 100 sub-parvas is usually understood to end with the Harivamsha (including its Bhavishya section), which is one reason the Harivamsha is regarded as belonging to the larger Mahabharata.
Modern Critical-Edition-based listings of the 18 parvas give 98 sub-parvas, with the Harivamsha counted separately to complete the traditional 100.

Sub-parvas per parva (Critical-Edition-based listing totalling 98): Adi 19 | Sabha 9 | Vana 16 | Virata 4 | Udyoga 11 | Bhishma 5 | Drona 8 | Karna 1 | Shalya 4 | Sauptika 3 | Stri 5 | Shanti 3 | Anushasana 2 | Ashvamedhika 2 | Ashramavasika 3 | Mausala 1 | Mahaprasthanika 1 | Svargarohana 1.
The sub-parva divisions in printed editions do not always match the Parvasamgraha list exactly, so counts other than 100 or 98 may be found in different editions.

Examples of named sub-parvas: the Bhagavad Gita Parva lies within the Bhishma Parva; the Rajadharma, Apaddharma and Mokshadharma sub-parvas make up the Shanti Parva; the Anugita Parva lies within the Ashvamedhika Parva.
Size and Length of the Epic: The Mahabharata is traditionally called the shatasahasri samhita, the 'collection of one hundred thousand verses'.

Size estimates: traditional figure roughly 100,000 shlokas | Critical Edition about 75,000–90,000 verses depending on how verses and prose are counted | Bharata 'without the subsidiary tales' 24,000 verses (as the Adi Parva itself states).

The longest versions of the Mahabharata are commonly said to total about 1.8 million words, which is why the epic is often described as roughly ten times the length of the Iliad and the Odyssey combined; such comparisons are approximate.
The Mahabharata is usually described as the longest epic poem known; its exact length depends on which recension and which counting method is used.

Critical Edition chapters (adhyayas) per parva: Adi 225 | Sabha 72 | Vana 299 | Virata 67 | Udyoga 197 | Bhishma 117 | Drona 173 | Karna 69 | Shalya 64 | Sauptika 18 | Stri 27 | Shanti 353 | Anushasana 154 | Ashvamedhika 96 | Ashramavasika 47 | Mausala 9 | Mahaprasthanika 3 | Svargarohana 5.

Critical Edition total chapters: 1,995 across the 18 parvas (the sum of the per-parva figures); vulgate editions divide the text into somewhat more chapters, so chapter numbers differ between editions.
The Adi Parva states that Vyasa took three years to compose the epic.

Passages in the opening chapter of vulgate texts make a mythic claim that Vyasa composed a far larger version for gods, ancestors and celestial beings, of which only 100,000 verses circulate among humans; this is a statement of cosmic scale, not a textual fact, and such passages are not uniform across manuscripts.
Parvas 1–5: From Origins to the Eve of W: Adi Parva (Book 1): the frame stories, the origins of the Kuru dynasty, Shantanu and Bhishma, the births of the Pandavas, Kauravas and Karna, the princes' education under Drona, the lac-house plot, Draupadi's swayamvara, the founding of Indraprastha and the burning of the Khandava forest; it also contains tales such as Shakuntala, Yayati, Garuda, the churning of the ocean and Astika.

Sabha Parva (Book 2): the assembly hall built by the demon architect Maya, the killing of Jarasandha, Yudhishthira's Rajasuya sacrifice, the killing of Shishupala, the dice game, Draupadi's humiliation, the second dice game and the sentence of exile.

Vana or Aranyaka Parva (Book 3): the twelve years of forest exile, Arjuna's quest for divine weapons including the Pashupata, the long pilgrimage to sacred fords, embedded tales such as Nala and Damayanti, Savitri and Satyavan and the Ramopakhyana, Jayadratha's attempted abduction of Draupadi, Karna's gift of his armour to Indra and the Yaksha's questions.

Virata Parva (Book 4): the thirteenth year spent in disguise at King Virata's court in Matsya, Bhima's killing of Kichaka, the Kaurava cattle raid repelled by Arjuna as Brihannala, and the marriage of Uttara to Abhimanyu.

Udyoga Parva (Book 5): preparations for war, Duryodhana and Arjuna seeking Krishna's help, embassies of peace including Sanjaya's and Krishna's, Vidura's counsel, Krishna's and Kunti's meetings with Karna, Bhishma's account of Amba, and the assembly of the armies at Kurukshetra.
Parvas 6–10: The War Books: Bhishma Parva (Book 6): the opening ten days of the Kurukshetra war under Bhishma's command, including the Bhagavad Gita before the fighting and Bhishma's fall onto a bed of arrows.

Drona Parva (Book 7): days 11–15 under Drona's command, including Abhimanyu's death in the chakravyuha formation, Arjuna's killing of Jayadratha, Karna's killing of Ghatotkacha in a night battle, and Drona's death after hearing the half-true report of Ashvatthama's death.
Karna Parva (Book 8): days 16–17 under Karna's command, with Shalya as his charioteer, Bhima's killing of Duhshasana and Arjuna's killing of Karna when Karna's chariot wheel is stuck.

Shalya Parva (Book 9): day 18 under Shalya's command, the deaths of Shalya and Shakuni, Duryodhana's hiding in a lake, Balarama's pilgrimage along the Sarasvati, and the mace duel in which Bhima breaks Duryodhana's thigh.

Sauptika Parva (Book 10): Ashvatthama's night attack on the sleeping Pandava camp with Kripa and Kritavarma, the deaths of Dhrishtadyumna and Draupadi's five sons, and the clash of divine weapons that ends with Krishna's curse on Ashvatthama.
War days per parva: Bhishma 10 | Drona 5 | Karna 2 | Shalya 1 | Sauptika 0 (the night after day 18).

Kaurava commanders and days of command: Bhishma 10 (days 1–10) | Drona 5 (days 11–15) | Karna 2 (days 16–17) | Shalya 1 (day 18); after Duryodhana's defeat, the dying Duryodhana appoints Ashvatthama commander for the night attack.
The Pandava army's supreme commander throughout the war is Dhrishtadyumna, proposed by Arjuna and endorsed by Krishna in the Udyoga Parva, with seven generals leading the seven Pandava akshauhinis.
The Bhagavad Gita occupies chapters 23–40 of the Bhishma Parva in the Critical Edition (chapters 25–42 in the vulgate numbering).
Parvas 11–18: Aftermath and Endings: Stri Parva (Book 11): the women of both sides lament on the battlefield, Gandhari curses Krishna, the funeral rites are performed, and Kunti reveals that Karna was her son.
Shanti Parva (Book 12): the grieving Yudhishthira is instructed by Bhishma on the duties of kings (Rajadharma), conduct in emergencies (Apaddharma) and liberation (Mokshadharma).
Anushasana Parva (Book 13): Bhishma's further instruction on gifts, duties and devotion, including the Vishnu Sahasranama (thousand names of Vishnu), followed by Bhishma's death.

Ashvamedhika Parva (Book 14): Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice, Krishna's further teaching to Arjuna known as the Anugita, Krishna's revival of the stillborn Parikshit, and Arjuna's campaign following the sacrificial horse.
Ashramavasika Parva (Book 15): Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, Kunti and Vidura retire to the forest; Vyasa makes the dead warriors appear for one night; the three elders later die in a forest fire.
Mausala Parva (Book 16): the Yadavas destroy one another in a drunken brawl at Prabhasa, Balarama and Krishna depart from the world, and Dwaraka is swallowed by the sea.
Mahaprasthanika Parva (Book 17): the Pandavas and Draupadi renounce the kingdom and walk toward the Himalaya; all fall on the way except Yudhishthira and the dog that follows him.

Svargarohana Parva (Book 18): Yudhishthira reaches heaven, is shown a vision of his brothers in hell and Duryodhana in heaven, passes this final test and is united with his family in a divine form; the frame narration then closes.
Time Spans Within the Story: Story durations: exile in the forest 12 years | incognito year 1 | total exile 13 years | Kurukshetra war 18 days.
Bhishma lies on his bed of arrows for 58 nights before choosing to die, according to the Anushasana Parva.
The Mausala Parva opens in the 36th year after the war, fulfilling Gandhari's curse that the Yadavas would perish after 36 years.
Dhritarashtra lives in Hastinapura under Yudhishthira's rule for about 15 years after the war before retiring to the forest.
Gandhari's pregnancy lasts two years in the epic's account before she delivers a mass of flesh that Vyasa divides into her children.

When Arjuna was recognised during the cattle raid, Duryodhana claimed the thirteenth year was not yet over; in the Virata Parva Bhishma calculates, allowing for intercalary months, that the full term had already been completed.
Post-war milestones: Yudhishthira's coronation | Bhishma's death after 58 nights | horse sacrifice | elders' retirement after about 15 years | Yadava destruction in year 36 | final journey.
The Recurring Number Eighteen: The number eighteen recurs in the Mahabharata's structure and story, a pattern often noted by commentators.
Eighteen in the epic: parvas 18 | days of war 18 | akshauhinis (army divisions) 18 | chapters of the Bhagavad Gita 18.
Armies at Kurukshetra: Kaurava 11 akshauhinis | Pandava 7 akshauhinis | total 18.
One akshauhini as defined in the Adi Parva: chariots 21,870 | elephants 21,870 | horses 65,610 | foot soldiers 109,350.

Units in one akshauhini (sum of the Adi Parva figures): 218,700 | in 18 akshauhinis by simple multiplication: 3,936,600; the multiplied total is arithmetic, not a figure the epic states, and these numbers are traditional and symbolic rather than historical.
Whether the recurrence of eighteen is deliberate symbolism or a product of later editorial arrangement is a matter of interpretation.
Didactic and Philosophical Sections: The Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna before the war, is part of the Bhishma Parva; both the vulgate and the Critical Edition give it 700 verses in 18 chapters (a verse found in some manuscripts and later tradition speaks of 745 verses).
The Viduraniti, Vidura's counsel on statecraft and ethics to Dhritarashtra, and the Sanatsujatiya, a dialogue on death and the self, are in the Udyoga Parva.
The Yaksha Prashna, a riddle-dialogue between Yudhishthira and a yaksha (later revealed as the god Dharma), is near the end of the Vana Parva.
The Shanti and Anushasana Parvas together form the largest body of instruction in the epic, delivered mainly by Bhishma from his bed of arrows.
The Anugita in the Ashvamedhika Parva is a later teaching by Krishna to Arjuna after Arjuna says he has forgotten the Gita.
Large didactic sections are often considered by scholars to be among the later layers of the text, though this is debated.
Embedded Tales (Upakhyanas): The Mahabharata contains many embedded stories called upakhyanas, told to characters by sages and elders.
Shakuntala and Dushyanta, whose son Bharata gives his name to the Bharata lineage, is told in the Adi Parva.
Nala and Damayanti is told to the exiled Yudhishthira in the Vana Parva by the sage Brihadashva, as the story of another king who lost his kingdom at dice.
Savitri and Satyavan, the story of a wife who wins back her husband's life from Yama, is told by Markandeya in the Vana Parva.
The Ramopakhyana, a shorter version of the story of Rama, is told by Markandeya in the Vana Parva.
Other notable embedded tales include Yayati, Garuda, the churning of the ocean, Astika and the snake sacrifice, Rishyashringa, Shibi and the dove, and the flood story of Manu and the fish.
The Adi Parva notes that the Bharata core is 24,000 verses 'without the subsidiary tales', implying that the upakhyanas account for much of the epic's size.
Verse Form and Style: Most of the Mahabharata is composed in the anushtubh shloka metre of four eight-syllable quarters (32 syllables per verse).
Longer trishtubh verses (four eleven-syllable quarters) appear especially in older-sounding narrative and battle passages.
The epic includes some prose passages, notably in the Adi Parva genealogies and some didactic sections.
The Mahabharata is largely dialogue: nearly every passage is framed as one character speaking to another, beginning with formulas such as 'Vaishampayana said' or 'Sanjaya said'.
Harivamsha: The Appendix (Khila): The Harivamsha is regarded as a khila (supplement or appendix) of the Mahabharata, not one of its 18 parvas.
The Harivamsha narrates the genealogy of the Yadavas and the life of Krishna, including his childhood among the cowherds of Vraja, which the main Mahabharata hardly covers.
Vulgate editions divide the Harivamsha into three parts: Harivamsha Parva, Vishnu Parva and Bhavishya Parva.
Harivamsha size: vulgate about 16,000 verses (a figure of 16,374 is commonly given) | Critical Edition about 6,000 verses (about 6,073 commonly given).
The Harivamsha Critical Edition was edited by P. L. Vaidya and published by BORI in 1969–1971.
Scholars generally consider the Harivamsha to be later than much of the Mahabharata, though parts of it are old.
The Epic's Description of Itself: The Mahabharata calls itself an itihasa, a traditional narrative of what happened, and also a treatise on dharma, artha (prosperity), kama (desire) and moksha (liberation).

The Mahabharata is often called the 'fifth Veda'; the Adi Parva describes Vyasa teaching the Vedas with the Mahabharata as the fifth, and the title is often explained by the epic being open to listeners excluded from Vedic study.
The epic claims a comprehensive scope: in paraphrase, whatever is found here may be found elsewhere, but what is not found here is found nowhere.
The Adi Parva opens with two summaries of the whole work: the Anukramanika (table of contents, chapter 1) and the Parvasamgraha (summary of the books, chapter 2).
The title 'Mahabharata' is explained in the text as 'the great (story of the) Bharatas', and also, by a playful etymology, as great in size and weight.
The epic is also traditionally called 'Jaya' ('victory'), a name used at the start of many recitations.

Overview of the Nested Frames: The Mahabharata is told as a story within a story within a story; each layer has its own narrator and listener.
Outer frame: the bard Ugrashravas (called Sauti, 'son of the charioteer-bard') tells the epic to the sage Shaunaka and other sages at a twelve-year sacrifice in the Naimisha forest.
Middle frame: Ugrashravas repeats what he heard Vaishampayana recite to King Janamejaya during Janamejaya's snake sacrifice.
Inner frames: within Vaishampayana's narration, characters such as Sanjaya, Markandeya, Bhishma and many sages narrate further stories to other characters.
Narration layers: author Vyasa | Vaishampayana to Janamejaya | Ugrashravas to Shaunaka at Naimisharanya | Sanjaya to Dhritarashtra for the war | many embedded narrators.
Because of the frames, the epic is presented as an oral recitation passed from teller to teller, not as a written book.
The frames make Vyasa both the author of the epic and a participant in its story, since he is the biological grandfather of the Pandavas and Kauravas.
Vyasa: Author and Participant: Vyasa, called Krishna Dvaipayana, is traditionally the composer of the Mahabharata; 'Krishna' refers to his dark complexion and 'Dvaipayana' to his birth on an island in the Yamuna river.
Vyasa is the son of the sage Parashara and Satyavati, born before Satyavati's marriage to King Shantanu.
Vyasa is also called Veda Vyasa ('arranger of the Vedas') because tradition credits him with dividing the Veda into its branches.
At his mother Satyavati's request, Vyasa fathered Dhritarashtra, Pandu and Vidura by niyoga, making him the biological grandfather of the Pandavas and Kauravas.
Vyasa appears repeatedly in the story to advise, console and warn the characters, for example dividing Gandhari's embryo into a hundred and one parts and granting Sanjaya divine sight.
Vyasa teaches the Mahabharata to his disciples and his son Shuka, and at Janamejaya's snake sacrifice he asks his disciple Vaishampayana to recite it.
The Adi Parva says Vyasa took three years to compose the epic.
In later (largely post-epic, Puranic and popular) tradition, Vyasa is counted among the chiranjivins, beings who live on through the ages.
Janamejaya and the Snake Sacrifice: Janamejaya is a Kuru king, the son of Parikshit, grandson of Abhimanyu and great-grandson of Arjuna.

Janamejaya's father Parikshit died from the bite of the serpent king Takshaka, fulfilling a curse laid on him by Shringin, son of the sage Shamika, after Parikshit insulted Shamika by draping a dead snake over his shoulders.
Urged on by the sage Utanka, who had his own grievance against Takshaka, Janamejaya performed a snake sacrifice (sarpa-sattra) designed to draw all serpents into the fire.
The snake sacrifice was halted by the young sage Astika, son of the sage Jaratkaru and the naga woman Jaratkaru (sister of the serpent king Vasuki), who won a boon from Janamejaya to stop it.
Vyasa came to Janamejaya's sacrifice with his disciples, and Janamejaya asked to hear the story of his ancestors, the Pandavas and Kauravas.
Vaishampayana recited the Mahabharata to Janamejaya in the intervals of the sacrificial rite.
Janamejaya repeatedly interrupts Vaishampayana with questions, which gives the epic its dialogue form ('Janamejaya said ... Vaishampayana said ...').

The background to the snake sacrifice (Utanka's grievance, the origin of the serpents, Parikshit's death and Astika's intervention) is told directly by Ugrashravas to the sages in the opening sub-parvas of the Adi Parva (the Paushya, Pauloma and Astika sub-parvas), before Vaishampayana's recitation begins.
Vaishampayana: Vyasa's Disciple and Reci: Vaishampayana is a disciple of Vyasa who recites the Mahabharata to King Janamejaya at the snake sacrifice.
Most of the Mahabharata as we have it is formally Vaishampayana's narration, introduced by the formula 'Vaishampayana said'.
Vaishampayana is also associated in Vedic tradition with the Black Yajurveda (Krishna Yajurveda) as its teacher.
Vaishampayana's recitation follows the order of events from the Kuru origins to the Pandavas' ascent to heaven.
Within Vaishampayana's telling, the war books are largely given as Sanjaya's report to Dhritarashtra, so the listener hears the war through two narrators at once.
Ugrashravas Sauti at Naimisharanya: Ugrashravas is a bard (suta), son of Lomaharshana, and is often called Sauti; he is the narrator of the outermost frame.
Ugrashravas arrives at the Naimisha forest (Naimisharanya), where the sage Shaunaka and other sages are performing a twelve-year sacrifice (sattra).
Ugrashravas tells the sages that he heard the Mahabharata recited by Vaishampayana at Janamejaya's snake sacrifice, and then retells it for them.
The Adi Parva begins with Ugrashravas greeting the sages and summarising the work, before the narration passes to Vaishampayana's telling.
The Naimisha forest frame with Ugrashravas and Shaunaka is also used by several Puranas, which present themselves as told by Lomaharshana or Ugrashravas to the same sages.
Some scholars see the Ugrashravas-Shaunaka frame as a later Bhargava (descendants of Bhrigu) layer added around the older Vaishampayana-Janamejaya frame; this is a scholarly hypothesis.
Sanjaya and the Narration of the War: Sanjaya is the charioteer and counsellor of the blind king Dhritarashtra.
Vyasa offered Dhritarashtra sight to watch the war; Dhritarashtra declined, and Vyasa instead granted Sanjaya divine sight so he could see and report all events of the battle.
In the Bhishma Parva, Sanjaya first reports to Dhritarashtra that Bhishma has fallen (on day 10) and then narrates the first ten days of the war in flashback.
The Bhagavad Gita is presented as Sanjaya reporting to Dhritarashtra the conversation between Krishna and Arjuna.
Sanjaya's narration of the war continues through the Drona, Karna and Shalya Parvas into the Sauptika Parva; according to the Sauptika Parva, his divine sight leaves him when Duryodhana dies.
Sanjaya survives the war and later accompanies Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti to the forest; he escapes the forest fire that kills them, according to the Ashramavasika Parva.
Sanjaya frequently speaks frankly to Dhritarashtra, telling him that his own indulgence of Duryodhana caused the disaster.
Ganesha as Scribe — a Later Addition: A popular story says that Vyasa dictated the Mahabharata and the elephant-headed god Ganesha wrote it down.
In this story Ganesha agrees on condition that Vyasa never pauses, and Vyasa counters that Ganesha must understand every verse before writing it, so Vyasa composes difficult verses to gain time.
The Ganesha-as-scribe episode is absent from the Critical Edition; it appears only in some manuscripts of the Adi Parva and was relegated by the editors to the critical apparatus.
Scholars consider the Ganesha episode a later addition; it conflicts with the epic's own presentation of itself as an oral recitation passed from teller to teller.
The Ganesha story is nonetheless widely known in India and appears in most popular retellings, art and television adaptations.

The idea of Vyasa's deliberately difficult verses connects to a statement in the vulgate Adi Parva about 8,800 riddling verses (kuta-shlokas) that only Vyasa, his son Shuka and perhaps Sanjaya understand; in vulgate texts this statement sits beside the Ganesha passage.
Vyasa's Disciples and Parallel Transmiss: Vyasa's disciples in the Mahabharata tradition include Sumantu, Jaimini, Paila, Vaishampayana and his son Shuka.

The epic says Vyasa taught the Mahabharata to these disciples; passages (notably in vulgate texts) add that other reciters told it to gods, ancestors and celestial beings, while Vaishampayana's version is the one told among humans.
The Jaimini Bharata is attributed to Vyasa's disciple Jaimini, but only its Ashvamedha portion (the Jaimini Ashvamedha) survives as a separate later work.
Shuka, Vyasa's son, is famed as a renunciant and is the traditional narrator of the Bhagavata Purana, a separate text.
The Adi Parva notes that some begin the story with Manu, some with Astika and some with Uparichara Vasu, which suggests that several recitation traditions existed.
Other Narrators Within the Epic: Markandeya, an ancient long-lived sage, narrates many stories to the exiled Pandavas in the Vana Parva, including Savitri, the Ramopakhyana and the fish who saved Manu.
Brihadashva tells Yudhishthira the story of Nala and Damayanti in the Vana Parva.
Lomasha, a sage who accompanies the Pandavas on their pilgrimage, tells the stories of the holy places they visit, including Rishyashringa.
Narada, the travelling divine sage, visits the Pandavas several times and tells stories such as the account of Sunda and Upasunda to warn them about quarrelling over Draupadi.
Bhishma narrates most of the Shanti and Anushasana Parvas, answering Yudhishthira's questions from his bed of arrows.
Krishna is the speaker of the Bhagavad Gita and the Anugita.
Vidura counsels Dhritarashtra in the Viduraniti, and the sage Sanatsujata teaches him about death and the self.
Three Beginnings and Self-Referential Cl: The Adi Parva itself says the Bharata may begin in three places: with Manu, with Astika, or with Uparichara Vasu.
The Adi Parva distinguishes a 24,000-verse Bharata without the subsidiary tales from the larger work with them.

The vulgate Adi Parva mentions 8,800 riddling verses (kuta-shlokas) whose meaning is hard to grasp; some modern writers have taken this number as the size of an original 'Jaya' poem, but that reading is speculative and not supported by the text.
Epic size statements (Adi Parva; the 8,800 figure from the vulgate): riddling verses 8,800 | Bharata core 24,000 verses | full work about 100,000 verses.
The epic describes the merit gained by hearing it recited, a common feature of texts intended for public recitation.
At the end of the Svargarohana Parva the narration returns to Janamejaya's sacrifice and to Ugrashravas and the sages, closing the frames.

Lunar Dynasty Ancestry: From Soma to Kur: The Kurus belong to the lunar dynasty (Chandravamsha), which traces descent from Soma, the Moon.

Lunar dynasty outline: Soma (Moon) → Budha (with Ila) → Pururavas (with the apsara Urvashi) → Ayu → Nahusha → Yayati → Puru → ... → Dushyanta → Bharata → ... → Hastin → ... → Kuru → ... → Pratipa → Shantanu.
Yayati had five sons: Yadu and Turvasu by Devayani, and Druhyu, Anu and Puru by Sharmishtha.
Puru, Yayati's youngest son, took on his father's old age and was rewarded with the kingdom; his line, the Pauravas, leads to the Kurus.
Yadu, Yayati's eldest son, founded the Yadava line into which Krishna and Kunti were born, so the Kurus and Yadavas share descent from Yayati.
Bharata, son of King Dushyanta and Shakuntala, gives his name to the Bharata lineage; the epic's title means 'the great (tale of the) Bharatas'.
Hastin, a later descendant, is traditionally said to have founded Hastinapura, which takes his name.
The Adi Parva gives two genealogies of the Puru-Kuru line (one in verse, one in prose) that do not fully agree, so the names between Bharata and Shantanu vary.
Kuru, Pratipa and the Kings Before Shant: Kuru, son of King Samvarana and Tapati (a daughter of the Sun), is the ancestor from whom the Kuru dynasty takes its name.
Kuru is said to have tilled and sanctified the field that became Kurukshetra, 'the field of Kuru'.
King Pratipa, a later Kuru, had three sons: Devapi, Bahlika and Shantanu.
Devapi, Pratipa's eldest son, was set aside from the throne because of a skin disease and became an ascetic.
Bahlika, Pratipa's second son, went to live with his mother's kin; his son Somadatta and grandson Bhurishravas later fight for the Kauravas.
Shantanu, Pratipa's youngest son, inherited the throne of Hastinapura.
Bahlika survives into the Kurukshetra war as the eldest warrior on the field and is killed by Bhima.
In the Adi Parva, Shantanu is the rebirth of King Mahabhisha, who was cursed by Brahma to be born as a mortal for gazing at the river goddess Ganga in heaven.
Shantanu, Ganga and the Eight Vasus: King Shantanu met the goddess Ganga in human form beside the river and asked her to marry him.
Ganga agreed to marry Shantanu on condition that he never question or oppose anything she did; if he did, she would leave.
Ganga drowned each of their first seven sons in the river at birth, and Shantanu kept silent to honour the promise.
When Ganga was about to drown the eighth son, Shantanu protested; Ganga then revealed that the sons were the eight Vasus under a curse, and she departed with the child.
Ganga's sons: born 8 | returned to heaven by drowning 7 | survived 1 (Devavrata, later Bhishma).
Years later, Ganga returned the grown son, Devavrata, to Shantanu as a prince trained in scripture and arms.
Shantanu made Devavrata heir apparent (yuvaraja) before meeting Satyavati.
The Vasus are a group of eight gods; in the Mahabharata they are listed as Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Ahah, Anila, Anala, Pratyusha and Prabhasa.
The Vasus stole the wish-granting cow Nandini from the sage Vasishtha, prompted by the wife of one of the Vasus who wanted the cow.
Vasishtha cursed all eight Vasus to be born as mortals.
Vasishtha softened the curse: seven Vasus would be freed at birth, but the Vasu who actually seized the cow would live a long life on earth, have no offspring and be renowned for virtue.
The Vasus asked Ganga to be their mortal mother and to free them by drowning them at birth, which explains her actions as Shantanu's wife.
The Vasu who took Nandini is named Dyaus (Dyu) in the epic's story of the theft (some retellings instead name Prabhasa); he was born as Devavrata (Bhishma).
Devavrata Becomes Bhishma — the Vow: According to the Adi Parva, Devavrata, son of Shantanu and Ganga, learned the Vedas from the sage Vasishtha, mastered the political sciences associated with Brihaspati and Shukra (Ushanas), and learned arms from Parashurama (Rama Jamadagnya).
Shantanu fell in love with Satyavati, but her father, the fisher chief, demanded that Satyavati's son inherit the throne.
Devavrata renounced his own claim to the throne so that Satyavati's sons could rule.
When the fisher chief objected that Devavrata's future sons might still claim the throne, Devavrata vowed lifelong celibacy (brahmacharya).
Because of this terrible vow, the gods and sages called him Bhishma, 'the one of the terrible (vow)'.
Shantanu granted Bhishma the boon of dying only when he himself chose (iccha-mrityu, death at will).
Bhishma's two vows: renounce the throne | never marry or father children.
Bhishma serves as protector and regent of the Kuru throne through several generations and commands the Kaurava army for the first ten days of the war.
Bhishma is also called Gangeya (son of Ganga), Shantanava (son of Shantanu) and Pitamaha (grandfather), the last as an honorific from the Pandavas and Kauravas.
Satyavati and Her Sons: Satyavati was raised by the chief of the fishermen; the Adi Parva says she was actually born from the seed of King Uparichara Vasu and a fish who was the cursed apsara Adrika.
Satyavati was first called Matsyagandha ('fish-scented'); the sage Parashara gave her a fragrance that earned her the name Yojanagandha ('fragrant for a yojana').
Before her marriage, Satyavati bore the sage Parashara a son, Krishna Dvaipayana (Vyasa), on an island in the Yamuna; her virginity was restored by Parashara's boon.
Satyavati married King Shantanu after Bhishma's vow; they had two sons, Chitrangada and Vichitravirya.
Satyavati's sons: Vyasa (by Parashara, before marriage) | Chitrangada (by Shantanu) | Vichitravirya (by Shantanu).
After Shantanu's death, Chitrangada became king but was killed by a gandharva of the same name, Chitrangada, in battle.
Vichitravirya then became king while still young, with Bhishma as regent.
Vichitravirya died young of consumption (a wasting disease) without children, leaving the Kuru line without an heir.
After the line's crisis, Satyavati first asked Bhishma to father heirs or take the throne; he refused because of his vow, and she then summoned her elder son Vyasa.
After Pandu's death, on Vyasa's advice, Satyavati withdrew to the forest with her daughters-in-law Ambika and Ambalika, where the three queens died, according to the Adi Parva.
The Princesses of Kashi: Amba, Ambika, A: Bhishma carried off the three daughters of the king of Kashi, Amba, Ambika and Ambalika, from their svayamvara (bride-choice ceremony) to marry Vichitravirya, defeating the assembled kings.
Amba, the eldest princess, told Bhishma she had already chosen King Shalva; Bhishma released her, but Shalva rejected her because she had been carried off.
Amba held Bhishma responsible for her ruin; when Bhishma refused to marry her because of his vow, she sought revenge.
The Udyoga Parva says Bhishma's teacher Parashurama fought Bhishma on Amba's behalf in a duel that lasted 23 days and ended without victory.
Amba performed austerities, received a boon from Shiva that she would cause Bhishma's death in another life, and entered a fire.
Amba was reborn as Shikhandini, daughter of King Drupada of Panchala, who later became the male warrior Shikhandi; Arjuna fights from behind Shikhandi when Bhishma falls.
Ambika and Ambalika married Vichitravirya, who died childless.
Kashi princesses: Amba (refused marriage, reborn as Shikhandi) | Ambika (mother of Dhritarashtra) | Ambalika (mother of Pandu).
Niyoga by Vyasa: Dhritarashtra, Pandu an: To continue the Kuru line after Vichitravirya's death, Satyavati asked her son Vyasa to father children with the widowed queens through niyoga.
Ambika closed her eyes in fear of Vyasa's ascetic appearance, so her son Dhritarashtra was born blind.
Ambalika turned pale at the sight of Vyasa, so her son Pandu ('the pale one') was born pale.
When Satyavati asked for another son, Ambika sent a maidservant in her place; the maid received Vyasa calmly and bore Vidura, wise and healthy.
Vidura is said to be an incarnation of the god Dharma (Yama), born as the son of a servant because of a curse by the sage Mandavya.
Sons of Vyasa by niyoga: Dhritarashtra (Ambika, born blind) | Pandu (Ambalika, born pale) | Vidura (a maidservant, wise).
Legally the three sons counted as heirs of Vichitravirya; biologically they were sons of Vyasa, so Vyasa is the grandfather of both the Pandavas and the Kauravas.
Dhritarashtra was the eldest son but was passed over for kingship because of his blindness; Pandu was crowned king of Hastinapura.
Vidura was ineligible for the throne because of his mother's servant status and served as minister and adviser, known for his wisdom and his loyalty to dharma.
Pandu conquered many neighbouring kingdoms and enlarged the Kuru realm before retiring to the forest.
Dhritarashtra married Gandhari, princess of Gandhara; Pandu married Kunti at her svayamvara and Madri of Madra, for whom Bhishma paid a bride-price to her brother Shalya.
After Pandu retired to the forest, Dhritarashtra governed in Hastinapura and later held the throne as king.
Vidura repeatedly warns Dhritarashtra against Duryodhana's schemes, most famously the dice game, and secretly helps the Pandavas escape the lac house at Varanavata.
Pandu's Curse, Kunti, Madri and the Divi: While hunting, Pandu shot the sage Kindama and his wife while they were mating in the form of deer.
The dying sage Kindama cursed Pandu to die if he ever approached his wife in love.
Pandu renounced the kingship and went to live as an ascetic with Kunti and Madri on the Shatashringa mountain in the Himalaya.
Kunti revealed that the sage Durvasa had given her a mantra to summon any god and bear his child.
At Pandu's request, Kunti summoned Dharma and bore Yudhishthira, summoned Vayu (the wind) and bore Bhima, and summoned Indra and bore Arjuna.
Kunti shared the mantra with Madri, who summoned the twin Ashvins and bore the twins Nakula and Sahadeva.
Divine fathers of the Pandavas: Yudhishthira — Dharma | Bhima — Vayu | Arjuna — Indra | Nakula — Ashvins | Sahadeva — Ashvins.
Pandu later died when he embraced Madri, fulfilling Kindama's curse; Madri joined him on the funeral pyre, and Kunti returned with the five boys to Hastinapura.
Sons by mother: Kunti 3 Pandavas (plus Karna before marriage) | Madri 2 Pandavas (twins).

Kunti, also called Pritha, was the daughter of the Yadava chief Shura and sister of Vasudeva (Krishna's father); she was given in adoption to her father's cousin King Kuntibhoja, from whom she took her name.
Madri was a princess of Madra and sister of King Shalya, who later fights for the Kauravas as Karna's charioteer.
Yudhishthira was the eldest of the Pandavas and was born before Duryodhana, which became central to the succession dispute.
The Adi Parva says Bhima and Duryodhana were born on the same day.
Krishna is the Pandavas' maternal cousin, since his father Vasudeva is Kunti's brother.
Gandhari and the Hundred Kauravas: Gandhari, daughter of King Subala of Gandhara and sister of Shakuni, married the blind Dhritarashtra and bound her own eyes with a cloth for life to share his condition.
In the Critical Edition, Vyasa granted Gandhari a boon of a hundred sons; some versions and retellings attribute the boon to Shiva.
Gandhari's pregnancy lasted two years; hearing that Kunti had already borne a son, she struck her womb and delivered a hard mass of flesh.
Vyasa divided the mass into 101 parts, placed them in pots of clarified butter, and from them were born 100 sons and one daughter.
Duryodhana, the eldest Kaurava, was born first; his birth was accompanied by ill omens, and Vidura and others advised Dhritarashtra to abandon him, which Dhritarashtra refused to do.
Dushala, the only daughter of Dhritarashtra and Gandhari, married Jayadratha, king of Sindhu.
Yuyutsu was born to Dhritarashtra by a vaishya maidservant who attended him during Gandhari's long pregnancy; he joined the Pandava side just before the war and survived it.

Prominent Kauravas include Duryodhana (also called Suyodhana in some passages), Duhshasana (the second son), Vikarna (who protested Draupadi's treatment) and Chitrasena; the Adi Parva lists all hundred names, with variations between manuscripts.
Dhritarashtra's offspring: sons by Gandhari 100 | daughter by Gandhari 1 | son by a maid 1 | total 102.
Of Dhritarashtra's sons, only Yuyutsu survives the Kurukshetra war; all hundred sons of Gandhari are killed.
Karna's Birth and Adoption: Before her marriage, Kunti tested Durvasa's mantra by summoning the sun god Surya, who gave her a son despite her fear.
Karna was born with natural armour (kavacha) and earrings (kundala), according to the epic; later versions elaborate these details differently.
Afraid of scandal, Kunti placed the infant in a basket and set him adrift on a river; the Vana Parva traces the basket's journey from the Ashva river to the Charmanvati, the Yamuna and the Ganga.
The charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Radha found the baby near Champa in the land of Anga and raised him as their own; he was called Vasushena and Radheya ('son of Radha').
Karna, as the son of Kunti born before her marriage, was by birth the eldest of Kunti's sons and so the elder brother of the Pandavas.

Karna's true parentage was known before the war to Kunti, Surya and Krishna, and also to Bhishma, who tells Karna so from his bed of arrows; the Pandavas learn it only when Kunti publicly reveals it after Karna's death, in the Stri Parva.
Karna became Duryodhana's close friend after Duryodhana made him king of Anga at the princes' tournament.
Kunti's sons: Karna (Surya, before marriage) | Yudhishthira (Dharma) | Bhima (Vayu) | Arjuna (Indra) — 4 in all.
The Succession Dispute: The rival claims to Hastinapura arise from a double ambiguity: Dhritarashtra was the elder son but blind, while Pandu was the younger son but was crowned king.
The Pandava claim: Pandu was the crowned king, and Yudhishthira, his eldest son, was also the eldest of all the princes of his generation, born before Duryodhana.
The Kaurava claim: Dhritarashtra was the elder brother and the ruling king, so Duryodhana as his eldest son should inherit.

Yudhishthira was named crown prince (yuvaraja) in Hastinapura, which intensified Duryodhana's jealousy; Duryodhana had already tried to poison and drown Bhima in their youth, and the lac-house plot followed.

After the Pandavas' marriage to Draupadi revealed that they were alive, Dhritarashtra, to ease the conflict, gave them half the kingdom, the forested region of Khandavaprastha, where they built Indraprastha.

Had Karna's birth been known, he would have been the eldest claimant of the Pandava line; Krishna offers him this position before the war, and Karna refuses out of loyalty to Duryodhana and his adoptive parents.

Bhishma's renunciation of the throne is often seen as a root of the dispute, since it handed the succession to Satyavati's line, which then had to be continued through niyoga; this is an interpretive reading rather than a claim the epic makes in these words.
Next Generations: To Parikshit and Janam: Draupadi bore one son to each Pandava, known as the Upapandavas: Prativindhya (by Yudhishthira), Sutasoma (by Bhima), Shrutakarman (by Arjuna), Shatanika (by Nakula) and Shrutasena (by Sahadeva); name spellings vary between manuscripts.
All five sons of Draupadi were killed by Ashvatthama in the night attack described in the Sauptika Parva.
Bhima's son by the rakshasi Hidimbi was Ghatotkacha, who is killed by Karna during the night battle of the 14th day.
Arjuna's sons were Shrutakarman (by Draupadi), Iravan (by the naga princess Ulupi), Babhruvahana (by Chitrangada of Manipura) and Abhimanyu (by Subhadra, Krishna's sister).

The Adi Parva also lists sons by other wives: Yaudheya (Yudhishthira by Devika), Sarvaga (Bhima by Balandhara of Kashi), Niramitra (Nakula by Karenumati of Chedi) and Suhotra (Sahadeva by Vijaya of Madra).
Abhimanyu married Uttara, daughter of King Virata; he was killed on the 13th day of the war, and their son Parikshit was born after his death.
Parikshit was stillborn after Ashvatthama aimed a divine weapon at the wombs of the Pandava women; Krishna revived him, and he became the sole heir of the Kuru line.
Before the Pandavas' final journey, Yudhishthira crowned Parikshit king at Hastinapura, with Yuyutsu and Kripa to guide him, and installed Krishna's great-grandson Vajra at Indraprastha.
Parikshit's son Janamejaya is the king who hears the Mahabharata recited by Vaishampayana at his snake sacrifice.
Generation Count and Family Numbers: Generations from Shantanu to Janamejaya: Shantanu 1 | Bhishma, Chitrangada, Vichitravirya 2 | Dhritarashtra, Pandu, Vidura 3 | Pandavas, Kauravas, Karna 4 | Abhimanyu, Upapandavas, Ghatotkacha 5 | Parikshit 6 | Janamejaya 7.

Generation detail: Gen 1 Shantanu with Ganga and Satyavati | Gen 2 Bhishma (son of Ganga), Chitrangada and Vichitravirya (sons of Satyavati), plus Vyasa (Satyavati's son by Parashara) | Gen 3 Dhritarashtra, Pandu, Vidura (fathered by Vyasa) | Gen 4 the five Pandavas, the hundred Kauravas, Dushala, Yuyutsu, Karna | Gen 5 Abhimanyu, the five Upapandavas, Ghatotkacha, Iravan, Babhruvahana | Gen 6 Parikshit | Gen 7 Janamejaya.

Bhishma's life touches five generations: he is son of Shantanu (generation 1), regent for his half-brothers, guardian of his nephews Dhritarashtra, Pandu and Vidura, guardian and elder of his grand-nephews the Pandavas and Kauravas (whose formal weapons teachers were Kripa and Drona), and an opponent in battle of his great-grand-nephew Abhimanyu.
Children: Dhritarashtra 100 sons + 1 daughter (+ Yuyutsu by a maid) | Pandu 5 sons (via divine fathers).
Wives: Shantanu 2 (Ganga, Satyavati) | Vichitravirya 2 (Ambika, Ambalika) | Pandu 2 (Kunti, Madri) | Dhritarashtra 1 chief queen (Gandhari) plus a vaishya maid who bore Yuyutsu.
Sons of Vyasa by niyoga: 3 (Dhritarashtra, Pandu, Vidura).
Sons of Draupadi: 5 (one by each Pandava).
Kuru heirs surviving the war: Parikshit (born after the war, revived by Krishna) | Yuyutsu (Dhritarashtra's son by a maid) | the five Pandavas.
Janamejaya is Arjuna's great-grandson: Arjuna → Abhimanyu → Parikshit → Janamejaya.
Marriage Alliances Linking Dynasties: The Kuru line is linked to the Yadavas through Kunti (Krishna's aunt) and through Arjuna's marriage to Subhadra (Krishna's sister).
The Kurus are linked to Gandhara through Gandhari, which brings her brother Shakuni to Hastinapura.

The Kurus are linked to Madra through Madri, whose brother Shalya is maternal uncle of Nakula and Sahadeva (and an uncle-figure to all five Pandavas) but fights for Duryodhana after being tricked into accepting his hospitality.
The Pandavas are linked to Panchala through Draupadi, daughter of King Drupada, which makes Drupada and his son Dhrishtadyumna key Pandava allies.
The Pandavas are linked to Matsya through Abhimanyu's marriage to Uttara, daughter of King Virata.
The Kauravas are linked to Sindhu through Dushala's marriage to Jayadratha.

Yudhishthira — eldest Pandava, son of Dh: Yudhishthira is the eldest of the five Pandavas, born to Kunti through the god Dharma (Yama-Dharma), invoked with the mantra Kunti received from the sage Durvasa; Pandu was his legal father.
Yudhishthira's epithets include Dharmaraja (king of righteousness), Ajatashatru (one whose enemy is not born) and Dharmaputra; he is the embodiment of truthfulness and restraint in the epic.

Yudhishthira was trained by Drona, and the Adi Parva singles him out as the best of the pupils at fighting from a chariot; in the war he is most remembered for the spear (shakti) with which he killed Shalya, and his conch is Anantavijaya.

Yudhishthira was crowned king of Indraprastha and performed the Rajasuya sacrifice, at which his brothers conquered the four directions: Bhima the east, Arjuna the north, Nakula the west and Sahadeva the south.

Yudhishthira lost his wealth, kingdom, brothers, himself and finally Draupadi to Shakuni in the first dice game at Hastinapura; after Dhritarashtra restored everything, a second game (the anudyuta) staked exile, and its loss led to twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth year incognito.

In the Yaksha episode (Vana Parva) Yudhishthira answered the riddles of a yaksha who was Dharma in disguise; offered one brother's life, he chose Nakula so that a son of Madri would also survive, and all four brothers were restored.
During the year in Virata, Yudhishthira lived disguised as Kanka, a brahmin courtier and dice companion of King Virata.

On day 15 of the war Yudhishthira told Drona 'Ashvatthama is dead' about an elephant of that name, muttering that it was an elephant; the Drona Parva says his chariot, which had always moved a little above the ground, then touched the earth.
On day 18 of the war Yudhishthira killed King Shalya of Madra, the last Kaurava supreme commander, with a spear.
After the war Yudhishthira grieved deeply, learned that Karna was his elder brother, and (Shanti Parva) cursed womankind never to be able to keep a secret because Kunti had hidden Karna's birth.
Yudhishthira was crowned at Hastinapura, received Bhishma's long teachings on kingship and dharma (Shanti and Anushasana Parvas) and performed the Ashvamedha horse sacrifice.

Yudhishthira ruled for about thirty-six years after the war (the Mausala Parva places the Yadava destruction in the thirty-sixth year), then crowned Parikshit and set out on the final journey to the Himalaya.
Yudhishthira's wives were Draupadi (son Prativindhya) and Devika, daughter of Govasana of the Shaibyas (son Yaudheya), per the Adi Parva genealogy.

At the end of the Mahaprasthanika Parva Yudhishthira refused to enter Indra's chariot to heaven without the dog that had followed him (Dharma in disguise), and alone of the group he reached heaven in his own body; in the Svargarohana Parva he faced a further test, an illusory vision of his brothers and Draupadi in hell.

Contested point: readers have long debated whether Yudhishthira's gambling, his staking of Draupadi and his half-truth to Drona compromise his reputation for dharma; the epic makes him pay for the half-truth with that brief sight of hell, while its judgement of the gambling is left more open and is argued over by characters within the story.
Bhima — second Pandava, son of Vayu: Bhima (Bhimasena) is the second Pandava, born to Kunti through the wind god Vayu; his epithet Vrikodara means 'wolf-bellied' for his huge appetite.
Bhima is the strongest of the brothers; his weapon is the mace (gada), the Sabha Parva says Maya brought him a great mace from Lake Bindu, and his conch is Paundra.

As a boy Bhima was poisoned and thrown into the Ganga by Duryodhana; in the widely known (vulgate) version he sank to the realm of the Nagas, who gave him a drink that made him immensely strong, but the episode's details vary between recensions.
Bhima carried his mother and brothers out of the burning lac house at Varanavata and then killed the rakshasa Hidimba, whose sister Hidimbi became Bhima's wife.

Bhima killed the rakshasa Baka (Bakasura) at Ekachakra, the rakshasas Kirmira and Jatasura during the exile, and King Jarasandha of Magadha in a wrestling bout that the Sabha Parva says lasted about two weeks, ending when Bhima whirled him and broke his back; popular and Puranic retellings stress Bhima tearing his body into two halves, undoing the joining by the rakshasi Jara at his birth.
In the Vana Parva Bhima met Hanuman, also a son of Vayu and so his elder brother, while seeking Saugandhika flowers for Draupadi.
During the year in Virata, Bhima served as Ballava the cook and wrestler, and secretly killed Kichaka, who had harassed Draupadi, followed by Kichaka's 105 kinsmen (the Upakichakas).
In the dice hall Bhima vowed to break Duryodhana's thigh (Duryodhana had bared it to Draupadi) and to drink Dushasana's blood; he fulfilled both vows in the war.
On day 17 Bhima killed Dushasana and tasted his blood; in the Stri Parva Bhima tells Gandhari that the blood did not pass beyond his lips and teeth.

On day 18 Bhima struck Duryodhana's thighs with his mace in their duel, a blow below the navel that broke the rules of mace combat and enraged Balarama; on Krishna's hint, Arjuna had reminded Bhima of his vow by slapping his own thigh.
The epic credits Bhima with killing the great majority of Dhritarashtra's hundred sons, traditionally all of them, including Vikarna on day 14.
Bhima's wives were Draupadi (son Sutasoma), Hidimbi (son Ghatotkacha) and Valandhara, a princess of Kashi (son Sarvaga), per the Adi Parva genealogy.
Bhima was the last to fall on the final journey; Yudhishthira said he fell for gluttony and boasting of his strength.
Contested point: Bhima's violence (the blood-drinking, the foul blow) is judged differently by commentators, some seeing righteous vengeance for Draupadi, others excess.
Arjuna — third Pandava, son of Indra: Arjuna is the third Pandava, born to Kunti through Indra, king of the gods; he is the epic's greatest archer and Drona's favourite pupil.

In the Virata Parva Arjuna explains his ten names to Prince Uttara: Arjuna, Phalguna, Jishnu, Kiritin, Shvetavahana (of the white horses), Bibhatsu, Vijaya, Krishna, Savyasachin (able to shoot with either hand) and Dhananjaya; elsewhere he is also called Partha and Gudakesha.

Arjuna's bow is Gandiva, which Agni (obtaining it from Varuna) gave him at the burning of the Khandava forest along with two inexhaustible quivers and a chariot bearing the monkey (Hanuman) banner, the Kapidhvaja.
Arjuna's conch is Devadatta, which the Sabha Parva says Maya brought from Lake Bindu; his charioteer in the war is Krishna.
At Drona's school Arjuna passed the famous test of seeing only the bird's eye; he captured King Drupada as Drona's teacher's fee.

Arjuna won Draupadi at her svayamvara in Panchala by stringing a huge bow and hitting a target through the opening of a mechanical device; the popular image of a revolving fish aimed at by its reflection in water comes from later and regional retellings, not the Critical Edition's description.
For breaking the brothers' rule about intruding on Draupadi with another brother, Arjuna went on a twelve-year pilgrimage, during which he married Ulupi, Chitrangada and Subhadra.
With Krishna, Arjuna burned the Khandava forest for Agni and spared the asura architect Maya, who then built the Pandavas' hall at Indraprastha.

During the exile Arjuna fought Shiva disguised as a Kirata (hunter) and received the Pashupata weapon; he then spent five years in Indra's heaven, gaining divine weapons and destroying the Nivatakavachas and Kalakeyas.

In heaven the apsara Urvashi cursed Arjuna to live as a eunuch after he refused her; the curse was limited to one year and served as his disguise as Brihannala, dance teacher to Princess Uttaraa in Virata.
At the end of the year in Virata, Arjuna single-handedly repelled the Kaurava cattle raid with Prince Uttara as his charioteer, using a stupefying weapon on the Kuru warriors.
Before the first day of battle Arjuna's refusal to fight his kin prompted Krishna's teaching, the Bhagavad Gita (Bhishma Parva).

In the war Arjuna brought down Bhishma on day 10 shooting from behind Shikhandi, killed Bhagadatta, killed Jayadratha on day 14 to avenge Abhimanyu, and killed Karna on day 17 while Karna's chariot wheel was stuck.
Arjuna's sons were Shrutakarma (with Draupadi), Iravan (with Ulupi), Babhruvahana (with Chitrangada) and Abhimanyu (with Subhadra).

During the Ashvamedha, Arjuna was killed in battle by his son Babhruvahana and revived by Ulupi with a Naga gem; after Krishna's death he could not protect the Yadava women from robbers and found his strength gone.
Arjuna fell fourth on the final journey; Yudhishthira said it was for pride in his prowess and contempt for other archers.
Nakula — fourth Pandava, son of the Ashv: Nakula is the elder of Madri's twin sons, born through the twin Ashvin gods (the Ashvins, divine physicians); Pandu was his legal father.
Nakula is described as the most handsome man of his age, a master swordsman and an expert in horses; his conch is Sughosha.
After Madri's death Nakula and his twin Sahadeva were raised by Kunti alongside her own three sons.
In the Rajasuya conquests Nakula subdued the western regions.
In the Yaksha episode, offered the life of one brother, Yudhishthira chose Nakula so that a son of Madri as well as of Kunti would survive; pleased, the yaksha (Dharma) restored all four.
During the year in Virata, Nakula served as Granthika (also called Damagranthi in some versions), keeper of King Virata's horses.
Nakula's sons were Shatanika (with Draupadi) and Niramitra (with Karenumati, a princess of Chedi), per the Adi Parva genealogy.
Nakula fought on the Pandava side through all eighteen days and survived the war.
Nakula fell third on the final journey; Yudhishthira said it was for pride in his beauty.
Nakula and Sahadeva were nephews of King Shalya of Madra, Madri's brother, who nonetheless fought for the Kauravas.
Sahadeva — fifth Pandava, son of the Ash: Sahadeva is the younger of Madri's twin sons, born through the Ashvins; he is the youngest Pandava.
Sahadeva is noted for wisdom and learning (including astronomy/astrology in many traditions), skill with the sword and knowledge of cattle; his conch is Manipushpaka.
In the Rajasuya conquests Sahadeva subdued the south; at the sacrifice he offered the first honour (agrapuja) to Krishna on Bhishma's advice, which provoked Shishupala.
In the dice hall Sahadeva vowed to kill Shakuni.
During the year in Virata, Sahadeva served as Tantipala (also named Arishtanemi), keeper of King Virata's cattle.
On day 18 of the war Sahadeva killed Shakuni and Shakuni's son Uluka, fulfilling his vow.
Sahadeva's sons were Shrutasena (with Draupadi) and Suhotra (with Vijaya, a Madra princess), per the Adi Parva genealogy.
Sahadeva fell second on the final journey, after Draupadi; Yudhishthira said it was for pride in his wisdom.
Later folklore (especially in South India) makes Sahadeva a seer who knew the future of the war but was bound not to reveal it; this is not in the Sanskrit epic's main text.
Draupadi — Panchali, wife of the five Pa: Draupadi, daughter of King Drupada of Panchala, emerged as a grown woman from Drupada's sacrificial fire, together with her brother Dhrishtadyumna; a heavenly voice foretold she would bring about the destruction of the Kshatriyas.

Draupadi's names include Krishnaa (the dark one), Panchali (of Panchala), Yajnaseni (born of the sacrifice) and Sairandhri (her disguise in Virata); the Adi Parva makes her a partial incarnation of the goddess Shri.
Arjuna won Draupadi at her svayamvara; after Kunti unknowingly told her sons to share what they had brought, she became the wife of all five brothers.

Vyasa justified the polyandrous marriage to Drupada by a previous-birth story in which she asked Shiva five times for a husband; the epic presents the marriage as exceptional and debated even by Drupada.

Draupadi's five sons, the Upapandavas, were Prativindhya (by Yudhishthira), Sutasoma (by Bhima), Shrutakarma (by Arjuna), Shatanika (by Nakula) and Shrutasena (by Sahadeva); all five were killed by Ashwatthama in the night massacre.

In the dice hall Draupadi was dragged in by Dushasana and asked whether Yudhishthira, having already lost himself, had the right to stake her; the elders gave no clear answer, Vikarna alone among the Kauravas spoke for her, and Vidura also protested.

When Dushasana tried to strip Draupadi, her garment was miraculously replaced again and again; the Critical Edition keeps the miracle but places her prayer to Krishna in an appendix, and popular retellings make Krishna the explicit rescuer.
Dhritarashtra, alarmed by omens, granted Draupadi boons; she used them to free Yudhishthira and then the other four brothers, asking nothing for herself beyond that.
During the exile Draupadi was abducted by Jayadratha and rescued by Bhima and Arjuna; she debated dharma and anger with Yudhishthira and counselled Satyabhama on married life (Vana Parva).
In Virata, as the maid Sairandhri of Queen Sudeshna, Draupadi was harassed and kicked by Kichaka; Bhima killed him at her urging.

Draupadi's unbound hair is a recurring sign of her humiliation; the vow to bind it only after washing it in Dushasana's blood is developed chiefly in later drama (e.g. the Venisamhara) and popular retellings.
The story that Draupadi laughed at Duryodhana in the Maya Sabha with a taunt about his blind father is a popular addition; in the Critical Edition it is Bhima and others who laugh.
Draupadi was the first to fall on the final journey; Yudhishthira said it was because she loved Arjuna more than the others.
Draupadi is worshipped as a goddess in the Draupadi Amman cult of Tamil Nadu and neighbouring regions, with its own regional epic traditions.
Kunti — Pritha, mother of the Pandavas a: Kunti was born Pritha, daughter of the Yadava chief Shura and sister of Vasudeva (making her Krishna's paternal aunt); she was adopted by her father's cousin King Kuntibhoja, hence the name Kunti.
Kunti served the irascible sage Durvasa and received a mantra to summon any god and bear his child.

Before marriage Kunti tested the mantra on the sun god Surya and bore Karna, born with armour and earrings; she set the baby afloat in a basket on the river Ashva, and he was found and raised by the charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Radha.
Kunti chose Pandu at her svayamvara; after Pandu was cursed never to approach his wives, she used the mantra to bear Yudhishthira (Dharma), Bhima (Vayu) and Arjuna (Indra), and shared it with Madri.
After Pandu's and Madri's deaths Kunti brought the five boys to Hastinapura and raised Madri's twins as her own.

Kunti's unthinking instruction, before she saw Draupadi, that her sons should all enjoy together what they had brought home is the epic's immediate occasion for Draupadi's marriage to all five brothers.
At Ekachakra Kunti volunteered Bhima to face the rakshasa Baka in place of their brahmin host's family.
Before the war Kunti met Karna, revealed she was his mother and asked him to join the Pandavas; he refused but promised to spare all her sons except Arjuna, so she would still have five.
Through Krishna, Kunti sent the Pandavas the story of Vidula, a mother who roused her defeated son to fight (Udyoga Parva).
After the war Kunti publicly revealed Karna's parentage, and Yudhishthira performed Karna's funeral rites as his brother's.
Kunti chose to retire to the forest with Dhritarashtra and Gandhari despite her sons' pleas; all three died in a forest fire (Ashramavasika Parva).
Madri — second wife of Pandu, mother of: Madri was a princess of Madra and sister of King Shalya; Bhishma obtained her for Pandu by paying a bride-price, which was the Madra custom.
Pandu was cursed by the sage Kindama, whom he shot while the sage and his wife mated in deer form, to die if he ever approached a wife in love.
Using Kunti's mantra, Madri invoked the twin Ashvins and bore the twins Nakula and Sahadeva.
Pandu died when he embraced Madri in the forest, fulfilling Kindama's curse.
Madri chose to join Pandu on his funeral pyre, entrusting her sons to Kunti (Adi Parva).
Through Madri, Nakula and Sahadeva were nephews of Shalya, who was lured to fight for Duryodhana.
Abhimanyu — son of Arjuna and Subhadra: Abhimanyu was the son of Arjuna and Subhadra, Krishna's sister, raised partly in Dwaraka; the Adi Parva makes him an incarnation of Varchas, son of the moon god Soma, who allowed his son on earth for only sixteen years.
Abhimanyu married Uttaraa, daughter of King Virata, after the Pandavas' year incognito; their son Parikshit was born after Abhimanyu's death.

On day 13 of the war, with Arjuna drawn away by the Samshaptakas, Abhimanyu broke into Drona's chakravyuha (circular array); in the Drona Parva he says he knows how to enter it but not how to get out.
The popular story that Abhimanyu learned to enter the chakravyuha while in his mother's womb, hearing Arjuna explain it, is a later and popular addition not found in the Critical Edition.
Jayadratha, using a boon from Shiva, held back the other Pandavas at the breach, leaving Abhimanyu alone inside the formation.
Inside the array Abhimanyu killed many warriors, including Duryodhana's son Lakshmana and King Brihadbala of Kosala.

Abhimanyu was attacked by several great warriors at once, including Drona, Karna, Kripa, Ashwatthama and Kritavarma; Karna cut his bow from behind, and he was finally killed by Dushasana's son with a mace blow.
Abhimanyu's death led Arjuna to vow to kill Jayadratha before sunset the next day or enter fire himself.
Abhimanyu's killing by many warriors together is often cited as the moment the war's rules of fair combat collapsed.
Ghatotkacha — son of Bhima and Hidimbi: Ghatotkacha was the son of Bhima and the rakshasi Hidimbi; he grew to adulthood soon after birth, as rakshasa children do in the epic, and was named for his pot-like hairless head.
Ghatotkacha promised to come whenever the Pandavas called him; he carried them through difficult mountain country during the exile.
Ghatotkacha had powers of flight and illusion (maya) and fought for the Pandavas, growing especially strong at night.
On the night of day 14 Ghatotkacha devastated the Kaurava army, killing rakshasa champions including Alayudha.
Karna, under pressure from Duryodhana, used the Vasavi shakti, Indra's spear usable only once, to kill Ghatotkacha; Karna had been saving it for Arjuna.
Krishna rejoiced at Ghatotkacha's death because Arjuna was now safe from the Vasavi spear, a reaction the epic itself highlights.
Ghatotkacha's son Anjanaparvan is named in the Drona Parva as killed by Ashwatthama.
Barbarika, worshipped as Khatu Shyam in Rajasthan, is presented in later traditions (e.g. the Skanda Purana and folk tales) as Ghatotkacha's son; he does not appear in the Critical Edition.
Uttara (Prince Bhuminjaya) — son of King: Prince Uttara, also called Bhuminjaya, was the son of King Virata of Matsya and Queen Sudeshna.
When the Kauravas raided Virata's northern cattle herds, Uttara boasted that he would defeat them, taking the eunuch dance teacher Brihannala (Arjuna) as his charioteer.
On seeing the Kaurava army, Uttara panicked and fled; Arjuna caught him, revealed the Pandavas' identities and had Uttara drive while Arjuna fought.
Arjuna retrieved the Pandavas' weapons from a shami tree near the cremation ground with Uttara's help.
After the victory Uttara told his father that a godlike youth had won the battle, until the Pandavas revealed themselves.
Uttara fought for the Pandavas and was killed by King Shalya on the first day of the war; his brother Shveta was killed by Bhishma on the same day.
Uttaraa (Princess) — daughter of Virata,: Princess Uttaraa was the daughter of King Virata of Matsya; Arjuna, disguised as Brihannala, was her dance teacher during the year incognito.
Virata offered Uttaraa to Arjuna in marriage; Arjuna declined because he had been her teacher, like a father, and accepted her instead as wife for his son Abhimanyu.
Uttaraa had asked Brihannala to bring back fine cloth from the battle for her dolls, and Arjuna took the garments of the stupefied Kuru warriors.
Uttaraa was widowed while pregnant when Abhimanyu died on day 13.
After the night massacre, Ashwatthama's Brahmashira weapon was directed at Uttaraa's womb; the child was born dead and was revived by Krishna.
Uttaraa's son Parikshit became the sole heir of the Kuru line.
Parikshit — grandson of Arjuna, heir of: Parikshit was the son of Abhimanyu and Uttaraa and the grandson of Arjuna and Subhadra.
Parikshit was stillborn because of Ashwatthama's Brahmashira weapon and was revived by Krishna (Ashvamedhika Parva).

The Ashvamedhika Parva explains his name as given because he was born when the Kuru line had dwindled (parikshina); the Bhagavata Purana explains it as 'one who examines', seeking the figure he saw in the womb.
When the Pandavas set out on their final journey Yudhishthira crowned Parikshit at Hastinapura, with Yuyutsu entrusted to oversee the kingdom and Kripa as his teacher.

In the Adi Parva Parikshit, while hunting, draped a dead snake over the silent sage Shamika; the sage's son Shringin cursed him to die within seven days by the bite of the serpent Takshaka, and the curse was fulfilled.
Parikshit's son Janamejaya held a great snake sacrifice to avenge him, and it was there that Vaishampayana recited the Mahabharata.
The Bhagavata Purana frames its whole narration as told to Parikshit by the sage Shuka during his last seven days; this is a Puranic frame, not part of the Mahabharata.
Hidimbi — rakshasi wife of Bhima: Hidimbi (Hidimba) was a rakshasi, sister of the rakshasa Hidimba, who lived in the forest the Pandavas entered after escaping the lac house.
Sent by her brother to lure the Pandavas, Hidimbi fell in love with Bhima, warned them, and took a beautiful human form.
Bhima killed Hidimba in single combat.
With Kunti's and Yudhishthira's consent Hidimbi married Bhima on the condition that he stay with her by day and return at night, until a son was born.
Hidimbi's son was Ghatotkacha; she left with him once he was born, and he promised to return whenever the Pandavas needed him.
Hidimbi is worshipped as a goddess at the Hidimba Devi temple in Manali, Himachal Pradesh, in local tradition.
Ulupi — Naga princess wife of Arjuna: Ulupi was a Naga princess, daughter of the Naga king Kauravya, who drew Arjuna into her underwater realm while he bathed in the Ganga during his pilgrimage.
Arjuna spent a night with Ulupi; she granted him invincibility in water.
Ulupi's son by Arjuna was Iravan (Iravat); the Bhishma Parva describes Ulupi as a widow whose earlier husband had been killed by Garuda.
Iravan fought for the Pandavas and was killed on day 8 by the rakshasa Alambusha.

In Tamil tradition Iravan becomes Aravan, who offers himself as a sacrifice to Kali before the war and is honoured at the annual Koovagam festival, especially important to Tamil Nadu's transgender (thirunangai) community; this is regional tradition, not the Sanskrit epic.

During the Ashvamedha, Ulupi urged Babhruvahana to fight Arjuna and then revived Arjuna with a Naga jewel after Babhruvahana killed him; the Ashvamedhika Parva says this released Arjuna from the curse of the Vasus for killing Bhishma.
Chitrangada — princess of Manipura, wife: Chitrangada was the daughter of King Chitravahana of Manipura, whom Arjuna met during his pilgrimage.
Chitravahana allowed the marriage on condition that Chitrangada's son would remain in Manipura as his heir (an appointed-daughter arrangement).
Chitrangada's son by Arjuna was Babhruvahana, who became king of Manipura.
During the Ashvamedha Babhruvahana fought and killed Arjuna, who was revived by Ulupi; Chitrangada later came to Hastinapura.
The location of the epic's Manipura is debated: it is popularly identified with Manipur in northeast India, while some scholars place it elsewhere, such as on the eastern coast.
Rabindranath Tagore's verse play Chitrangada (Bengali, 1892; English version Chitra, 1913) reimagines Chitrangada as a warrior princess raised as a man; this is a modern retelling.
Subhadra — Krishna's sister, wife of Arj: Subhadra was the daughter of Vasudeva and the sister of Krishna and Balarama; texts differ on whether her mother was Rohini or Devaki.
Arjuna fell in love with Subhadra at the festival on Mount Raivataka near Dwaraka and, on Krishna's advice, carried her off in his chariot.
Balarama and the Yadavas were furious at the abduction until Krishna persuaded them to accept the marriage; the Yadavas then sent rich wedding gifts.
On arriving at Indraprastha Subhadra dressed as a cowherd woman to win Draupadi's goodwill (Adi Parva).
Subhadra was the mother of Abhimanyu and grandmother of Parikshit.
The idea that Balarama meant Subhadra to marry Duryodhana appears in later texts and retellings, not clearly in the Critical Edition.
Subhadra is worshipped with her brothers Jagannatha (Krishna) and Balabhadra (Balarama) in the temple at Puri, Odisha.
Dhrishtadyumna — Panchala prince, Pandav: Dhrishtadyumna was the son of King Drupada, born fully armed from the sacrificial fire (with Draupadi) to kill Drona; the Adi Parva makes him a portion of Agni.
Although he knew the prophecy, Drona taught Dhrishtadyumna the use of weapons.
Dhrishtadyumna announced the conditions of Draupadi's svayamvara and secretly followed the disguised Pandavas afterward to learn who had won her.
Dhrishtadyumna was supreme commander (senapati) of the Pandava army for all eighteen days and was one of its seven akshauhini commanders.
On day 15 Dhrishtadyumna beheaded Drona after Drona had laid down his weapons and sat in yogic meditation; Arjuna and others condemned the act, and it was bitterly debated in the Pandava camp.
Dhrishtadyumna was killed in his sleep by Ashwatthama in the night massacre, kicked and strangled rather than slain with a weapon, so that he would not reach a warrior's heaven.
Shikhandi — Amba reborn, Drupada's child: Shikhandi was born to King Drupada as a daughter, Shikhandini, after Shiva promised Drupada a child who would be a girl and then a man; the Udyoga Parva identifies Shikhandi as the princess Amba reborn to destroy Bhishma.
Shikhandini was raised as a son and married to a princess of Dasharna; when the bride's father threatened war, a yaksha named Sthunakarna exchanged sexes with Shikhandi.
Kubera cursed Sthunakarna to remain female until Shikhandi's death, so Shikhandi lived thereafter as a man.
Bhishma refused to fight Shikhandi because he regarded him as born female, and he told the Pandavas this on the night of day 9.

On day 10 Arjuna shot Bhishma while Shikhandi was placed in front of him; Bhishma fell onto a bed of arrows. Popular images often put Shikhandi in Arjuna's own chariot, a detail the epic does not make clear.
Shikhandi was one of the seven commanders of the Pandava army.
Shikhandi was killed by Ashwatthama in the night massacre.
Shikhandi is today discussed as a gender-variant or transgender figure; the epic's own framing centres on rebirth, vow and Bhishma's code.
Drupada — King of Panchala: Drupada, son of Prishata, was king of Panchala and a boyhood friend of Drona at the hermitage of Drona's father Bharadvaja.
When Drona, poor, came to claim friendship, Drupada scorned him, saying a king and a poor brahmin could not be friends.
As his teacher's fee Drona had the Kuru princes capture Drupada; Arjuna defeated him, and Drona took northern Panchala (Ahichchhatra), leaving Drupada the south (Kampilya).
Seeking revenge, Drupada held a sacrifice performed by the brahmins Yaja and Upayaja, from which Dhrishtadyumna and Draupadi were born.
Drupada held Draupadi's svayamvara hoping Arjuna would win her, and became the Pandavas' father-in-law and chief ally.
Drupada was one of the seven commanders of the Pandava army.
Drupada was killed by Drona on day 15 of the war, the morning of Drona's own death.
Virata — King of Matsya: Virata was king of the Matsyas; the Pandavas and Draupadi spent their thirteenth year of exile incognito in his court.
Virata's queen Sudeshna was the sister of Kichaka, commander of Virata's army.
During the year in disguise Virata struck Yudhishthira (disguised as Kanka) in the face with dice for praising Brihannala over Uttara; Draupadi caught the blood so it would not fall on the ground.
After Kichaka's death the Trigartas under Susharma and the Kauravas raided Virata's cattle; Virata was captured by Susharma and rescued by Bhima.
Virata offered his daughter Uttaraa to Arjuna; she married Abhimanyu instead.
The Pandavas used Upaplavya in Virata's kingdom as their base before the war; Virata was one of the seven Pandava commanders.
Virata lost his sons Uttara and Shveta on the first day of the war and was killed by Drona on day 15.

Pandava mothers: Yudhishthira Kunti | Bhima Kunti | Arjuna Kunti | Nakula Madri | Sahadeva Madri
Karna, Kunti's first son, was fathered by Surya, making the Pandava-Karna kinship: Karna Surya | Yudhishthira Dharma | Bhima Vayu | Arjuna Indra
Pandava conches (Bhagavad Gita 1.15-16): Yudhishthira Anantavijaya | Bhima Paundra | Arjuna Devadatta | Nakula Sughosha | Sahadeva Manipushpaka | Krishna Panchajanya
Pandava chief weapons: Yudhishthira spear | Bhima mace | Arjuna Gandiva bow | Nakula sword | Sahadeva sword
Rajasuya digvijaya directions: Bhima east | Arjuna north | Nakula west | Sahadeva south
Order of falling on the final journey (Mahaprasthanika Parva): Draupadi 1 | Sahadeva 2 | Nakula 3 | Arjuna 4 | Bhima 5; Yudhishthira alone reached heaven in his body
Reasons Yudhishthira gave for each fall: Draupadi partiality to Arjuna | Sahadeva pride in wisdom | Nakula pride in beauty | Arjuna pride in prowess | Bhima gluttony and boasting
Wives and sons of the Pandavas (chart ta: Sons of Draupadi (Upapandavas): Prativindhya by Yudhishthira | Sutasoma by Bhima | Shrutakarma by Arjuna | Shatanika by Nakula | Shrutasena by Sahadeva; all five were killed by Ashwatthama in the night massacre
Arjuna's wives and sons: Draupadi Shrutakarma | Ulupi Iravan | Chitrangada Babhruvahana | Subhadra Abhimanyu
Bhima's wives and sons: Draupadi Sutasoma | Hidimbi Ghatotkacha | Valandhara Sarvaga
Yudhishthira's wives and sons: Draupadi Prativindhya | Devika Yaudheya
Nakula's wives and sons: Draupadi Shatanika | Karenumati Niramitra
Sahadeva's wives and sons: Draupadi Shrutasena | Vijaya Suhotra
Number of wives per Pandava in the Adi Parva genealogy: Yudhishthira 2 | Bhima 3 | Arjuna 4 | Nakula 2 | Sahadeva 2

Sons of the Pandavas who died in the war: Abhimanyu (day 13) | Iravan (day 8) | Ghatotkacha (night of day 14) | Upapandavas 5 (night massacre); Babhruvahana survived as king of Manipura, and the epic says little about the fates of Yaudheya, Sarvaga, Niramitra and Suhotra
The Pandava line continued only through Parikshit, son of Abhimanyu, whose son Janamejaya heard the Mahabharata recited.
Pandava disguises during the year in Vir: Pandava disguises in Virata: Yudhishthira Kanka the dice-playing brahmin courtier | Bhima Ballava the cook and wrestler | Arjuna Brihannala the eunuch dance teacher | Nakula Granthika the horse-keeper | Sahadeva Tantipala the cowherd | Draupadi Sairandhri the queen's maid
The Pandavas hid their weapons in a shami tree near a cremation ground outside Virata's city before entering in disguise.
The thirteenth year incognito was a condition of the dice game: if discovered, the Pandavas would have to repeat the twelve years of exile.
Duryodhana claimed the Pandavas were discovered before the year ended; Bhishma calculated (allowing for intercalary months) that the full term had been completed.
Arjuna's disguise as a eunuch drew on Urvashi's curse, which Indra had limited to one year.
Pandava side roster, roles and fates: Pandava army size: 7 akshauhinis, against 11 for the Kauravas.
Pandava akshauhini commanders (seven): Drupada | Virata | Dhrishtadyumna | Shikhandi | Satyaki | Chekitana | Bhima; Dhrishtadyumna was supreme commander for all 18 days.
Pandava-side survivors per the Sauptika Parva: the five Pandavas, Krishna and Satyaki, seven in all; Yuyutsu, who changed sides, also survived.

Pandava-side deaths by war day: Uttara 1 | Shveta 1 | Iravan 8 | Abhimanyu 13 | Ghatotkacha 14 (night) | Drupada 15 | Virata 15 | Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandi and the Upapandavas in the night massacre after day 18

Key Pandava-side kills: Bhishma by Arjuna (day 10) | Drona by Dhrishtadyumna (15) | Karna by Arjuna (17) | Dushasana by Bhima (17) | Shalya by Yudhishthira (18) | Shakuni by Sahadeva (18) | Duryodhana by Bhima (18)

Pandava allies by kingdom: Panchala (Drupada) | Matsya (Virata) | Yadava contingent under Satyaki | Chedi (Dhrishtaketu) | Magadha (Jarasandha's son Sahadeva) | Kashi | Kekaya brothers loyal to the Pandavas
Krishna joined the Pandavas as Arjuna's unarmed charioteer and counsellor, while his Narayana troops fought for Duryodhana.

Duryodhana — eldest Kaurava, rival of th: Duryodhana was the eldest of the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra and Gandhari; some regional traditions and modern retellings call him Suyodhana, a name the epic uses only rarely.
At Duryodhana's birth jackals howled and other bad omens appeared, and Vidura and others advised Dhritarashtra to abandon the child; Dhritarashtra refused.
The Adi Parva's list of partial incarnations makes Duryodhana a portion of Kali, the spirit of the dark age.
Duryodhana trained in the mace under Drona and later Balarama, who favoured him; Bhima was his lifelong rival with the same weapon.
As a youth Duryodhana poisoned Bhima and threw him into the Ganga, and later, with Shakuni and Karna, plotted the burning of the lac house at Varanavata through his agent Purochana.
At the tournament Duryodhana made Karna king of Anga so that he could challenge Arjuna, beginning their lifelong friendship.
At the Maya Sabha in Indraprastha Duryodhana mistook a crystal floor for water and fell into a pool he took for floor; the Pandavas' laughter fed his envy and led to the dice game.
Duryodhana had his uncle Shakuni play the dice game in his place and won the Pandavas' kingdom; in the dice hall he bared his thigh to Draupadi, provoking Bhima's vow.

During the exile Duryodhana's cattle-inspection trip (ghosha-yatra) ended with his capture by the gandharva Chitrasena and his humiliating rescue by the Pandavas; he then tried to fast to death until persuaded otherwise.
Duryodhana refused the Pandavas even five villages, declaring he would not give up land as much as the point of a needle could pierce (Udyoga Parva).

When Krishna let Arjuna choose first between Krishna unarmed and Krishna's troops, and Arjuna chose Krishna, Duryodhana gladly took the Narayana army; he also tricked Shalya into his camp and commanded 11 akshauhinis.
On day 18, with his army destroyed, Duryodhana hid in a lake (Dvaipayana) by stilling its waters, then fought Bhima in a mace duel and fell when Bhima struck his thighs against the rules.
Dying, Duryodhana defended his life as a ruler, flowers fell from the sky on him, and he appointed Ashwatthama commander; he died after hearing of the night massacre.
