In the Svargarohana Parva Yudhishthira finds Duryodhana in heaven, earned by dying as a warrior on the field of Kurukshetra.
The popular story that Gandhari's gaze made Duryodhana's body invulnerable except where he covered himself is a later folk addition, not in the Critical Edition.

Duryodhana's wife is unnamed in most of the epic and is commonly called Bhanumati in later retellings; his son Lakshmana was killed by Abhimanyu, and the Bhagavata Purana and related later texts add a daughter Lakshmanaa, whom Krishna's son Samba carried off and married.
Duryodhana is honoured as a deity at a temple at Poruvazhy in Kerala, and some modern retellings present him sympathetically as a loyal friend and capable king.
Dushasana — second Kaurava, Draupadi's t: Dushasana (Duhshasana) was the second son of Dhritarashtra and Gandhari and Duryodhana's closest brother and accomplice.
After the dice game Dushasana dragged Draupadi by her hair from the women's quarters into the assembly hall.
Dushasana tried to strip Draupadi in the assembly, but her garments were miraculously replaced again and again until he gave up exhausted.
Bhima vowed in the dice hall to tear open Dushasana's chest and drink his blood.
On day 17 of the war Bhima killed Dushasana and fulfilled the vow; in the Stri Parva Bhima says the blood did not pass beyond his lips and teeth.
Dushasana's son killed Abhimanyu on day 13 with a mace blow after Abhimanyu had been surrounded and disarmed.
Karna — Radheya, Kunti's first son, king: Karna was born to the unmarried Kunti through the sun god Surya, with natural armour (kavacha) and earrings (kundala); Kunti set him afloat in a basket on the river Ashva.
Karna was found and raised by the charioteer (suta) Adhiratha and his wife Radha, hence the names Radheya and Sutaputra; his birth name was Vasusena.
Karna studied arms under Drona and then under Parashurama, pretending to be a brahmin; when Parashurama discovered he was not, he cursed Karna to forget the Brahmastra at the moment of greatest need.
A brahmin whose cow Karna accidentally killed cursed him that his chariot wheel would sink into the earth in his decisive battle.
At the tournament Karna challenged Arjuna; when his low birth was mocked, Duryodhana crowned him king of Anga, and Karna became Duryodhana's devoted friend.
Popular versions have Draupadi reject Karna at her svayamvara because he was a suta's son; the Critical Edition omits that line.
In the dice hall Karna called Draupadi a woman of many husbands and urged that she be stripped, a deed he is later made to regret in some passages.
Indra, disguised as a brahmin, asked Karna for his armour and earrings; though warned by Surya in a dream, Karna gave them and received in return the Vasavi shakti, a spear that could kill one enemy.
Before the war Krishna and then Kunti told Karna he was Kunti's son; he refused to abandon Duryodhana but promised Kunti to spare every brother except Arjuna.
Karna refused to fight while Bhishma was commander after Bhishma rated him only half a chariot-warrior (ardharatha); he entered the war on day 11.
On the night of day 14 Karna used the Vasavi spear to kill Ghatotkacha, losing the weapon he had saved for Arjuna.
Karna was Kaurava supreme commander on days 16 and 17, with King Shalya as his reluctant and discouraging charioteer.
On day 17 Karna's chariot wheel sank into the earth; while he struggled to free it, Arjuna, urged by Krishna, killed him.
Karna's bow was Vijaya; his son Vrishasena was killed by Arjuna on day 17.
Karna is famed for his generosity (he is called Danavira, the great giver) and his loyalty; modern works such as Dinkar's Rashmirathi and Shivaji Sawant's Mrityunjaya retell the epic from his side.
Details of Karna's armour and earrings, including whether they were grafted to his body and how they were cut away, vary between versions and are elaborated in popular retellings.
Shakuni — prince of Gandhara, master of: Shakuni was a prince of Gandhara, son of King Subala and brother of Gandhari, which made him maternal uncle to the Kauravas.
Shakuni was a master of dice, and the Adi Parva makes him an incarnation of Dvapara, the personified losing throw and the age before the Kali age.
Shakuni joined Duryodhana and Karna in the lac house plot and other schemes against the Pandavas.
Shakuni played on Duryodhana's behalf in the dice game, winning from Yudhishthira his wealth, kingdom, brothers, himself and Draupadi, and then the second game that sent the Pandavas into exile.
Shakuni's son Uluka carried Duryodhana's insulting message to the Pandavas before the war.
Sahadeva killed Uluka and then Shakuni on day 18 of the war, fulfilling his vow from the dice hall.

The story that Shakuni sought revenge on the Kurus for the imprisonment and starvation of his family, and that his dice were made from his father's bones, is a later folk tradition not found in the Sanskrit epic.
Gandhari — queen of Hastinapura, mother: Gandhari was a princess of Gandhara, daughter of King Subala and sister of Shakuni, married to the blind Dhritarashtra.
On learning that her husband was blind, Gandhari blindfolded herself for life.
Gandhari received a boon of a hundred sons (from Vyasa in the epic; some versions say Shiva).

Gandhari's pregnancy lasted two years; hearing that Kunti had already borne a son, she struck her womb and delivered a hard mass of flesh, which Vyasa divided into 101 portions kept in pots of ghee, producing a hundred sons and the daughter Duhshala.
Gandhari repeatedly urged Duryodhana toward peace and, when he asked for her blessing, said 'where there is dharma, there is victory' (yato dharmas tato jayah).
In the Stri Parva Gandhari's glance, through a gap in her blindfold, scorched Yudhishthira's toenails.
Gandhari blamed Krishna for not preventing the war and cursed him that his own clan would destroy itself in thirty-six years, which came true in the Mausala Parva.
Gandhari retired to the forest with Dhritarashtra and Kunti and died with them in a forest fire.
The Adi Parva makes Gandhari a partial incarnation of Mati (understanding).
Dhritarashtra — blind king of the Kurus: Dhritarashtra was born to Ambika, widow of Vichitravirya, through niyoga with Vyasa; he was born blind because Ambika shut her eyes at the sight of the sage.
Dhritarashtra was passed over for the throne in favour of his younger brother Pandu because of his blindness, and became ruler when Pandu retired to the forest.
Dhritarashtra had a hundred sons and one daughter (Duhshala) with Gandhari, and the son Yuyutsu with a vaishya maidservant.
Dhritarashtra repeatedly gave in to Duryodhana despite warnings from Vidura, Bhishma and Gandhari; his divided affection is a central theme of the epic.
After the dice game, frightened by omens, Dhritarashtra granted Draupadi boons that freed the Pandavas, but then allowed the second game that exiled them.
Vyasa offered Dhritarashtra sight to watch the war; he declined and Vyasa gave divine vision to his charioteer Sanjaya, who narrated the battle to him.
After the war Dhritarashtra embraced an iron statue of Bhima, substituted by Krishna, and crushed it in his grief and rage (Stri Parva).
Dhritarashtra lived about fifteen years under Yudhishthira's rule, then retired to the forest with Gandhari, Kunti, Vidura and Sanjaya; he died in a forest fire (Ashramavasika Parva).
Jayadratha — king of Sindhu, husband of: Jayadratha was king of Sindhu (Sindhu-Sauvira), son of Vriddhakshatra, and husband of Duhshala, the only daughter of Dhritarashtra.

During the exile Jayadratha abducted Draupadi from the hermitage in the Kamyaka forest; Bhima and Arjuna caught him, and Bhima shaved his head leaving five tufts, sparing his life for Duhshala's and Gandhari's sake.
Jayadratha then performed austerities to Shiva and won a boon to hold back all the Pandavas except Arjuna for one day.
On day 13 Jayadratha used the boon to block the Pandavas at the breach in the chakravyuha, leaving Abhimanyu alone inside.
Arjuna vowed to kill Jayadratha before sunset on day 14 or enter fire; the Kauravas hid him at the rear of a huge formation.
Popular versions say Krishna created an illusory sunset so that Jayadratha came out of hiding; accounts of exactly how Krishna intervened vary.

Jayadratha's father had pronounced that whoever made his son's head fall to the ground would have his own head shatter; Arjuna shot Jayadratha's head into the lap of the meditating Vriddhakshatra, whose head then burst.
Vikarna — the Kaurava who defended Draup: Vikarna was one of the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra and Gandhari; his place in the birth order differs between lists.
In the dice hall Vikarna alone among the Kauravas argued that Draupadi had not been lawfully won, since Yudhishthira had staked her after losing himself and under the pressure of gambling.
Karna rebuked Vikarna as a child for his protest, and the assembly ignored him.
Despite his protest Vikarna fought loyally for his brother in the war.
Vikarna was killed by Bhima on day 14, and the epic has Bhima lament having to kill him.
Vikarna is often cited as the voice of conscience on the Kaurava side, set against the silence of the elders.
Yuyutsu — Dhritarashtra's son who joined: Yuyutsu was a son of Dhritarashtra by a vaishya maidservant who attended him while Gandhari was pregnant; he was born in the same year as Duryodhana.
Just before the fighting began Yudhishthira invited anyone to change sides, and Yuyutsu crossed over to the Pandava army.
Yuyutsu survived the war, the only one of Dhritarashtra's sons to do so.
After the war Yuyutsu escorted the Kaurava women back to Hastinapura and helped with the rites.
When the Pandavas set out on their final journey Yudhishthira entrusted Yuyutsu with overseeing the kingdom for the young Parikshit.
Later tradition names Yuyutsu's mother Sughada; the epic does not clearly name her.
Ashwatthama — son of Drona, author of th: Ashwatthama was the son of Drona and Kripi (Kripa's sister); he was named for the horse-like cry he gave at birth.
The Adi Parva says Ashwatthama was born from portions of Mahadeva (Shiva), Yama, Kama and Krodha, and he bore a jewel on his forehead.
Ashwatthama fought for the Kauravas; on day 15 the Pandavas killed an elephant named Ashvatthama and told Drona his son was dead, which led to Drona's death.
After his father's death Ashwatthama released the Narayanastra; Krishna saved the Pandava army by telling them to lay down their weapons and get down from their chariots.
The dying Duryodhana made Ashwatthama the last Kaurava commander.
Inspired by seeing an owl kill sleeping crows, Ashwatthama attacked the Pandava camp at night with Kripa and Kritavarma (Sauptika Parva).
In the night massacre Ashwatthama killed Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandi, the five sons of Draupadi and many Panchala and Pandava warriors; the Pandavas, Krishna and Satyaki were away from the camp.

Pursued by the Pandavas, Ashwatthama released the Brahmashira weapon; Arjuna countered it, Vyasa and Narada intervened, Arjuna withdrew his, but Ashwatthama could not and turned his against the wombs of the Pandava women, aimed at Uttaraa's unborn child.

Ashwatthama surrendered his forehead jewel, which Bhima brought to Draupadi; Krishna cursed him to wander the earth for three thousand years, alone and diseased, and revived Uttaraa's child Parikshit.
Later tradition counts Ashwatthama among the seven chiranjivis (long-lived immortals), and folk legends report him still wandering; this goes beyond the epic's 3,000-year curse.
Shalya — king of Madra, uncle of the twi: Shalya was king of Madra and brother of Madri, which made him the maternal uncle of Nakula and Sahadeva.
Shalya set out with a large army to join the Pandavas, but Duryodhana entertained him lavishly on the way; when Shalya offered a boon to his host, Duryodhana asked him to fight for the Kauravas.
Shalya promised Yudhishthira that if he became Karna's charioteer he would undermine Karna's confidence.
Shalya killed Prince Uttara of Virata on day 1 of the war.
As Karna's charioteer on day 17 Shalya taunted and discouraged him, and the two exchanged bitter insults about each other's peoples.
Shalya was Kaurava supreme commander on day 18 and was killed by Yudhishthira with a spear.
Shalya brought one akshauhini to the Kaurava side.
Kichaka — commander of Virata's army: Kichaka was commander of King Virata's army and brother of Queen Sudeshna; the epic calls him a suta (of charioteer lineage).
Kichaka lusted after Sairandhri (the disguised Draupadi), and when she refused him he kicked her in Virata's court.
Draupadi turned to Bhima, who lured Kichaka to the dance hall at night and killed him with his bare hands, crushing his body.
Kichaka's kinsmen, the Upakichakas, numbering 105, tried to burn Draupadi on Kichaka's pyre; Bhima killed them all.
Kichaka's mysterious death made Duryodhana suspect the Pandavas were hiding in Matsya, which prompted the cattle raid on Virata.
Kichaka had earlier defended Matsya against the Trigartas under Susharma, who attacked after his death.
Bhagadatta — king of Pragjyotisha: Bhagadatta was king of Pragjyotisha in the east, son of the demon-king Naraka and an old friend of Pandu; Pragjyotisha is traditionally identified with the region of Assam.
Arjuna fought Bhagadatta during his conquest of the north before the Rajasuya, and Bhagadatta submitted and paid tribute.
Bhagadatta joined Duryodhana with an army that the Udyoga Parva says included Chinas and Kiratas, and fought from his great elephant Supratika.
On day 12 Bhagadatta hurled the Vaishnava weapon at Arjuna; Krishna took it on his own chest, where it turned into a garland, and Arjuna then killed Bhagadatta and his elephant.
Bhagadatta is portrayed as an aged but formidable warrior, one of the greatest elephant-fighters of the war.
Bhurishravas — Kuru kinsman on the Kaura: Bhurishravas was the son of Somadatta and grandson of Bahlika, Shantanu's elder brother, which made him a Kuru kinsman of both sides.
Bhurishravas fought for Duryodhana throughout the war and was a renowned performer of sacrifices.
An old family feud lay behind his duel with Satyaki: Satyaki's grandfather Shini had defeated and humiliated Bhurishravas's father Somadatta while winning Devaki as a bride for Vasudeva.

On day 14 Bhurishravas overpowered the exhausted Satyaki and was about to kill him when Arjuna, at Krishna's urging, cut off his sword arm from a distance; Bhurishravas rebuked Arjuna for striking a man engaged with someone else.
Bhurishravas then sat down to fast to death in yogic meditation, and Satyaki beheaded him, an act condemned by warriors on both sides; the Drona Parva lets Satyaki defend it by citing his own vow.
The hundred Kauravas and Duhshala: The Kauravas, in the narrow sense, are the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra and Gandhari; the name Kaurava also refers to all descendants of Kuru, including the Pandavas.
Dhritarashtra's children: sons by Gandhari 100 | daughter by Gandhari 1 (Duhshala) | son by a vaishya maidservant 1 (Yuyutsu)
Gandhari's hundred sons and daughter came from a single mass of flesh which Vyasa divided into 101 portions in pots of ghee.

Named Kaurava brothers include Duryodhana, Dushasana, Duhsaha, Vikarna, Vivimshati, Chitrasena, Durmukha, Durmarshana, Jalasandha and Sulochana; the Adi Parva gives the full list, which varies in order between manuscripts.
Duhshala, the only daughter, married Jayadratha of Sindhu; after the war, during the Ashvamedha, she brought her grandson to Arjuna to stop fighting with the Sindhus.
The epic credits Bhima with killing all or nearly all of the hundred brothers in the war.
Duryodhana's son Lakshmana was killed by Abhimanyu on day 13.
Kaurava side roster, commanders and fate: Kaurava army size: 11 akshauhinis, against 7 for the Pandavas.
Kaurava supreme commanders by war days: Bhishma 1-10 | Drona 11-15 | Karna 16-17 | Shalya 18 | Ashwatthama night after 18
Days as Kaurava supreme commander: Bhishma 10 | Drona 5 | Karna 2 | Shalya 1
Kaurava commanders and their slayers: Bhishma Arjuna (with Shikhandi) | Drona Dhrishtadyumna | Karna Arjuna | Shalya Yudhishthira | Ashwatthama survived

Kaurava-side deaths by war day: Bhishma falls 10 (dies after the war) | Bhagadatta 12 | Lakshmana son of Duryodhana 13 | Bhurishravas 14 | Jayadratha 14 | Vikarna 14 | Drona 15 | Dushasana 17 | Karna 17 | Shalya 18 | Shakuni 18 | Duryodhana 18 (dies that night)
Kaurava-side survivors per the Sauptika Parva: Ashwatthama, Kripa and Kritavarma, three in all.

Kaurava allies by kingdom: Gandhara (Shakuni) | Madra (Shalya) | Sindhu (Jayadratha) | Anga (Karna) | Pragjyotisha (Bhagadatta) | Kamboja (Sudakshina) | Trigarta (Susharma) | Bhoja-Andhaka Yadavas (Kritavarma) | Avanti (Vinda and Anuvinda)
Elders who fought for the Kauravas out of duty to Hastinapura despite sympathy for the Pandavas: Bhishma, Drona and Kripa.
Karna, Shalya and Kritavarma joined Duryodhana from friendship, obligation and alliance respectively; Yuyutsu, a son of Dhritarashtra, defected to the Pandavas.

Bhishma — Devavrata, grandsire of the Ku: Bhishma, born Devavrata, was the eighth son of King Shantanu and the river goddess Ganga, and the only one she did not drown; he was an incarnation of one of the eight Vasus cursed by the sage Vasishtha, the one the Adi Parva names Dyaus (Dyu), who stole Vasishtha's cow at his wife's urging; some later lists and retellings call this Vasu Prabhasa.
Devavrata was taught by Vasishtha, Brihaspati, Shukra and Parashurama, and was made crown prince of Hastinapura.
To let his father marry Satyavati, Devavrata renounced the throne and vowed lifelong celibacy so no child of his could claim it; the gods named him Bhishma ('the terrible one') for this vow.
Shantanu granted Bhishma the boon of choosing the time of his own death (icchamrityu).
Bhishma abducted the three princesses of Kashi, Amba, Ambika and Ambalika, from their svayamvara as brides for his half-brother Vichitravirya.
When Bhishma refused to marry Amba, his teacher Parashurama fought him on her behalf; the Udyoga Parva says the duel lasted twenty-three days without a victor.
Bhishma served as regent and protector of the Kuru throne for generations, under Chitrangada, Vichitravirya, Pandu, Dhritarashtra and Duryodhana; he saw his vow as binding him to Hastinapura.
Bhishma failed to answer Draupadi's question in the dice hall, saying the course of dharma was subtle, a silence that critics of the epic and its characters still debate.
Bhishma was Kaurava supreme commander for the first ten days of the war, though he declared he would not kill the Pandavas themselves.
On the night of day 9 Bhishma told the Pandavas he would not fight Shikhandi; on day 10 Arjuna, shooting from behind Shikhandi, brought him down onto a bed of arrows.
Lying on the bed of arrows, Bhishma asked for water, and Arjuna shot an arrow into the earth to bring up a spring.
Bhishma waited for the sun's northward course (uttarayana) to die; in the Anushasana Parva he says he has lain fifty-eight nights on the arrows.

From the bed of arrows Bhishma taught Yudhishthira on kingship, conduct in crisis and liberation (Shanti Parva) and on duty and gifts (Anushasana Parva), where the Vishnu Sahasranama, the thousand names of Vishnu, is placed in his mouth.
Bhishma's death and his mother Ganga's lament close the Anushasana Parva.
Drona — Dronacharya, teacher of the Kuru: Drona was the son of the sage Bharadvaja, born, as his name ('vessel') indicates, from his father's seed collected in a pot; the Adi Parva makes him a portion of Brihaspati.
Drona married Kripi, sister of Kripa, and their son was Ashwatthama.
Drona received weapons and the knowledge to use them from Parashurama, who was giving away all his possessions.
Poor and scorned by his boyhood friend King Drupada, Drona came to Hastinapura, where he retrieved the princes' ball from a well with blades of grass and was appointed their teacher by Bhishma.
As teacher's fee Drona demanded that his pupils capture Drupada; Arjuna did so, and Drona kept northern Panchala.
Drona demanded the right thumb of the Nishada archer Ekalavya, who had learned before a clay image of him, to keep his promise that Arjuna would be the greatest archer.
Drona tested his pupils by asking what they saw when aiming at a wooden bird; only Arjuna said he saw only the bird's eye.
Drona fought for the Kauravas and was supreme commander from day 11 to day 15, vowing to capture Yudhishthira alive.
On day 13 Drona's chakravyuha formation trapped Abhimanyu, and on day 15 Drona killed his old rival Drupada and King Virata.
On day 15 Bhima killed an elephant named Ashvatthama; Yudhishthira confirmed to Drona that 'Ashvatthama' was dead, adding indistinctly that it was an elephant, and Drona laid down his arms.
Seated in yogic meditation, Drona was beheaded by Dhrishtadyumna; the Drona Parva says his spirit had already left his body for heaven.

Drona is often criticised, in the epic and in modern readings, for his treatment of Ekalavya and for his partiality to Arjuna and his own son; the popular scene of Drona refusing to teach Karna because of his birth comes from later retellings, since in the epic Karna is listed among Drona's pupils.
Kripa — Kripacharya, first teacher of th: Kripa (Kripacharya) and his twin sister Kripi were born to the sage Sharadvan Gautama when his seed fell on a clump of reeds at the sight of the apsara Janapadi.
King Shantanu found the abandoned twins and raised them out of compassion (kripa), which gave them their names.
Kripa was the first teacher of arms to the Kuru princes before Drona arrived; his sister Kripi married Drona.
Kripa fought for the Kauravas throughout the war and repeatedly counselled Duryodhana to make peace.
Kripa was one of the three Kaurava survivors, with Ashwatthama and Kritavarma, and took part in the night raid by guarding the camp's gates.
After the war Kripa was appointed teacher of Parikshit; later tradition counts him among the seven chiranjivis (long-lived immortals).
Vidura — wise minister, son of Vyasa: Vidura was the son of Vyasa by a maidservant whom Ambika sent in her place for the niyoga; he was the half-brother of Dhritarashtra and Pandu.
Vidura was an incarnation of Dharma (Yama), cursed by the sage Animandavya to be born of a shudra mother for punishing him unjustly.
Because of his birth Vidura could not be king; he served as chief counsellor of Hastinapura and was famed for his wisdom and honesty.
Vidura warned the Pandavas of the lac house in a coded speech and sent a miner to dig their escape tunnel.
Vidura opposed the dice game, was abused by Duryodhana, and briefly left Hastinapura to visit the Pandavas in exile before Dhritarashtra recalled him.
Vidura's night-time counsel to the sleepless Dhritarashtra in the Udyoga Parva is known as the Vidura Niti.
During his peace mission Krishna refused Duryodhana's hospitality and stayed in Vidura's house, where Kunti was living.
Vidura did not fight in the war; some retellings say he broke his bow in protest, a detail that is not well attested in the Critical Edition.
Vidura retired to the forest with Dhritarashtra; when Yudhishthira found him, emaciated, Vidura passed his life force into Yudhishthira's body through yoga and died (Ashramavasika Parva).
Vyasa — Krishna Dvaipayana, author and g: Vyasa, called Krishna Dvaipayana ('the dark one born on an island'), was the son of the sage Parashara and Satyavati, born on an island in the Yamuna before her marriage to Shantanu.
Tradition credits Vyasa with arranging the Vedas, hence the title Vedavyasa, and with composing the Mahabharata; he is also a character in the story.
At his mother's request Vyasa fathered Dhritarashtra (with Ambika), Pandu (with Ambalika) and Vidura (with a maidservant) by niyoga, so he is the biological grandfather of both Kauravas and Pandavas.
Vyasa taught the epic to his pupil Vaishampayana, who recited it at Janamejaya's snake sacrifice; his son was the sage Shuka.

The Adi Parva says Vyasa composed a Bharata of 24,000 verses without the subsidiary tales, and speaks of a larger work; it also mentions 8,800 verses that only Vyasa, Shuka and perhaps Sanjaya understand.
The story that Ganesha wrote down the Mahabharata as Vyasa dictated it is a later addition; the Critical Edition places it outside the main text.
Vyasa intervenes repeatedly: dividing Gandhari's flesh into 101 pots, explaining Draupadi's marriage, giving Sanjaya divine sight, stopping the Brahmashira duel and urging Yudhishthira to rule.
In the Ashramavasika Parva Vyasa summoned the dead warriors from the Ganga for one night so their families could see them again.
After Krishna's death Vyasa told the grieving Arjuna that his time had passed, prompting the Pandavas' final journey.
Later tradition counts Vyasa among the seven chiranjivis (long-lived immortals).
Sanjaya — charioteer and narrator of the: Sanjaya, son of Gavalgana, was charioteer (suta) and counsellor to King Dhritarashtra.
Before the war Sanjaya went to the Pandavas as Dhritarashtra's envoy and brought back their message.
Vyasa gave Sanjaya divine sight so that he could see and narrate the whole war to Dhritarashtra, including the thoughts of the combatants.
Sanjaya narrates the Bhagavad Gita to Dhritarashtra in the Bhishma Parva, beginning with Dhritarashtra's question about what his sons and Pandu's sons did at Kurukshetra.
Sanjaya speaks frankly to Dhritarashtra, often telling him his own failings caused the disaster.
On day 18 Sanjaya was captured on the battlefield and spared, according to the Shalya Parva, after Vyasa's intervention.
Sanjaya accompanied Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti to the forest, survived the forest fire that killed them and went to the Himalaya.
Satyavati — fisher queen, matriarch of t: The Adi Parva says Satyavati was born from a fish (a cursed apsara) that swallowed the seed of King Uparichara Vasu, and was raised by the chief of the fisherfolk (Dasharaja).
Satyavati was called Matsyagandha for her fishy smell until the sage Parashara gave her a fragrance carried for a yojana (Yojanagandha); their son was Vyasa.
Satyavati's father agreed to her marriage with King Shantanu only if her sons would inherit, which led to Bhishma's vow.
Satyavati's sons by Shantanu were Chitrangada, killed by a gandharva of the same name, and Vichitravirya, who died childless of a wasting illness.
To save the dynasty Satyavati asked Bhishma to father heirs (he refused, citing his vow) and then summoned her first son Vyasa for niyoga with Vichitravirya's widows.
After Pandu's death, on Vyasa's advice, Satyavati withdrew to the forest with Ambika and Ambalika and died there.
Satyavati's descendants: sons 3 (Vyasa, Chitrangada, Vichitravirya) | grandsons by niyoga 3 (Dhritarashtra, Pandu, Vidura)
Shantanu — Kuru king, father of Bhishma: Shantanu was a Kuru king of Hastinapura, son of King Pratipa; the Adi Parva makes him a rebirth of King Mahabhisha.
The Adi Parva says Shantanu's touch made the old young again, which it uses to explain his name.
Shantanu married Ganga on condition that he never question her; she drowned seven newborn sons, and when he protested at the eighth she left, revealing the curse of the Vasus.
Ganga later returned his grown son Devavrata (Bhishma) to Shantanu, trained in scripture and arms.
Shantanu fell in love with Satyavati; Devavrata's vow of celibacy and renunciation made the marriage possible.
Shantanu gave Bhishma the boon that he would die only when he chose.
Shantanu's sons: by Ganga 8 (7 drowned, Devavrata survived) | by Satyavati 2 (Chitrangada, Vichitravirya)
Shantanu also found and raised the twins Kripa and Kripi.
Ganga — river goddess, mother of Bhishma: Ganga, goddess of the river Ganges, agreed to become the mother of the eight Vasus, who had been cursed by Vasishtha to be born as humans for stealing his wish-granting cow Nandini.
Ganga married Shantanu on condition that he never question her actions.
Ganga drowned seven of their sons at birth to free those Vasus at once; the eighth, the Vasu who had actually stolen the cow, had to live a long life on earth without offspring.
When Shantanu objected at the eighth birth, Ganga left him, taking the child, and later returned him as the accomplished Devavrata.
Ganga appears at the end of the Anushasana Parva mourning Bhishma's death, and Krishna and Vyasa console her.
Ganga as a sacred river runs through the epic, where the dead are honoured with water offerings and Vyasa calls up the slain warriors from its waters.
Amba — princess of Kashi, Bhishma's neme: Amba was the eldest of the three princesses of Kashi abducted by Bhishma from their svayamvara for Vichitravirya; her sisters were Ambika and Ambalika.
Amba told Bhishma she had chosen King Shalva of Saubha; Bhishma let her go, but Shalva rejected her because another man had carried her off.
Amba demanded that Bhishma marry her; bound by his vow, he refused.
Amba sought help from Parashurama, who fought Bhishma for twenty-three days without winning, and then turned to austerities.
Skanda (Kartikeya) gave Amba a garland of unfading lotuses, promising that its wearer would kill Bhishma; Drupada would not wear it, and it hung on his gate.
Shiva granted Amba that she would kill Bhishma in her next birth; she entered a fire and was reborn as Drupada's child Shikhandini, later Shikhandi.
Amba's story is told mainly in the Udyoga Parva (the Ambopakhyana), as Bhishma's own explanation for refusing to fight Shikhandi.
Ekalavya — the Nishada archer: Ekalavya was a Nishada (a forest people), son of the Nishada chief Hiranyadhanus.
Drona refused to accept Ekalavya as a pupil; Ekalavya made a clay image of Drona in the forest and practised archery before it until he became a superb archer.
When the Pandavas' dog barked at him, Ekalavya silenced it with seven arrows in its mouth without injuring it, which revealed his skill to the princes.
Drona, having promised Arjuna that no one would surpass him, asked Ekalavya for his right thumb as teacher's fee, and Ekalavya cut it off without hesitation.
After losing his thumb Ekalavya shot with his fingers and was less swift than before (Adi Parva).
Later passages and texts associate Ekalavya with Jarasandha and connect his death with Krishna; these references are brief and vary between versions.
Ekalavya's story is widely read today as a story of caste and exclusion, and as a critique of Drona.
Pandu — the pale king, father of the Pan: Pandu was the son of Vichitravirya's widow Ambalika by Vyasa through niyoga; the Adi Parva says he was born pale because Ambalika turned pale with fear at the sight of the sage, and his name means 'the pale one'.
Because Dhritarashtra was blind, Pandu was crowned king of Hastinapura, and the Adi Parva describes his campaigns of conquest that enlarged the Kuru realm.
Pandu married Kunti, who chose him at her svayamvara, and Madri of Madra, obtained by Bhishma for a bride-price.
While hunting, Pandu shot the sage Kindama, who was mating with his wife in the form of a deer; the dying sage cursed Pandu to die if he ever approached a wife in love.
Pandu renounced the throne and lived as an ascetic in the forest (the Adi Parva mentions the Shatashringa mountain) with Kunti and Madri, leaving Dhritarashtra to govern.
Desperate for heirs, Pandu urged Kunti to bear sons by others; she revealed Durvasa's mantra, and the five Pandavas were born to Kunti and Madri through the gods.
Pandu died in the forest when he embraced Madri in springtime, and Madri followed him onto his funeral pyre; the sages then brought Kunti and the five boys to Hastinapura.
Pandu is thus the legal father of the five Pandavas but the biological father of none of them, which shapes the later dispute over who is the rightful heir to the Kuru throne.
Partial incarnations of the main charact: The Adi Parva's list of partial incarnations (amshavatarana) gives a divine or demonic origin for many characters; these attributions vary somewhat between versions.
Divine origins of elders: Bhishma a Vasu | Drona Brihaspati | Ashwatthama Shiva, Yama, Kama and Krodha | Vidura Dharma | Kripa one of the Rudras
Divine origins on the Kaurava side: Duryodhana Kali | Shakuni Dvapara | Karna Surya | Gandhari Mati
Divine origins on the Pandava side: Krishna Narayana | Balarama the serpent Shesha | Draupadi Shri | Dhrishtadyumna Agni | Abhimanyu Varchas son of Soma | Kunti Siddhi | Madri Dhriti
The Adi Parva also places Satyaki, Kritavarma, Drupada and Virata among warriors born from the Maruts (storm gods).
The Pandavas are sons of the gods Dharma, Vayu, Indra and the Ashvins, and the same Adi Parva list also calls them portions of those gods; a separate Adi Parva story makes them five former Indras.
Teachers, pupils and lineages of learnin: Teachers and their pupils: Parashurama Bhishma, Drona, Karna | Drona Pandavas, Kauravas, Karna, Dhrishtadyumna | Kripa Kuru princes, later Parikshit | Balarama Duryodhana and Bhima (mace) | Arjuna Satyaki and Abhimanyu

Parashurama taught three great warriors of the epic: Drona received his weapons as a gift, Bhishma later fought him for 23 days over Amba, and Karna was cursed to forget the Brahmastra when his deception was discovered.
Vyasa's narrative lineage: Vyasa taught Vaishampayana, who recited to Janamejaya; Ugrashravas (Sauti) heard it there and retold it to the sages at Naimisha forest.
Ekalavya learned from a clay image of Drona, without Drona's consent.
Neutral, non-combatant and elder figures: Elders who fought for the Kauravas: Bhishma | Drona | Kripa | Shalya
Elders and others who did not fight: Vidura | Dhritarashtra | Gandhari | Kunti | Vyasa | Sanjaya (narrator) | Balarama (went on pilgrimage)

Generations of the Kuru story (oldest first): Shantanu, Ganga, Satyavati | Bhishma, Vyasa, Chitrangada, Vichitravirya | Dhritarashtra, Pandu, Vidura | Kauravas, Pandavas, Karna | Abhimanyu, Upapandavas, Ghatotkacha | Parikshit | Janamejaya

Fates of the elders: Bhishma died on the bed of arrows after the war | Drona killed on day 15 | Kripa survived | Vidura died in the forest | Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti died in a forest fire | Sanjaya went to the Himalaya | Vyasa lived on
Bhishma, Kripa and Vyasa span the whole story, from Shantanu's reign to after the war; Vidura spans from the generation after Shantanu to the elders' last years in the forest.

Krishna — birth, family and early life: Krishna was the son of the Yadava (Vrishni) prince Vasudeva and Devaki, sister of the tyrant Kamsa of Mathura; to escape Kamsa he was raised by the cowherd Nanda and his wife Yashoda in Gokula (Vraja).

Krishna's childhood and youth (the cowherd life, the slaying of demons, his love with the gopis and his killing of Kamsa) are told mainly in the Harivamsha (the Mahabharata's appendix) and the Puranas, especially the Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas; the Mahabharata itself mostly alludes to them, as in Shishupala's insults in the Sabha Parva.
Krishna was a cousin of the Pandavas: his father Vasudeva was the brother of Kunti (Pritha), so Kunti was Krishna's paternal aunt.
Krishna's family: father Vasudeva | mother Devaki | foster father Nanda | foster mother Yashoda | elder brother Balarama | sister Subhadra | maternal uncle Kamsa | paternal aunt Kunti
Krishna's names and epithets include Vasudeva, Keshava, Madhava, Govinda, Hrishikesha, Janardana, Madhusudana, Achyuta and Partha-sarathi (Arjuna's charioteer).
The epic identifies Krishna with Narayana (Vishnu) and Arjuna with Nara, the paired ancient sages, a link stated repeatedly in the Mahabharata.

After killing Kamsa, Krishna led the Yadavas from Mathura to Dwaraka on the western sea to escape the repeated attacks of Jarasandha of Magadha, Kamsa's father-in-law (Sabha Parva; the Puranas count the attacks as seventeen or eighteen).
Krishna — weapons, conch, chariot and at: Krishna's weapons: discus Sudarshana | mace Kaumodaki | bow Sharnga | sword Nandaka; his conch is Panchajanya.
Agni gave Krishna the discus and the mace Kaumodaki at the burning of the Khandava forest, when he gave Arjuna the Gandiva bow (Adi Parva).
Krishna's conch Panchajanya is named in the Bhagavad Gita (1.15); the Puranas say it came from the sea demon Panchajana.
Krishna's own chariot horses are named Shaibya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa and Balahaka, and his charioteer is Daruka.
Krishna's banner bears Garuda, the eagle mount of Vishnu.
Krishna is described as dark-skinned, dressed in yellow garments, and wearing the Kaustubha jewel and the Shrivatsa mark in Vaishnava descriptions.
Krishna and the Pandavas — friendship, K: Krishna first meets the Pandavas at Draupadi's svayamvara, where he recognises them in their brahmin disguise.
Krishna and Arjuna are close friends and cousins; Krishna approved Arjuna's elopement with his sister Subhadra and persuaded Balarama to accept it.
Krishna and Arjuna burned the Khandava forest together for the fire god Agni, fighting off Indra, and spared Maya, who built the Pandavas' assembly hall.

Krishna advised Yudhishthira that Jarasandha had to be removed before the Rajasuya; disguised as brahmins, Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna went to Magadha, where Bhima killed Jarasandha in a wrestling duel and the imprisoned kings were freed.

At the Rajasuya, Krishna received the first honour on Bhishma's advice; Shishupala of Chedi protested and insulted him, and Krishna killed Shishupala with his discus after exhausting the hundred offences he had promised Shishupala's mother to forgive.
Krishna was absent from the dice game; in the Vana Parva he explains that he was away fighting King Shalva of Saubha, who had attacked Dwaraka.
During the exile Krishna visited the Pandavas in the forest and promised Draupadi that her humiliation would be avenged.
Popular retellings make Krishna the rescuer of Draupadi's honour in the dice hall; the Critical Edition keeps the miracle of the endless garment but places her prayer to Krishna in an appendix.

The story of Krishna saving the exiled Pandavas from the hungry sage Durvasa and his disciples by eating a last morsel left in Draupadi's vessel belongs to the vulgate and popular tradition; it is not part of the Critical Edition's constituted text.
Krishna's peace embassy and the road to: Before the war Arjuna and Duryodhana both went to Dwaraka for Krishna's help; Krishna, waking to see Arjuna first, let him choose between Krishna alone, unarmed and not fighting, and Krishna's army.

Arjuna chose Krishna himself; Duryodhana gladly took Krishna's Narayana troops, which the Udyoga Parva describes as a huge force of cowherd warriors and which popular accounts often call one akshauhini.

Krishna went to Hastinapura as the Pandavas' envoy, stayed with Vidura and pleaded for peace in the Kuru assembly; the Pandavas' request was reduced to five villages (the names vary between passages and versions).
When Duryodhana plotted to seize him, Krishna revealed his cosmic form (vishvarupa) in the Kuru court (Udyoga Parva).

After the failed embassy Krishna met Karna alone, revealed that Karna was Kunti's eldest son and offered him the throne and Draupadi if he joined the Pandavas; Karna refused out of loyalty to Duryodhana.
Debate continues over whether Krishna sincerely sought peace or knew the war to be inevitable; the epic gives him speeches pointing both ways.
Krishna in the Kurukshetra war — chariot: Krishna served as Arjuna's charioteer throughout the war and vowed not to take up weapons.
Before the first day's battle Krishna taught Arjuna the Bhagavad Gita (Bhishma Parva), 700 verses in 18 chapters in the received text, and revealed his universal form.

On day 3 and again on day 9 Krishna, angered by Arjuna's mild fighting against Bhishma, leapt from the chariot to attack Bhishma himself, with his discus in some passages and a whip in others; popular retellings show him raising a chariot wheel. Arjuna held him back.
Krishna saved Arjuna from Bhagadatta's Vaishnava weapon on day 12 by taking it on his own chest, where it became a garland.
When Ashwatthama released the Narayanastra on day 15, Krishna saved the Pandava army by telling the warriors to lay down their arms.

Krishna advised or approved most of the stratagems by which the Kaurava champions fell: Shikhandi before Bhishma, the false report of Ashwatthama's death to Drona, the attack on Karna while his wheel was stuck, and Bhima's blow to Duryodhana's thigh.
Krishna also intervened on the day of Jayadratha's death and rejoiced at Ghatotkacha's death because it used up Karna's Vasavi spear.
When the heavens honoured the fallen Duryodhana, Krishna told the Pandavas that the Kaurava heroes could not have been killed by fair means, and defended the stratagems as necessary.
After the night massacre Krishna cursed Ashwatthama to wander for three thousand years and revived Uttaraa's stillborn son Parikshit.
Krishna after the war — teachings, curse: After the war Krishna urged the grieving Yudhishthira to rule and took him to hear Bhishma's teachings on the bed of arrows.

Gandhari cursed Krishna in the Stri Parva: since he had allowed the Kurus to destroy one another, his own clan would perish by fratricide in thirty-six years, and he would die alone; Krishna accepted the curse.
In the Ashvamedhika Parva Krishna retells his teaching to Arjuna, who says he has forgotten the Gita; this second teaching is called the Anugita.
Krishna's death (Mausala Parva): after the Yadavas destroyed themselves, he sat in meditation in the forest and was struck in the foot by the arrow of a hunter named Jara, who took him for a deer.
Krishna forgave Jara and departed to heaven; Arjuna arrived in Dwaraka to find Krishna gone and his father Vasudeva dying.
Traditional Indian reckoning dates the start of the Kali age to Krishna's departure (conventionally 3102 BCE); this is a traditional calculation, not a historically established date.
The Bhagavata Purana says Krishna lived about 125 years; the Mahabharata gives no explicit age.
Krishna's wives, sons and descendants: Krishna's chief wife is Rukmini, princess of Vidarbha, whom he carried off with her consent despite her brother Rukmi (a story told mainly in the Harivamsha and Puranas, and only alluded to in the Mahabharata); Satyabhama and Jambavati are among his other prominent wives.
The Puranas list eight principal wives (ashtabharya): Rukmini, Satyabhama, Jambavati, Kalindi, Mitravinda, Nagnajiti (Satya), Bhadra and Lakshmana; the eight vary slightly between texts.
The Mahabharata mentions sixteen thousand wives of Krishna; the Bhagavata Purana gives 16,100 women rescued from the demon Naraka in addition to the eight chief wives.
Krishna's wives (traditional counts): principal 8 | others 16,000 (Mahabharata) or 16,100 (Bhagavata Purana)
Krishna's best-known sons are Pradyumna (by Rukmini), Samba (by Jambavati) and Charudeshna; his grandson Aniruddha was Pradyumna's son.

The Bhagavata Purana and related later texts say Samba carried off and married Lakshmanaa, daughter of Duryodhana, making Krishna and Duryodhana relatives by marriage; the Mahabharata itself does not tell this story.
Krishna's great-grandson Vajra, son of Aniruddha, survived the Yadava destruction and was installed by Arjuna as ruler at Indraprastha (Mausala Parva).
In the Vana Parva Satyabhama asks Draupadi how she keeps her five husbands devoted, and Draupadi describes her conduct and service.
Balarama — Krishna's elder brother: Balarama (Baladeva, Sankarshana) was Krishna's elder brother, son of Vasudeva and Rohini; the Harivamsha and Puranas say he was transferred as an embryo from Devaki's womb to Rohini's.
Balarama carries the plough (hala), giving him the name Halayudha, and the pestle-club (musala); he is famed for his strength and fair complexion, and his wife was Revati.
The Adi Parva makes Balarama a partial incarnation of the cosmic serpent Shesha.
Balarama taught mace combat to both Duryodhana and Bhima and was fond of Duryodhana.
Balarama was angry when Arjuna carried off Subhadra, until Krishna persuaded him to accept the marriage.
Balarama refused to fight for either side and went on a pilgrimage along the Sarasvati river during the war; the Shalya Parva says he was away forty-two days.

Balarama returned in time to watch the mace duel between Bhima and Duryodhana; enraged at Bhima's blow below the navel, he raised his plough to attack Bhima, was calmed by Krishna and left for Dwaraka, declaring that Duryodhana would reach heaven.
At the end of the Yadavas, Balarama sat in yogic meditation by the sea and a great white serpent left his mouth and entered the ocean (Mausala Parva).
Balarama is worshipped as Balabhadra with Jagannatha and Subhadra at Puri, and in some traditions he replaces the Buddha in the list of Vishnu's ten avatars.
Satyaki (Yuyudhana) — Yadava champion of: Satyaki, also called Yuyudhana, was a Yadava warrior of the Shini (Shaineya) clan, grandson of Shini and son of Satyaka.
Satyaki learned archery from Arjuna and was devoted to both Arjuna and Krishna.
Satyaki accompanied Krishna on the peace embassy to Hastinapura and warned him of Duryodhana's plot to seize him.
Satyaki brought one akshauhini to the Pandavas and was one of the seven Pandava commanders.
On day 14 Satyaki, sent by Yudhishthira to help Arjuna, broke through the Kaurava formations.
On day 14 Satyaki was overpowered by Bhurishravas; Arjuna cut off Bhurishravas's arm, and when Bhurishravas sat down to fast to death, Satyaki beheaded him, an act condemned by many on both sides.
The feud between Satyaki's Shini clan and Bhurishravas's family went back to Shini's defeat of Somadatta when winning Devaki as a bride for Vasudeva.
Satyaki survived the war, one of the seven Pandava-side survivors.
Satyaki died in the drunken Yadava brawl at Prabhasa, killed by the Bhojas and Andhakas after he had beheaded Kritavarma.
Kritavarma — Yadava warrior on the Kaura: Kritavarma was a Yadava of the Bhoja (Andhaka) branch, son of Hridika.
Kritavarma brought one akshauhini to Duryodhana and fought for the Kauravas throughout the war, the most prominent Yadava on that side.
Kritavarma was one of the three Kaurava survivors with Ashwatthama and Kripa.
In the night raid Kritavarma and Kripa guarded the gates of the Pandava camp, cut down those who fled and set the camp on fire.

At Prabhasa, thirty-six years after the war, the drunken Satyaki mocked Kritavarma for the night massacre; Kritavarma taunted Satyaki over Bhurishravas, and Satyaki beheaded him, starting the brawl that destroyed the Yadavas.
The Puranas involve Kritavarma in the quarrel over the Syamantaka jewel and the killing of its owner Satrajit; that story belongs to the Puranic tradition, not the Mahabharata's main narrative.
The Yadava clan — branches, Dwaraka and: The Yadavas descend from Yadu, eldest son of King Yayati; the Adi Parva says Yayati cursed Yadu's line not to hold royal sovereignty after Yadu refused to give his father his youth.
The Yadava branches include the Vrishnis (Krishna's own line), Andhakas, Bhojas, Kukuras, Shainyas (Shini's line), Dasharhas and Satvatas, often grouped as the Vrishni-Andhaka confederacy.
The Yadavas were governed as a clan assembly; King Ugrasena, Kamsa's father, was restored as their nominal king after Krishna killed Kamsa.

Dwaraka, the Yadava capital, is described as a strongly fortified city on the western sea (some descriptions make it island-like, surrounded by water); it is traditionally identified with Dwarka in Gujarat, and claims about submerged ruins offshore are debated.
The Yadavas were split by the war: allegiances: Krishna Pandavas (unarmed) | Satyaki Pandavas | Chekitana Pandavas | Kritavarma Kauravas | Narayana troops Kauravas | Balarama neutral
Yadava festivals at Mount Raivataka near Dwaraka were the setting of Arjuna's elopement with Subhadra.
Leading Yadava figures include Ugrasena, Vasudeva, Akrura, Balarama, Krishna, Satyaki, Kritavarma, Uddhava, Pradyumna, Samba and Aniruddha.
Destruction of the Yadavas (Mausala Parv: In the thirty-sixth year after the war, fulfilling Gandhari's curse, the Yadavas destroyed themselves (Mausala Parva).

Some young Yadavas dressed Krishna's son Samba as a pregnant woman and asked the sages Vishvamitra, Kanva and Narada what she would bear; the sages cursed them that Samba would bear an iron pestle (musala) that would destroy the clan.
Samba gave birth to an iron pestle; King Ugrasena had it ground to powder and thrown into the sea, and liquor was banned in Dwaraka, but omens multiplied.
The powdered iron washed ashore and grew into eraka reeds.

The Yadavas went on a pilgrimage to Prabhasa by the sea, drank heavily, and quarrelled; Satyaki killed Kritavarma, Satyaki and Pradyumna were killed, and the Yadavas slaughtered one another with eraka reeds that turned into iron clubs in their hands.
Krishna himself joined the killing in fury, then left; Balarama departed in yoga, and Krishna was killed by the hunter Jara's arrow.
Arjuna came to Dwaraka, performed the rites for Vasudeva and led the surviving women, children and elders away; the sea then swallowed Dwaraka.
On the way, in the land of the five rivers (Panchanada), Abhira herdsmen attacked the convoy; Arjuna could barely string Gandiva, his divine weapons failed him and many women were carried off.
Arjuna settled the survivors in several places and installed Krishna's great-grandson Vajra as ruler at Indraprastha; some of Krishna's wives entered the fire and others withdrew to the forest.
Years after the Kurukshetra war: Gandhari's curse 0 | Yadava destruction 36 | Pandavas' final journey soon after 36
Yadava destruction was the immediate trigger for the Pandavas' renunciation: on Vyasa's advice Yudhishthira crowned Parikshit and the brothers and Draupadi set out for the Himalaya.

Kripa — First Teacher of the Kuru Prince: Kripa (Kripacharya) and his twin sister Kripi were born, as the Adi Parva tells it, when the seed of the sage Sharadvan Gautama fell on a clump of reeds after he saw the apsara Janapadi.
King Shantanu found the abandoned twins while hunting and raised them out of compassion (kripa), which the epic gives as the origin of the names Kripa and Kripi.
Kripa learned archery and weapon lore from his father Sharadvan and became the first instructor in arms of both the Pandava and Kaurava princes at Hastinapura.
Kripa's sister Kripi married Drona; their only son was Ashwatthama, which made Kripa Ashwatthama's maternal uncle.
Kripa remained attached to the Hastinapura court for life; he later fought on the Kaurava side at Kurukshetra and is one of the few warriors on that side who survived the war.
At the tournament (exhibition of arms), it was Kripa who challenged Karna to state his lineage before he could duel Arjuna, on the rule that princes fight only their equals in birth.
Drona — Origins, Poverty and the Feud wi: Drona was the son of the sage Bharadvaja; the epic says he was born from Bharadvaja's seed collected in a vessel (drona), which gives him his name.
As a youth Drona studied alongside Drupada, son of King Prishata of Panchala, and Drupada promised him friendship and, in some tellings, a share of his kingdom.
Drona obtained divine weapons and their lore from Rama Jamadagnya (Parashurama), who was giving away his possessions at the end of his life.
Drona lived in poverty after his marriage to Kripi; the Adi Parva tells that the boy Ashwatthama was once given flour mixed in water in place of milk, which drove Drona to seek wealth.
When Drona went to King Drupada claiming their old friendship, Drupada rejected him, saying friendship exists only between equals, and a poor brahmin could not be the friend of a king.
Humiliated by Drupada, Drona went to Hastinapura, where he lived for a time unknown in Kripa's house before Bhishma appointed him teacher of the Kuru princes.

Drona's first act at Hastinapura in the epic: the princes' ball (and, in the story, Drona's ring) had fallen into a well, and Drona retrieved it by shooting a chain of grass-blades (ishika), each piercing the one before.
Drona's teacher's fee (gurudakshina) from the princes was the capture of Drupada; the Kauravas attacked first and failed, and Arjuna with his brothers then defeated and captured Drupada.
Drona took the northern half of Panchala (capital Ahichchhatra) and returned the southern half (capital Kampilya, south of the Ganga) to Drupada, saying they were now equals and could be friends.
Drupada, nursing revenge, later performed a sacrifice through the brahmins Yaja and Upayaja to obtain a son who would kill Drona; from the sacrificial fire came Dhrishtadyumna and Draupadi.
Drona's Gurukul — Students and Specialit: Drona's students included the five Pandavas, the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra (the Kauravas), his own son Ashwatthama, princes of the Vrishni and Andhaka clans, and, according to the Critical Edition's text, Karna (called Radheya, son of the suta Adhiratha).

Popular retellings often say Drona refused to teach Karna because he was a charioteer's son; in the Critical Edition's Adi Parva Karna is listed among Drona's pupils, and his rivalry with Arjuna begins there.

The Adi Parva assigns specialities at the end of training: Arjuna excelled above all in archery and in every weapon; Bhima and Duryodhana in the mace; Nakula and Sahadeva in sword-fighting; Yudhishthira in chariot fighting; Ashwatthama in the secret lore of weapons.

Elsewhere the epic says that Bhima and Duryodhana also learned mace-fighting from Balarama, Krishna's elder brother; in the Shalya Parva Balarama calls both of them his pupils, and he is said to have favoured Duryodhana.
Drona promised Arjuna that he would make sure no archer in the world surpassed him, a promise that drives the Ekalavya episode.

The Adi Parva tells that when a gust of wind blew out the lamp while Arjuna was eating, he realised that practice could make the hand find its mark in darkness, and he began practising archery at night.

A story in the Adi Parva says Drona gave his pupils narrow-necked water pots to fill but gave Ashwatthama a wide-mouthed one so his son returned early for extra teaching; Arjuna filled his pot quickly with the Varuna weapon and so did not miss the lessons.

When a crocodile seized Drona while he bathed in the Ganga, Arjuna alone acted at once and killed it with arrows; as reward Drona gave him the Brahmashiras weapon, with the warning never to use it against ordinary human foes.
A local tradition associates Drona's teaching ground with Gurugram (Gurgaon) near Delhi; the epic itself places Drona's residence and teaching at Hastinapura.
The Bird's-Eye Test: To test his pupils' concentration, Drona set an artificial bird on a treetop as a target and asked each prince, bow drawn, what he saw.
Yudhishthira and the other princes answered that they saw the tree, the bird, Drona himself and their brothers; Drona sent each away without letting him shoot.
Arjuna answered that he saw only the bird; asked again, he said he saw only its head. Drona told him to shoot, and Arjuna severed the bird's head.

In the Critical Edition's Adi Parva the target is the bird's head (the bird is called a bhasa, a kind of bird of prey); the familiar detail that Arjuna saw only the bird's eye comes from later and popular retellings.
The episode is the epic's emblem of single-pointed concentration (ekagrata), and it is the reason the story gives for Drona's special affection for Arjuna.
Ekalavya: Ekalavya was the son of Hiranyadhanus, king of the Nishadas, a forest people; he came to Drona asking to be taught archery.

The Critical Edition says Drona refused him because he was a Nishada, and out of concern for the Kuru princes; interpretation of the refusal (caste exclusion, Drona's promise to Arjuna, royal patronage) is much debated.
Ekalavya went back to the forest, made a clay image of Drona, treated it as his teacher, and through practice became an outstanding archer.
When the princes went hunting, their dog barked at Ekalavya, and he silenced it by shooting seven arrows into its mouth at once without killing it.
Arjuna, troubled that a forest archer surpassed him, reminded Drona of his promise; Drona went to Ekalavya, who greeted him as his teacher.

Drona asked for Ekalavya's right thumb as gurudakshina, and Ekalavya cut it off and gave it without hesitation; afterwards, shooting with his fingers, he was no longer as swift as before, and Arjuna's anxiety ended.

Ekalavya reappears later as a Nishada king; in the Drona Parva Krishna names him, with Jarasandha and Shishupala, among enemies removed for the Pandavas' sake, and the Harivamsha shows him fighting the Yadavas on Jarasandha's side; accounts of his fate differ between texts.

Modern readers, writers and Dalit and Adivasi critics often read Ekalavya's thumb as a symbol of injustice by caste and birth; traditional readings stress his devotion to his teacher. Both readings are interpretations, not settled fact.
Bhima and Duryodhana — Childhood Enmity: Dhritarashtra and Gandhari had a hundred sons (the Kauravas), led by Duryodhana, and one daughter, Duhshala.

In childhood games Bhima bullied the Kauravas, pulling them under water, dragging them by the hair, and shaking trees until the boys climbing them fell; the Adi Parva gives this as a root of Duryodhana's hatred.
Duryodhana poisoned Bhima's food during a water-sport outing on the Ganga (at a place called Pramanakoti), bound the unconscious Bhima and threw him into the river.
Bhima sank to the realm of the Nagas, where snakebites counteracted the poison; the Naga Aryaka, a relative of Kunti's family, had Vasuki give him an elixir.
Bhima drank eight bowls (kundas) of the Naga elixir, which, the epic says, gave him the strength of ten thousand elephants; he returned to Hastinapura after eight days.
Number facts — Bhima and the Nagas: Bowls of elixir drunk 8 | Days before his return 8 | Elephants' strength gained 10000.
The Adi Parva says Duryodhana also tried snakes and other poisons against Bhima, and that Vidura advised the Pandavas to keep silent and stay alert rather than accuse him openly.
The Tournament and Karna's Entry: When training was complete, Drona asked Dhritarashtra to hold a public exhibition of the princes' skill (the ranga, or tournament); Vidura oversaw the arrangements, and Gandhari and Kunti watched from the stands.
The mace display between Bhima and Duryodhana turned into real rivalry, and Drona had Ashwatthama separate them before it became a fight.
Arjuna displayed mastery of divine weapons, including the fire, water, wind and cloud weapons and the weapon of invisibility (antardhana), to the crowd's acclaim.
Karna entered the arena uninvited, repeated all of Arjuna's feats, and challenged him to single combat; Duryodhana embraced him at once.
Kripa demanded that Karna declare his parents and lineage, because a prince did not have to fight an opponent of unknown birth; Karna lowered his head in shame.

Duryodhana answered that a man may be qualified for battle by birth, by valour or by leading an army, and had Karna consecrated king of Anga on the spot so that Arjuna could not refuse him as an unequal.
Asked what he wanted in return, Karna asked for Duryodhana's lifelong friendship; the bond between Karna and Duryodhana dates from this day.
When Karna's foster father, the charioteer Adhiratha, appeared, Karna bowed to him; Bhima mocked Karna as a charioteer's son who should take up the whip, not a kingdom.
Duryodhana defended Karna by arguing that the origins of heroes, like the sources of rivers, are hard to know, citing other great figures of irregular birth.
Kunti recognised Karna, her son born before her marriage (by his earrings and armour, according to the story), and fainted; Vidura revived her with sandal water, and she kept her secret.
Sunset ended the tournament before Karna and Arjuna could fight; their duel was postponed, symbolically, until the war at Kurukshetra.
Karna's Training and Curses: Before her marriage, Kunti used a mantra given to her by the sage Durvasa to invoke the sun god Surya and bore Karna; fearing disgrace, she set the baby afloat in a basket on a river, and he was found and adopted by the charioteer (suta) Adhiratha and his wife Radha.
Karna, son of Kunti by Surya and raised by Adhiratha and Radha, is called Radheya and Vasusena; he was born with armour (kavacha) and earrings (kundala), according to the epic.
The Shanti Parva (in Narada's account to Yudhishthira) says Karna went to Parashurama claiming to be a brahmin and learned the Brahmastra from him.

When an insect bored into Karna's thigh while Parashurama slept on his lap and Karna bore the pain without moving, Parashurama concluded he could not be a brahmin; he cursed Karna to forget the Brahmastra at the moment of greatest need.
Narada's account also says Karna accidentally killed a brahmin's cow, and the brahmin cursed that the earth would swallow his chariot wheel in his decisive battle.

Karna himself recalls these curses to Shalya in the Karna Parva, and both are fulfilled during his final duel with Arjuna; the order and details of the curse stories differ between the Shanti Parva, the Karna Parva and popular retellings.
Heir Apparent and Rising Jealousy: After the tournament Dhritarashtra named Yudhishthira heir apparent (yuvaraja), and the citizens openly said Yudhishthira should rule.
The Pandavas' popularity, conquests and fame deepened Duryodhana's jealousy, and he pressed Dhritarashtra to send them away from the capital.

The minister Kanika gave Dhritarashtra a famous speech of ruthless statecraft (known as Kanika's counsel), advising him to destroy rivals by craft; the Adi Parva places it just before the lac-house plot.
Dhritarashtra is shown as torn between love for his sons and duty to Pandu's sons, a tension that runs through the epic's account of the Kuru crisis.
The Lac House at Varanavata: Persuaded by Duryodhana, Dhritarashtra sent the Pandavas and Kunti to Varanavata on the pretext of a festival for Shiva (Pashupati) there.
Duryodhana's minister Purochana built them a house of highly flammable materials such as lac, resin, hemp and clay mixed with fat (the jatugriha), planning to burn them inside.

Vidura warned Yudhishthira before he left, speaking in riddles in a foreign (mleccha) tongue that only the two understood, about a fire in a dry forest from which one escapes like a creature in a burrow.
Vidura secretly sent a miner who dug an escape tunnel under the house, hidden from Purochana.
The Pandavas lived in the house for about a year, acting unsuspecting while Purochana waited for his moment.

Kunti held a feast; a Nishada woman and her five sons stayed the night drunk in the house; that night Bhima set fire to the house, beginning with Purochana's quarters, and the Pandavas and Kunti escaped through the tunnel.
Number facts — Lac house: Years lived in the house about 1 | Deaths in the fire: Nishada woman 1 | her sons 5 | Purochana 1.
Finding the bodies of the Nishada woman and her five sons, the people of Varanavata believed the Pandavas and Kunti had died; Dhritarashtra performed their funeral rites.
A boatman sent by Vidura ferried the fugitives across the Ganga, and they fled south into the forest; they later wandered as ascetics and, at Ekachakra, lived disguised as brahmins.
The deaths of the Nishada woman and her sons are an ethical problem much discussed by modern readers; the epic itself records them without comment.
Hidimba, Bakasura and the Road to Pancha: In the forest the rakshasa Hidimba sent his sister Hidimbi to kill the sleeping Pandavas; she fell in love with Bhima, who was keeping watch.

Bhima killed Hidimba in a wrestling fight, and with Kunti's and Yudhishthira's consent married Hidimbi, on condition that he would stay with her by day and return to his family at night until a son was born.
Their son Ghatotkacha grew to youth at once, as rakshasa children do in the epic, and promised to come whenever the Pandavas called him.
Vyasa visited the fugitives and directed them to the town of Ekachakra, where they lived in a brahmin's house disguised as brahmins, living on alms, with Bhima eating half of all food gathered.
The rakshasa Baka (Bakasura) near Ekachakra demanded a daily tribute of a cartload of rice, two buffaloes and the person who brought them.
Number facts — Baka's daily tribute: Cartloads of food 1 | Buffaloes 2 | Human victims 1.
When it was their host family's turn, Kunti sent Bhima in their place; Bhima ate the food himself and killed Baka, freeing the town.
On the way to Draupadi's swayamvara, Arjuna defeated the gandharva Angaraparna (also called Chitraratha) at the Ganga; the gandharva advised them to take a family priest, and they chose Dhaumya.
The gandharva Chitraratha also gave the Pandavas gandharva horses; these horses are later named among the stakes in the dice game.
Sources and Variants for the Youth Episo: These episodes are told in the Adi Parva (Book 1), mainly in the Sambhava, Jatugriha (lac house), Hidimba-vadha, Baka-vadha and Chaitraratha sub-parvas; the Critical Edition's Adi Parva has 225 chapters (adhyayas).

The Critical Edition (Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune, 1919–1966) reconstructs the oldest recoverable text from many manuscripts; passages found only in some recensions are relegated to footnotes and appendices.

Details such as the bird's eye as Arjuna's target, Drona refusing Karna as a pupil, and many dialogues in television versions come from later or popular retellings rather than the Critical Edition's text.

The Pandavas' and Kauravas' childhood and education are narrated to King Janamejaya by Vaishampayana, within Ugrashravas' telling at the Naimisha forest, so every episode reaches the reader through nested narrators.

Draupadi's Birth from the Fire: Draupadi was born, along with her twin brother Dhrishtadyumna, from the fire altar of a sacrifice King Drupada had the brahmins Yaja and Upayaja perform to obtain a son who would kill Drona.
Dhrishtadyumna rose first from the fire, armoured and armed; Draupadi then emerged from the altar (vedi) as a dark-complexioned young woman of great beauty.
A voice from the sky declared that Draupadi would bring about the destruction of the Kshatriyas and serve the purpose of the gods.
Draupadi's names: Krishnaa (the dark one), Draupadi (daughter of Drupada), Panchali (princess of Panchala), Yajnaseni (born of the sacrifice) and Sairandhri (her disguise in Virata).
Shikhandi, born first as a daughter and later living as a man, was also Drupada's child and a sibling of Draupadi and Dhrishtadyumna.
Setting of the Swayamvara: Draupadi's swayamvara (self-choice ceremony) was held at Kampilya, capital of southern Panchala, Drupada's kingdom.
Drupada secretly hoped Arjuna would win Draupadi, though the Pandavas were believed to have died at Varanavata.
Kings and princes came from across the land, including Duryodhana and his brothers, Karna, Shalya, Shishupala, Jarasandha and Ashwatthama; Krishna and Balarama attended with the Yadavas.
The festivities went on for many days, and the text says Draupadi entered the arena on the sixteenth day, holding the garland for the man she would choose.
The Pandavas, disguised as brahmins, sat among the brahmins; Krishna recognised them in spite of their disguise and told Balarama.
Dhrishtadyumna announced the contest and named the assembled suitors to his sister.
The Target and the Bow: Drupada had a very stiff bow made that few could string, and set up a target that had to be hit by shooting five arrows through an opening in a device hung high in the air.
In the Critical Edition the target is a revolving or aerial device (yantra) with a hole and a mark (lakshya) beyond it; the bow had to be strung and five arrows shot through the opening.

The famous image of a revolving fish (matsya) whose eye had to be hit while aiming at its reflection in a pool of water or oil comes from later retellings, some manuscripts and regional versions; it is not in the Critical Edition's constituted text.
Many powerful kings failed even to string the bow, and some were thrown to the ground by its recoil, which the crowd met with laughter.
Number facts — Swayamvara contest: Arrows required 5 | Day Draupadi entered 16 | Successful suitors 1 (Arjuna).
Karna at the Swayamvara — Differs by Rec: Karna's part in the swayamvara is one of the best-known recension differences in the Mahabharata.

In the vulgate (the version printed with Nilakantha's commentary) and many Northern manuscripts, Karna strings the bow and is about to shoot when Draupadi declares she will not choose a charioteer's son (suta); Karna laughs bitterly, looks at the sun and puts the bow down.

In the Critical Edition's constituted text, Draupadi's public rejection of Karna is relegated to the apparatus and is not in the main text; there Karna is simply counted among the great kings who fail at the contest (manuscripts differ on the exact details of his attempt).

Popular retellings, plays and television adaptations nearly always use the rejection scene, and it underlies many modern novels that treat Karna's humiliation as a cause of his later cruelty to Draupadi in the dice hall.
Because the evidence differs, an honest account says that in some versions Draupadi rejects Karna for his birth, while in the oldest reconstructed text Karna simply fails like the other kings.
Arjuna Wins Draupadi: After the kings had failed, Arjuna rose from among the brahmins, strung the bow at once, and shot the target down with the five arrows.
The brahmins cheered and waved their deerskins; Draupadi came forward and placed her white garland on Arjuna.
The assembled Kshatriyas were enraged that a brahmin had won a Kshatriya princess and attacked Drupada; Arjuna and Bhima defended him, with Bhima using an uprooted tree as a club.
Arjuna fought Karna, and Karna withdrew, saying he would not fight on against what seemed to be the power of a brahmin; Bhima defeated Shalya in wrestling.
Krishna calmed the kings, pointing out that Draupadi had been won according to the rules of the contest.
Dhrishtadyumna secretly followed the brahmins to the potter's house where they lived and reported to Drupada that their conduct and talk of weapons showed they were Kshatriyas.
Kunti's Words and the Shared Marriage: Arriving home with Draupadi, Bhima and Arjuna announced to their mother that they had brought alms; Kunti, from inside without looking, told them to share it all together.
Seeing that the alms was Draupadi, Kunti was distressed that her words might force wrongdoing, but the rule that a mother's word must not prove false weighed on the brothers.
Yudhishthira saw that all five brothers desired Draupadi and feared that rivalry over her would split them; he decided that she would be the wife of all five.
Drupada and Dhrishtadyumna objected that one woman marrying several men was against the Vedas and customary law, and a debate on dharma followed at Drupada's court.
The marriage took place on successive days in order of seniority, Yudhishthira first; the family priest Dhaumya officiated.

The text adds that Draupadi became a maiden again after each wedding day; the claim that each brother lived with her for one year in turn is a later and popular tradition rather than a rule stated at the wedding.
Number facts — Draupadi's marriage: Husbands 5 | Wedding days 5 (one per brother, in order of age).
Justifications Offered for the Polyandry: Justification 1, Kunti's word: Kunti's instruction to share must not be made false, which the brothers treat as binding.

Justification 2, precedent: Yudhishthira cites old precedents of polyandry, such as Jatila of the Gautama lineage, said to have married seven sages, and Varkshi, a sage's daughter said to have married ten brothers, the Prachetas.

Justification 3, Draupadi's previous birth: Vyasa tells Drupada that in an earlier life Draupadi, a sage's daughter, asked Shiva for a husband five times, and Shiva granted her five husbands in her next birth; later tradition names this earlier woman Nalayani.

Justification 4, the five Indras: Vyasa tells a story in which five former Indras were reborn as the Pandavas and the goddess Shri (Lakshmi) was born as Draupadi to be their common wife; Vyasa gives Drupada divine sight to see their divine forms.
Justification 5, family unity: the story itself makes it clear that the arrangement keeps the five brothers from fighting over Draupadi.

Many scholars read the episode as a narrative effort to explain an unusual polyandrous marriage; whether it reflects an older custom is debated, and the epic itself presents the marriage as needing exceptional justification.
Narada's Rule and its Consequences: To prevent quarrels over Draupadi, the sage Narada told the brothers the story of the asura brothers Sunda and Upasunda, who killed each other over the apsara Tilottama.
The brothers agreed that if one of them intruded while another was alone with Draupadi, the intruder would go into exile as a celibate (brahmacharin) for twelve years.

Arjuna broke the rule to fetch his weapons from the room where Yudhishthira was with Draupadi so he could help a brahmin whose cattle had been stolen; he insisted on going into exile even though Yudhishthira forgave him.

The rule specified twelve years of exile, but the epic's account of Arjuna's journey is chronologically loose, and readers have noted that his marriages during the 'celibate' exile sit uneasily with the vow.
Number facts — Narada's rule: Exile for intrusion 12 years.
Draupadi's Sons and the Pandavas' Other: Draupadi bore each Pandava one son, together called the Upapandavas: Prativindhya (by Yudhishthira), Sutasoma (by Bhima), Shrutakarman (by Arjuna), Shatanika (by Nakula) and Shrutasena (by Sahadeva).
All five sons of Draupadi were killed by Ashwatthama in the night raid on the Pandava camp after the war.

The Adi Parva also lists the Pandavas' other wives and sons: Yudhishthira and Devika (son Yaudheya); Bhima and Hidimbi (son Ghatotkacha) and Bhima and Balandhara (son Sarvaga); Nakula and Karenumati (son Niramitra); Sahadeva and Vijaya (son Suhotra).
Arjuna married Ulupi (son Iravat), Chitrangada of Manipura (son Babhruvahana) and Subhadra, Krishna's sister (son Abhimanyu), during and after his exile.
Number facts — sons of Draupadi: Prativindhya 1 | Sutasoma 1 | Shrutakarman 1 | Shatanika 1 | Shrutasena 1 (total 5).
Return to Hastinapura and the Half-Kingd: News that the Pandavas were alive and allied to Panchala by marriage reached Hastinapura, where Duryodhana and Karna debated how to respond.
Duryodhana proposed covert schemes, such as sowing discord between the brothers or turning Draupadi against them; Karna argued instead for an immediate open attack before the Pandavas grew stronger.
Bhishma and Drona advised Dhritarashtra to welcome the Pandavas back and give them half the kingdom, and Vidura was sent to bring them, with Kunti and Draupadi, to Hastinapura.
Dhritarashtra gave Yudhishthira the region of Khandavaprastha, a forested and undeveloped half of the realm, where the Pandavas built Indraprastha.
These events form the Vaivahika (wedding), Viduragamana (Vidura's coming) and Rajyalabha (gaining the kingdom) sub-parvas of the Adi Parva.

Founding of Indraprastha: Dhritarashtra gave the Pandavas Khandavaprastha, and with Krishna's help they built a city there named Indraprastha, described in the epic as rich, walled and moated, with broad streets and splendid buildings.
Some retellings say the divine architect Vishvakarma built Indraprastha at Indra's command; the Critical Edition describes the city's building more generally.
Indraprastha is traditionally identified with the area of present-day Delhi, often with the site of the Purana Qila; the epic itself gives no map coordinates.
Yudhishthira ruled Indraprastha justly, and the epic describes the kingdom as prosperous and well-governed under him.
Arjuna's Exile, Pilgrimage and Marriages: Under Narada's rule Arjuna left Indraprastha on a twelve-year exile and pilgrimage after intruding on Yudhishthira and Draupadi to fetch his weapons for a brahmin.
At the Ganga, Ulupi, a Naga princess, drew Arjuna to the Naga realm and married him; their son was Iravat (Iravan).
At Manipura Arjuna married Chitrangada, the king's only daughter, on condition that her son would stay to continue her father's line; their son was Babhruvahana.
In the far south Arjuna freed five apsaras who had been cursed to live as crocodiles in sacred bathing places.
At Prabhasa and Dvaraka, with Krishna's encouragement, Arjuna carried off Subhadra, Krishna's sister; Balarama was angry at first but was reconciled, and the marriage was celebrated.
Subhadra's son by Arjuna was Abhimanyu, later married to Uttara, princess of Virata, and father of Parikshit.
Draupadi was hurt at first by Arjuna's marriage to Subhadra; Subhadra came to her dressed as a cowherd woman and won her acceptance.
These events are told in the Arjuna-vanavasa, Subhadra-harana and Harana-harika sub-parvas of the Adi Parva.
Burning of the Khandava Forest: Agni, the fire god, had become sick from consuming too much ghee offered in King Shvetaki's sacrifices, and was told by Brahma that eating the creatures and plants of the Khandava forest would cure him.

The vulgate expands the Shvetaki story at length (including a twelve-year rite and the sage Durvasa serving as priest); much of this elaboration is not in the Critical Edition's main text, so its details should be treated as variant material.
Agni had tried seven times to burn Khandava, but Indra protected it because his friend the Naga Takshaka lived there, and put out the fires with rain.
Agni came to Krishna and Arjuna, picnicking on the bank of the Yamuna, disguised as a brahmin, and asked them to help him burn the forest.

To equip them, Varuna gave Arjuna the Gandiva bow, two inexhaustible quivers and a chariot with white horses and a monkey banner (kapidhvaja); Krishna received the Sudarshana discus and the mace Kaumodaki.

Krishna and Arjuna circled the forest in their chariots and shot down creatures that tried to escape, while fighting off Indra and the gods; Indra finally withdrew, and a heavenly voice told him Takshaka was away at Kurukshetra.
The epic says the fire burned for fifteen days, and that only six beings escaped: Takshaka's son Ashvasena, the asura Maya, and four Sharngaka birds, sons of the sage Mandapala and the bird Jarita.
Number facts — Khandava: Agni's failed attempts before 7 | Days the fire burned 15 | Survivors named 6 (Ashvasena 1, Maya 1, Sharngaka birds 4).
Indra was pleased with Arjuna and promised him divine weapons once Arjuna had pleased Shiva; Krishna asked for eternal friendship with Arjuna.

Takshaka's son Ashvasena, whose mother died in the fire, bears a lasting grudge: in the Karna Parva he enters Karna's arrow to strike Arjuna, and Krishna saves Arjuna by pressing the chariot down so the arrow only knocks off his diadem.

In the frame story Takshaka later kills Arjuna's grandson Parikshit, but the epic gives a sage's curse (by Shringin, son of Shamika) as the cause, not the Khandava fire; linking the two as revenge is an interpretation.

Modern readers often see the Khandava burning as ethically troubling, and some scholars read it as a mythic memory of clearing forest land for settlement; these are interpretations, not statements of the text.
Maya and the Maya Sabha: The asura architect Maya, spared by Arjuna during the Khandava fire, offered to build something in gratitude, and at Krishna's suggestion built an assembly hall (sabha) for Yudhishthira.
Maya brought materials from the lake Bindusaras near Mount Kailasa, including a great mace that he gave to Bhima and the conch Devadatta that he gave to Arjuna.
