Bhishma teaches that the king must wield the rod of punishment (danda) justly, since without danda the strong would devour the weak.
Rajadharma covers the appointment and testing of ministers, the use of spies, the protection of treasury and fortress, diplomacy, alliances, war and the treatment of conquered peoples.

Rajadharma teaching emphasises that the king should tax moderately, like a bee taking honey without harming the flower, or a calf drinking milk without hurting the cow; a sixth share of produce is the traditional royal portion in Indian dharma literature.
Bhishma lists qualities of a good king including truthfulness, self-control, generosity, accessibility, readiness to act and care for the weak, widows, the old and the poor.
Rajadharma acknowledges hard political realities: Bhishma discusses deceit toward enemies, secret policy and when a king may use crookedness, an unresolved tension with the ideal of truthfulness.
Bhishma includes the seven limbs of the state (king, ministers, territory, fortress, treasury, army, allies), a scheme shared with the Arthashastra tradition.
Rajadharma names classical teachers of statecraft such as Brihaspati and Ushanas (Shukra), whose views Bhishma cites.
Rajadharma — Origins of Kingship and the: Bhishma explains the origin of kingship in the Shanti Parva: in an age without kings, people preyed on one another like big fish eating small (matsya-nyaya), so they sought a king to protect them.
In one Shanti Parva account the people approach Manu to be their king, offering a share of their produce in return for protection.
Bhishma also recounts the story of the wicked king Vena, killed by sages for his unrighteousness, from whose body the righteous king Prithu was produced; the earth was named Prithvi after Prithu.
Bhishma describes Danda (the rod of punishment) as a quasi-divine force created to uphold dharma, without which society collapses.
Bhishma states in a well-known passage that the king makes the age: whether the age is Krita or Kali depends on the king's conduct.
A passage in the Anushasana Parva holds that subjects may justly rise against a king who fails to protect them, one of the epic's limits on royal power.
Apaddharma — Dharma in Times of Distress: Apaddharma, the second section of the Shanti Parva, discusses what is permissible in emergencies (apad), when normal rules cannot be followed without catastrophe.

In the apaddharma story of Vishvamitra and the outcaste (chandala), the starving sage Vishvamitra, during a long famine, steals dog's flesh to survive and argues that preserving life in extremity can justify breaking normal rules.

In the apaddharma fable of the cat and the mouse, the mouse Palita makes a temporary alliance with the cat Lomasha to escape an owl and a mongoose, then wisely ends the friendship once the danger passes; the moral concerns prudent alliances with enemies.
The fable of the three fish in the Apaddharma contrasts a fish that plans ahead, one that improvises in the moment and one that procrastinates and perishes.

The story of the pigeon and the fowler (Shanti Parva) tells of a pigeon who offers his own body as hospitality to the fowler who had caught his mate, after which the fowler renounces his violent life.
The story of the ungrateful brahmin Gautama and the crane Rajadharma (Nadijangha) in the Shanti Parva condemns ingratitude as the worst of offences.
Apaddharma teaching insists that emergency measures are temporary and should be atoned for once normal conditions return.
Apaddharma shows the epic's view of dharma as context-sensitive rather than a fixed code, a theme also captured by the phrase dharma-sukshma (the subtlety of dharma).
Mokshadharma — Liberation and Philosophy: Mokshadharma, the third and largest section of the Shanti Parva, turns from worldly duty to liberation (moksha) from the cycle of rebirth.
Mokshadharma contains extensive discussions of Samkhya (the enumeration of principles, including the distinction between spirit, purusha, and matter, prakriti) and of Yoga practice.

The Narayaniya, a section within the Mokshadharma, describes Narada's journey to Shvetadvipa (the White Island) and the worship of Narayana; it is an important early source for the Pancharatra (Bhagavata) tradition.
The Narayaniya names five systems of knowledge: Samkhya, Yoga, Pancharatra, the Vedas (including Aranyakas) and Pashupata.
The Mokshadharma tells the story of Shuka, son of Vyasa, who seeks liberation, is sent to King Janaka of Mithila for instruction, and finally attains release.
King Janaka of Mithila is quoted in the Mokshadharma as saying, in substance, that if Mithila were burning nothing of his own would burn, an emblem of detachment amid kingship.

In the Mokshadharma, the female ascetic Sulabha debates King Janaka and challenges his claim to be liberated while still attached to kingship; the dialogue is often cited in discussions of women's voices in the epic.
Other Mokshadharma dialogues include Bhrigu and Bharadvaja on creation and the elements, and Yajnavalkya instructing Janaka.
Mokshadharma teachings often stress renunciation of desire, equanimity in pleasure and pain, and knowledge as the means of release, standing in tension with the activist rajadharma of the same book.
Embedded 'Gitas' and Wisdom Dialogues: Beyond the Bhagavad Gita, the Mahabharata contains several shorter teachings traditionally called 'gitas', many of them in the Shanti Parva.

Gitas traditionally located in the Shanti Parva include the Pingala Gita (sayings of the courtesan Pingala, who found peace by abandoning hope), the Manki Gita, the Bodhya Gita, the Hamsa Gita, the Vritra Gita and the Parashara Gita.
The Bodhya Gita teaches detachment through lessons the sage Bodhya learned from several 'teachers', among them Pingala, an osprey, a serpent and an arrow-maker.
The Vritra Gita presents the demon Vritra, defeated by Indra, as a philosopher who accepts his fall with insight into the cycle of existence.
In the Tuladhara–Jajali dialogue (Shanti Parva), the merchant Tuladhara teaches the proud ascetic Jajali that non-harm (ahimsa) and fair dealing with all beings are higher than ascetic display.
The Anugita in the Ashvamedhika Parva and the Vidura Niti and Sanatsujatiya in the Udyoga Parva are other major wisdom texts embedded in the epic.
Lists of 'Mahabharata gitas' are traditional and vary in number; not all were labelled 'gita' in the text itself.
Anushasana Parva — Instruction on Gifts,: The Anushasana Parva ('Book of Instruction') continues Bhishma's teaching after the Shanti Parva, with emphasis on gifts (dana), duties of the social orders, rites and the glory of brahmins and gods.

The Anushasana Parva opens with the story of Gautami, a hunter, a snake, Death (Mrityu) and Time (Kala), who debate who is responsible for a boy's death, concluding that a person's own past karma is decisive.

Anushasana Parva chapter 6 (in standard references) presents a dialogue on destiny (daiva) versus human effort (purushakara), using an agricultural simile of seed and field to argue that destiny bears fruit only with human effort.

The story of King Bhangasvana in the Anushasana Parva tells of a king transformed into a woman who, when offered the choice to return, chose to remain a woman, saying women's pleasure is greater; it is often discussed in modern gender readings.
The Anushasana Parva contains extended praise of gifts of cows, land, food, gold and water, and accounts of the merit of pilgrimage sites (tirthas).
The Anushasana Parva includes a thousand-name hymn of Shiva (Shiva Sahasranama) taught by Krishna, who recounts the sage Upamanyu's devotion to Shiva.
The Anushasana Parva includes the Uma–Maheshvara dialogue, in which Shiva instructs Parvati on dharma; scholars generally regard it as late material.

Other Anushasana stories include Ashtavakra's test by the northern goddess Disha, Nachiketa's report of Yama's realm, and Sudarshana and Oghavati, whose hospitality to the disguised god Dharma conquers Death.
The Anushasana Parva closes with Bhishma's farewell and death.
Vishnu Sahasranama: The Vishnu Sahasranama ('Thousand Names of Vishnu') is part of the Anushasana Parva, taught by Bhishma to Yudhishthira.
Location of the Vishnu Sahasranama as commonly cited: Critical Edition Anushasana Parva 13.135 | vulgate (e.g. Gita Press) Anushasana Parva 13.149

Yudhishthira opens the Vishnu Sahasranama by asking six questions: who is the one god, what is the one supreme refuge, by praising whom and worshipping whom humans attain good, what is the highest dharma, and by repeating what is one freed from the bondage of birth and rebirth.
Number of questions Yudhishthira asks at the start of the Vishnu Sahasranama: 6
Bhishma answers Yudhishthira that the supreme deity is Vishnu, and recites the thousand names, which identify Vishnu with the highest reality.
A commentary on the Vishnu Sahasranama is attributed to Adi Shankara; Parashara Bhattar wrote an influential Sri Vaishnava commentary (Bhagavad Guna Darpana) in the twelfth century.
The Vishnu Sahasranama is among the most widely recited hymns in Hindu devotional practice; some names occur more than once, a point discussed by commentators.
The Vishnu Sahasranama is included in the Critical Edition's constituted text, although scholars generally treat the Anushasana Parva as a whole as relatively late.
Bhishma's Death and Uttarayana: When the sun turned north, Yudhishthira returned with the family, Krishna and priests to Kurukshetra, bringing materials for Bhishma's funeral.
Bhishma took leave of all, asked Yudhishthira to treat Dhritarashtra as a father, and by yogic control released his life-breaths, which rose through the crown of his head.
The Kurus cremated Bhishma and then went to the Ganga to offer water for him, and the goddess Ganga, his mother, emerged from the river lamenting her son.
Ganga lamented that her son had been brought down by Shikhandi; Krishna consoled her, saying that Bhishma had attained heaven and had in truth been felled by Arjuna, as destined.
Bhishma's dying in uttarayana became a classic example of the belief that dying in the sun's northern course leads to a higher destination, an idea also found in Bhagavad Gita 8.24.
Anugita and Teaching in the Ashvamedhika: The Anugita ('after-song') is a teaching in the Ashvamedhika Parva, given by Krishna to Arjuna after the war.

In the Anugita frame, Arjuna confesses that he has forgotten what Krishna taught him on the battlefield; Krishna rebukes him and says he cannot repeat the Bhagavad Gita, being then in a state of yogic absorption, but teaches him again through old stories.

The Anugita includes a dialogue between a sage Kashyapa and a perfected being (siddha), a brahmin's dialogue with his wife (often called the Brahmana Gita), and a teacher-disciple dialogue on Samkhya-Yoga themes.
The Anugita is generally regarded as less integrated and later than the Bhagavad Gita and focuses more on renunciation and knowledge than on action in battle.
Parva of Each Major Teaching: Parva numbers of major teachings embedded in the Mahabharata: Yaksha Prashna 3 | Dharmavyadha teaching 3 | Vidura Niti 5 | Sanatsujatiya 5 | Bhagavad Gita 6 | Vidura's man-in-the-well parable 11 | Rajadharma 12 | Apaddharma 12 | Mokshadharma 12 | Narayaniya 12 | Shiva Sahasranama 13 | Vishnu Sahasranama 13 | Anugita 14

Parva names of major teachings: Yaksha Prashna – Vana (Aranyaka) Parva | Vidura Niti and Sanatsujatiya – Udyoga Parva | Bhagavad Gita – Bhishma Parva | man in the well – Stri Parva | Rajadharma, Apaddharma, Mokshadharma, Narayaniya – Shanti Parva | Vishnu and Shiva Sahasranamas – Anushasana Parva | Anugita – Ashvamedhika Parva
The Bhagavad Gita occupies chapters 23–40 of the Bhishma Parva in the Critical Edition (chapters 25–42 in the vulgate), eighteen chapters in all.

Teachers of the major embedded teachings: Bhagavad Gita – Krishna to Arjuna | Anugita – Krishna to Arjuna | Shanti and Anushasana – Bhishma to Yudhishthira | Vidura Niti – Vidura to Dhritarashtra | Sanatsujatiya – the sage Sanatsujata to Dhritarashtra | Yaksha Prashna – the Yaksha (Dharma) questioning Yudhishthira
Debates on the Didactic Books: Many scholars regard large parts of the Shanti and Anushasana Parvas as later expansions added to the narrative core, though others argue the didactic material is integral to the epic's design.
V. S. Sukthankar argued that the epic underwent a 'Bhrguization', a reworking by brahmins of the Bhrigu clan who added much didactic and mythological material (The Bhrgus and the Bharata, 1936).

James L. Fitzgerald has argued that the epic, including the Shanti Parva's teachings on kingship and violence, was shaped partly as a brahminical response to the Mauryan (especially Ashokan) political world; this is a scholarly hypothesis, not a settled conclusion.
The Anushasana Parva is widely considered among the latest parts of the Mahabharata, partly because of its sectarian hymns and its emphasis on gifts to brahmins.
The post-war didactic books make the Mahabharata a 'dharma-shastra' as well as an epic; the text itself claims to be a treatise on dharma, artha, kama and moksha.

Post-War Timeline in Years: Post-war timeline as stated or implied in the epic (years after the war): Dhritarashtra leaves for the forest ~15 | Yadava destruction and Krishna's death 36 | Pandavas' final journey shortly after 36
Dhritarashtra lived in Hastinapura under Yudhishthira's care for fifteen years after the war before retiring to the forest (Ashramavasika Parva).
Years Dhritarashtra lived at Hastinapura after the war: 15
The Mausala Parva opens in the thirty-sixth year after the war, fulfilling Gandhari's curse of Krishna.

Yudhishthira's reign of about thirty-six years is a traditional figure inferred from the Mausala Parva timing; the epic does not give a separate exact regnal count, so the number should be treated as approximate.

The deaths of Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti in a forest fire came some years after they retired; summaries commonly place the fire about two to three years after their departure, and the exact interval is not consistently given.
Traditional Hindu chronology links Krishna's departure from the world with the beginning of the Kali Yuga, conventionally dated to 3102 BCE; this is a traditional reckoning, not a historical date.
Elders Retire to the Forest and Vidura's: In the Ashramavasika Parva, Dhritarashtra, hurt by Bhima's occasional harsh words and weary of life, asked Yudhishthira's permission to retire to the forest as a vanaprastha (forest-dweller).
Gandhari accompanied Dhritarashtra to the forest, and Kunti, refusing her sons' pleas to stay, chose to go with them to serve the elders.
Kunti explained that she had urged her sons to fight for their kingdom out of duty, not because she wanted to enjoy royal comforts, and now wished to live in austerity.
Vidura and Sanjaya also went to the forest with Dhritarashtra.
Before leaving, Dhritarashtra asked for wealth to perform funeral offerings (shraddha) for his sons and for Bhishma and others; Yudhishthira and Arjuna supported this, while Bhima at first objected.
The elders lived in an ashram in the forest near Kurukshetra (the hermitage of the royal sage Shatayupa is named), practising severe austerities.
Sub-books of the Ashramavasika Parva: Ashramavasa (life in the hermitage) | Putradarshana (seeing the sons) | Naradagamana (Narada's arrival with news of the fire)
When the Pandavas visited the elders in the forest, Yudhishthira found Vidura emaciated by austerities and followed him into the woods.
Vidura, standing against a tree, fixed his gaze on Yudhishthira and by yogic power passed his life-breath and senses into Yudhishthira's body, leaving his own body lifeless.
Vidura's merging into Yudhishthira reflects the epic's teaching that both were born of Dharma: Vidura as an incarnation of Dharma (Yama) cursed by the sage Mandavya, and Yudhishthira as Dharma's son.
A voice instructed Yudhishthira not to cremate Vidura's body, since Vidura had attained the state of a renunciant.
Vyasa Raises the Dead for One Night: In the Putradarshana section of the Ashramavasika Parva, Vyasa summoned the dead warriors of both armies from the waters of the Ganga for a single night so that the bereaved could see them.
On the night of the reunion, the dead warriors appeared free of enmity and anger, and Dhritarashtra, given sight by Vyasa, saw his sons; Kunti saw Karna, and Draupadi saw her sons and brothers.
At dawn the dead departed, and Vyasa allowed widows who wished to join their husbands to enter the Ganga and attain their husbands' worlds.
The one-night reunion is one of the epic's most consoling scenes and provides a kind of reconciliation between the living and the dead before the final books.
In the Mahabharata frame, Janamejaya hears of this event and asks to see his own father Parikshit; Vyasa grants this, a sign of the frame narrative intersecting with the story.
Forest Fire: Deaths of Dhritarashtra, Ga: Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti died in a forest fire while practising austerities; the fire arose from Dhritarashtra's own sacrificial fires, which had been left to spread in the forest.
Facing the forest fire, Dhritarashtra sent Sanjaya away to save himself and sat with Gandhari and Kunti in meditation, facing east, accepting death.
Sanjaya escaped the forest fire and went to the Himalaya as an ascetic, according to the Ashramavasika Parva.
The sage Narada brought news of the forest fire to Yudhishthira, who lamented especially for Kunti; this section is the Naradagamana.
Narada reassured Yudhishthira that the elders had died in fire from their own sacrificial fires and attained a good end; Yudhishthira then performed their funeral rites and water offerings.

Elders' fates in the Ashramavasika Parva: Dhritarashtra – died in forest fire | Gandhari – died in forest fire | Kunti – died in forest fire | Vidura – entered Yudhishthira by yoga | Sanjaya – escaped to the Himalaya
Mausala Parva — Omens and the Curse on t: The Mausala Parva ('Book of the Clubs') narrates the self-destruction of the Yadava (Vrishni, Andhaka and Bhoja) clans of Dwaraka in the thirty-sixth year after the war.
Evil omens appeared in Dwaraka before the Yadava destruction: strange winds, rats, disordered birds and animals, and disturbances in households.
Yadava youths mocked the visiting sages Vishvamitra, Kanva and Narada by dressing Samba, son of Krishna and Jambavati, as a pregnant woman and asking what child she would bear.
The insulted sages cursed the Yadavas: Samba would bring forth an iron club (musala) that would destroy the race, with only Balarama and Krishna escaping its direct effect.
Samba produced an iron club the next day; King Ugrasena had it ground to powder and cast into the sea, and Dwaraka banned intoxicating drink.

In the Mausala Parva the eraka grass on the shore turns into iron clubs through the sages' curse; later retellings such as the Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas make the iron powder cast into the sea grow into those reeds.

Puranic retellings such as the Bhagavata and Vishnu Puranas add that a leftover lump of iron was swallowed by a fish and made into the arrowhead of the hunter Jara; this detail is not part of the Mausala Parva's own account.
Krishna, recognising that Gandhari's curse was coming true, did not prevent the destruction.
Prabhasa — Yadava Self-Destruction: The Yadavas went on pilgrimage to Prabhasa by the sea, where they drank heavily despite the ban.
At Prabhasa, Satyaki mocked Kritavarma for slaughtering sleeping men in the Sauptika night massacre, and Pradyumna supported Satyaki.
Kritavarma retorted by reproaching Satyaki for killing Bhurishravas, whose arm had been cut off and who was seated in meditation (prayopavesha) on the battlefield.
Satyaki beheaded Kritavarma at Prabhasa, and the Bhoja and Andhaka Yadavas then killed Satyaki and Pradyumna.
Krishna plucked a handful of eraka grass that turned into an iron club, and the eraka reeds in every Yadava's hand became clubs; the Yadavas slaughtered one another, fathers and sons alike.
Krishna's son Pradyumna, his grandson Aniruddha, Samba, Charudeshna, Gada and other Yadava heroes died at Prabhasa; Krishna's great-grandson Vajra survived and was later installed at Indraprastha.
The Yadava self-destruction at Prabhasa mirrors the Kurukshetra war in miniature: kin killing kin, and the war's unresolved crimes (the night massacre, Bhurishravas' death) resurfacing as quarrels.
Deaths of Balarama and Krishna: Balarama withdrew into yogic meditation, and from his mouth a great white serpent (understood as Shesha, whose incarnation he was) emerged and entered the ocean, received by the Nagas.
Krishna sent his charioteer Daruka to Hastinapura to summon Arjuna to protect the Yadava women, and arranged the protection of the women in Dwaraka.
Krishna took leave of his father Vasudeva and went to the forest, where he lay down in yogic meditation.

A hunter named Jara ('old age'), mistaking Krishna for a deer, shot him in the sole of the foot with an arrow; Krishna consoled the horrified hunter and then ascended to heaven, filling the sky with radiance.
Krishna's death by Jara's arrow fulfils Gandhari's curse that he would die alone in the forest by ignoble means.

Popular later tradition (not the Mahabharata or the major Puranic accounts of Krishna's death) adds that Jara was a rebirth of the monkey-king Vali, whom Rama had shot from hiding, so that Krishna's death settled that old account.
The Bhagavata Purana tradition holds that Krishna lived 125 years; the Mahabharata does not state his age at death, so this figure should be treated as Puranic.
Krishna's father Vasudeva died soon after, and Arjuna performed his funeral rites; some of Vasudeva's wives joined his pyre.
Arjuna at Dwaraka — Evacuation, Submerge: Arjuna came to Dwaraka at Krishna's summons, lamented over the destroyed Yadavas, and led the surviving women, children and elders out of the city toward Indraprastha.
After the survivors left, the ocean flooded and submerged Dwaraka; the Mausala Parva describes the sea engulfing the city as they watched.
In the region of the five rivers (Panchanada), Abhira herdsmen-robbers attacked Arjuna's convoy.
Arjuna found that he could barely string the Gandiva bow, could not recall his celestial weapons, and that his once-inexhaustible arrows ran out; the robbers carried off many of the women.
Arjuna's loss of power at Panchanada is the epic's starkest image of decline: the greatest archer of the war is helpless once Krishna is gone and his time has passed.
Of Krishna's wives, the Mausala Parva says some, including Rukmini and Jambavati, entered the funeral fire, while Satyabhama and others went to the forest for austerities.
Arjuna went to Vyasa, who told him that time (kala) is the root of all things, that the Yadavas' end was destined, and that the Pandavas' purpose was fulfilled and it was time for them to depart.

According to the Mausala Parva, Arjuna settled Krishna's great-grandson Vajra at Indraprastha, Kritavarma's son with the remaining Bhoja people at the city of Martikavata, and Satyaki's son by the river Sarasvati.
Succession: Parikshit, Vajra and Yuyutsu: Before the final journey, Yudhishthira crowned Parikshit, Abhimanyu's son, as king of Hastinapura (Mahaprasthanika Parva).
Yudhishthira confirmed Vajra, Krishna's great-grandson through Pradyumna and Aniruddha, as king at Indraprastha, where Arjuna had already settled him.
Yudhishthira entrusted the kingdom's management to Yuyutsu and placed Parikshit under the guidance of Kripa as teacher, asking Subhadra to protect the young king.
Yudhishthira performed funeral offerings for Krishna, Balarama and the departed elders and made generous gifts before departing.
Ulupi entered the Ganga and Chitrangada returned to Manipura when the Pandavas departed, according to the Mahaprasthanika Parva.
Heirs after the Pandavas: Hastinapura – Parikshit (Kuru line) | Indraprastha – Vajra (Yadava line) | regent-adviser – Yuyutsu | royal teacher – Kripa
Mahaprasthanika — Departure and Route: In the Mahaprasthanika Parva ('Book of the Great Departure'), the five Pandavas and Draupadi renounced the kingdom, dressed as ascetics in bark garments, and set out on foot; a dog followed them from Hastinapura.
The citizens followed the departing Pandavas for some distance before returning.

The Pandavas first went east to the Lauhitya (red) sea, where Agni appeared and asked Arjuna to give up the Gandiva bow and the inexhaustible quivers to Varuna, from whom they had come; Arjuna cast them into the water.
From the east the Pandavas turned south, then southwest, then west, where they saw Dwaraka covered by the sea, and then turned north.
Route of the Pandavas' final journey: east (Lauhitya sea) → south → southwest → west (submerged Dwaraka) → north → Himalaya → great sand desert → Mount Meru
The route amounts to a clockwise circuit of the earth (east, south, west, then north), resembling a ritual circumambulation (pradakshina) before the ascent into the Himalaya.
Crossing the Himalaya, the Pandavas saw a vast sand desert and then the great mountain Meru, where they began to fall one by one.
Order of Falling and Yudhishthira's Reas: In the Mahaprasthanika Parva, the companions fall one by one in this order: Draupadi first, then Sahadeva, Nakula, Arjuna and finally Bhima; only Yudhishthira and the dog continue.
Order of falling on the final journey (1 = first): Draupadi 1 | Sahadeva 2 | Nakula 3 | Arjuna 4 | Bhima 5
At each fall, Bhima asks Yudhishthira why, and Yudhishthira gives a reason; Yudhishthira himself does not look back.
Draupadi fell first because, Yudhishthira said, she was partial to Arjuna above her other husbands.
Sahadeva fell second because, Yudhishthira said, he thought no one equal to him in wisdom.
Nakula fell third because, Yudhishthira said, he thought no one equal to him in beauty.
Arjuna fell fourth because, Yudhishthira said, he had boasted he would burn all enemies in a single day and did not, and he disregarded other archers.
Bhima fell fifth and, as he fell, asked the reason for his own fall; Yudhishthira said he had eaten too much and boasted of his strength without regard for others.

Reasons for falling given by Yudhishthira: Draupadi – partiality to Arjuna | Sahadeva – pride in wisdom | Nakula – pride in beauty | Arjuna – boastfulness about destroying enemies, disdain for other archers | Bhima – gluttony and boasting of strength
Many readers find Yudhishthira's verdicts harsh, especially toward Draupadi, and modern interpreters read the scene as revealing Yudhishthira's own coldness as much as the faults of the fallen.
The Dog Revealed as Dharma: When only Yudhishthira and the dog remained, Indra arrived in his chariot to take Yudhishthira to heaven in his bodily form.
Yudhishthira refused to enter heaven without his brothers and Draupadi; Indra told him they had already gone ahead, having cast off their human bodies.
Indra told Yudhishthira that there was no place in heaven for people with dogs and that he must leave the dog behind.

Yudhishthira refused to abandon the dog, saying that abandoning one who is devoted and seeks protection is as great a sin as killing a brahmin, and that he would never give up a devoted companion even for heaven.
The dog then revealed itself as Dharma (Yama), Yudhishthira's divine father, who praised his compassion and loyalty.
Dharma had tested Yudhishthira before, as the Yaksha at the lake in the Vana Parva (Yaksha Prashna); the dog was the second test, and the vision of hell in the Svargarohana Parva is the third.
Tests of Yudhishthira by Dharma: 1 – Yaksha at the lake (Vana Parva) | 2 – the dog (Mahaprasthanika Parva) | 3 – the illusion of hell (Svargarohana Parva)

Yudhishthira then ascended to heaven in Indra's chariot in his human body, whereas his brothers and Draupadi had to cast off their bodies (Arjuna had, however, visited Indra's heaven bodily during the exile, in the Vana Parva).
Svargarohana — Duryodhana in Heaven and: In the Svargarohana Parva ('Book of the Ascent to Heaven'), Yudhishthira found Duryodhana seated in splendour in heaven and was indignant, refusing to share heaven with the man who caused the war.
Narada told Yudhishthira that Duryodhana had attained heaven by kshatriya dharma, having died fearlessly in battle at the holy field of Kurukshetra, and that enmity has no place in heaven.
Yudhishthira asked to see his brothers, Draupadi and Karna, and declared that heaven without them was not heaven to him.
A divine messenger led Yudhishthira down a dark, foul and frightening path; when he turned to go back, voices begged him to stay, since his presence brought them relief.

The voices in hell identified themselves as Karna, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva, Dhrishtadyumna, Draupadi and Draupadi's sons; Yudhishthira, angry at the gods and at dharma, chose to stay with them.
Indra and Dharma then appeared, and the vision of hell vanished; Indra explained that it had been an illusion (maya).
Indra explained that every king must see hell, and that Yudhishthira was shown hell by a deception because he had deceived Drona about the death of Ashwatthama.
Yudhishthira bathed in the celestial Ganga (Mandakini), cast off his human body, and with it his grief and enmity.
Final Reconciliation — Heroes Return to: After his bath in the celestial Ganga, Yudhishthira saw his family and the heroes of both sides in divine forms, reconciled.
Yudhishthira saw Krishna in his divine form as Vishnu (Govinda), with Arjuna attending him.

Divine identities revealed in the Svargarohana Parva: Krishna – Vishnu/Narayana | Arjuna – attending Krishna (traditionally understood as Nara beside Narayana) | Karna – among the Adityas, with Surya | Bhima – with Vayu and the Maruts | Nakula and Sahadeva – with the Ashvins | Draupadi – Shri (Lakshmi) | Abhimanyu – with Soma (the Moon) | Bhishma – among the Vasus | Drona – with Brihaspati | Vidura and Yudhishthira – with Dharma
Svargarohana's ending matches the Adi Parva's list of partial incarnations (amshavatarana), in which the epic's heroes are portions of gods and demons who return to their sources at death.

According to the Adi Parva's incarnation list, Duryodhana was a portion of Kali and Shakuni of Dvapara, the personifications of the late world-ages; the Svargarohana's closing summary likewise sends each hero, Kauravas included, back to the being of which he was a portion.
The epic's conclusion presents war, curse and enmity as ultimately part of a cosmic drama, while still having Yudhishthira's anger and choice to stay in hell show that the human cost was real.
At the close of the Svargarohana Parva, Vyasa laments in a famous verse that he cries out with raised arms but no one listens: from dharma come wealth and pleasure, so why is dharma not pursued.
The closing verses (the 'Bharata Savitri') also urge that dharma should never be abandoned for desire, fear, greed or even to save one's life.
The Mahabharata ends with Vaishampayana completing his narration at Janamejaya's snake sacrifice and Ugrashravas completing his retelling to the sages of the Naimisha forest, closing both frames.

How Places Are Described Here: Places in this graph are described as the Mahabharata describes them; their real-world locations are not proven.
Modern sites are mentioned only as traditional identifications, often supported by local tradition, place names or archaeology, but none confirms that the epic's events happened there.

The epic's geography centres on the upper Ganga-Yamuna plain (the Kuru-Panchala region), with journeys reaching the Himalaya, the western coast at Dwaraka, and eastern kingdoms such as Magadha and Anga.

Epic regions (approximate): north — Himalaya, Gandhara, Madra | upper Ganga plain — Hastinapura, Indraprastha, Kurukshetra, Panchala, Naimisharanya, Varanavata | west — Dwaraka, Prabhasa, Matsya, Sindhu | east — Magadha, Anga, Kashi, and (by some local traditions; location uncertain) Ekachakra.
Many places in the epic, especially sacred fords (tirthas) on the pilgrimage of the Vana Parva, have several competing local claimants.
Hastinapura: Hastinapura is the capital of the Kuru kingdom in the epic, on the bank of the Ganga, and is traditionally said to be named after King Hastin.

Hastinapura is where the Kuru princes grow up, where Drona trains them, where the princes' tournament takes place and where the dice game is held in an assembly hall that Dhritarashtra had built for the occasion.
After the war, Yudhishthira is crowned king at Hastinapura, and later Parikshit is crowned there before the Pandavas' final journey.
Hastinapura is traditionally identified with Hastinapur in Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, India.

Excavations at Hastinapur in the 1950s led by B. B. Lal found Painted Grey Ware settlement layers and evidence of a major flood, which Lal linked to a Puranic account (not the Mahabharata itself) that a later king moved the capital to Kaushambi after the Ganga washed Hastinapura away; this link is debated.
Story locations within Hastinapura: royal palace | assembly hall (sabha) | training ground of Drona | tournament arena | the dice hall.
Indraprastha and Khandavaprastha: Indraprastha is the city the Pandavas build on the Yamuna after Dhritarashtra gives them half the kingdom, the wild region of Khandavaprastha.
Arjuna and Krishna help the fire god Agni burn the Khandava forest, sparing the demon architect Maya, who in gratitude builds a magnificent assembly hall (the Maya Sabha) for Yudhishthira.

Yudhishthira performs the Rajasuya sacrifice at Indraprastha, where Shishupala is killed; Duryodhana, envious of the Pandavas' wealth and humiliated when the hall's illusions make him mistake floor for water and water for floor, returns home resentful (the popular line in which Draupadi mocks him as a blind man's son is not in the Critical Edition).

Indraprastha is traditionally identified with the area of the Purana Qila (Old Fort) in Delhi, India, where excavations found Painted Grey Ware sherds; whether this identification is correct is debated.
After the Yadava destruction, Arjuna brings the surviving Yadavas to Indraprastha, and Krishna's great-grandson Vajra is made its king.
Story events at Indraprastha: Khandava burning | founding of the city | Maya Sabha | Jarasandha's killing planned | Rajasuya | Shishupala's death.
Kurukshetra: Kurukshetra ('the field of Kuru') is the plain where the 18-day war is fought; the first verse of the Bhagavad Gita calls it dharmakshetra, 'the field of dharma'.
Kurukshetra was sacred long before the war: Vedic texts describe it as a place of sacrifice, and the epic says King Kuru tilled it to make it holy.
The epic associates Kurukshetra with Samantapanchaka, the five lakes that Parashurama filled with the blood of the kshatriyas he slew, according to the Adi Parva.
The epic places Kurukshetra in the region between the Sarasvati and Drishadvati rivers; the Pandava army camps near the river Hiranvati.
Armies gathered on the field of Kurukshetra: Kaurava 11 akshauhinis | Pandava 7 akshauhinis | total 18.
On the 18th day, after his army is destroyed, Duryodhana hides in a lake near the battlefield, called Dvaipayana in the Shalya Parva, before the mace duel with Bhima.
Kurukshetra is traditionally identified with the Kurukshetra region (around Thanesar) in Haryana, India, which has many pilgrimage sites linked by local tradition to the war.
Story events at Kurukshetra: the Bhagavad Gita | all 18 days of battle | Bhishma's bed of arrows | the mace duel | the night attack on the camp | the women's lament and funeral rites.
Naimisharanya: Naimisharanya (the Naimisha forest) is the sacred forest where the sage Shaunaka and other sages hold a twelve-year sacrifice, and where Ugrashravas Sauti recites the Mahabharata to them.
Naimisharanya is the setting of the outermost frame of the epic, and also the frame setting of several Puranas.
The Mahabharata also mentions Naimisha as a holy place visited on pilgrimage.
Naimisharanya is traditionally identified with Nimsar (Naimisharanya) in Sitapur district, Uttar Pradesh, India, on the Gomti river.
Naimisharanya's role: it is not a site of the main story's action, but the place where the story is told.
Dwaraka and Prabhasa: Dwaraka is the fortified city of the Yadavas on the western sea, ruled by Krishna's clan; the epic and the Harivamsha say Krishna led the Yadavas there from Mathura to escape repeated attacks by Jarasandha of Magadha.
Near Dwaraka stands Mount Raivataka, where Arjuna carries off Subhadra during a festival with Krishna's approval.
In the Mausala Parva, after Krishna's departure, the sea floods and swallows Dwaraka, as Arjuna leads the survivors away.
Prabhasa, a sacred ford on the western coast, is where the Yadavas go on pilgrimage and destroy one another in a drunken brawl, and near where Krishna is struck by the hunter Jara's arrow.

Dwaraka is traditionally identified with Dwarka in Gujarat, India; underwater surveys off Dwarka and Bet Dwarka from the 1980s reported submerged structures, but their date and significance are disputed.
Prabhasa is traditionally identified with Prabhas Patan near Somnath in Gujarat, India.
Mount Raivataka is often identified with Girnar in Gujarat, though this is a traditional identification.
Panchala: Kampilya and Ahichchhatra: Panchala is the kingdom of King Drupada, east of the Kurus, divided by the Ganga into northern and southern halves.
After the Kuru princes captured Drupada as Drona's tuition fee, Drona kept northern Panchala with its capital Ahichchhatra and returned southern Panchala, with its capital Kampilya, to Drupada.
Drupada performed a sacrifice to obtain a son who could kill Drona; from it emerged Dhrishtadyumna and Draupadi.
Draupadi's svayamvara, where Arjuna wins her by hitting the target, takes place in Drupada's capital in Panchala.
Kampilya is traditionally identified with Kampil in Farrukhabad district, Uttar Pradesh, India.
Ahichchhatra is traditionally identified with the ruins near Ramnagar in Bareilly district, Uttar Pradesh, India.
Panchala division: northern half (Ahichchhatra) to Drona | southern half (Kampilya) kept by Drupada.
Matsya Kingdom: Virata and Upaplavya: Matsya is the kingdom of King Virata, where the Pandavas and Draupadi spend the thirteenth year of exile in disguise.

Pandava disguises at Virata's court: Yudhishthira as Kanka, a dice-playing courtier | Bhima as Ballava, a cook | Arjuna as Brihannala, a dance teacher living as a eunuch | Nakula as a horse-keeper (Granthika) | Sahadeva as a cowherd (Tantipala) | Draupadi as Sairandhri, a maid to Queen Sudeshna; the twins' names vary between versions.
At Virata's capital, Bhima kills Kichaka, the queen's brother and army commander, who had harassed Draupadi.

At the end of the hidden year, King Susharman of Trigarta raids Matsya's cattle from one side while the Kauravas raid from the other; Virata, aided by the disguised Pandavas, repels the Trigartas, and Arjuna, with Prince Uttara as his charioteer, defeats the Kaurava host.

Upaplavya is a town in the Matsya kingdom where the Pandavas settle after revealing themselves, where Abhimanyu marries Uttara, and from where the Pandavas conduct the peace negotiations and set out for war.
Virata's capital is traditionally identified with Bairat (Viratnagar) in northeastern Rajasthan, India (historically part of Jaipur district); the location of Upaplavya is uncertain.
Matsya is traditionally placed in the region of present-day northeastern Rajasthan (around Jaipur, Alwar and Bharatpur).
Kamyaka and Dwaita Forests: Kamyaka is a forest where the Pandavas spend much of their twelve-year exile; the epic places it near the Sarasvati river, at the edge of the desert.
Bhima kills the rakshasa Kirmira at the entrance to the Kamyaka forest early in the exile.
Jayadratha's attempt to abduct Draupadi takes place while the Pandavas are living in the Kamyaka forest.
Dwaitavana (the Dwaita forest) is a forest with a lake where the Pandavas also live during the exile, moving between it and Kamyaka.
Duryodhana's 'cattle expedition' (ghosha-yatra) to Dwaitavana, meant to flaunt his wealth before the exiled Pandavas, ends with his capture by the gandharva Chitrasena and his rescue by the Pandavas.
The Yaksha's questions to Yudhishthira take place at a lake in the forest while the Pandavas are chasing a deer that carried off a Brahmin's fire-sticks, near the end of the forest years.
Kamyaka and Dwaitavana are traditionally associated with sites in the Kurukshetra region of Haryana, though identifications are uncertain.
Forest exile locations: Kamyaka | Dwaitavana | the pilgrimage circuit of sacred fords | the Himalayan region (Gandhamadana, Badari).
Varanavata and Ekachakra: Varanavata is the town where Duryodhana's agent Purochana builds a house of lac and other flammable materials to burn the Pandavas and Kunti alive.
Warned by Vidura in veiled language, the Pandavas escape through a tunnel dug by a miner Vidura sends; they set the fire themselves, and Purochana dies in it.
A Nishada woman and her five sons who were sleeping in the house die in the fire, so the Kauravas believe the Pandavas and Kunti are dead.
Varanavata is traditionally identified with Barnawa in Baghpat district, Uttar Pradesh, India.
After the lac house, the Pandavas wander in the forest, where Bhima kills Hidimba and marries Hidimbi, and then live disguised as Brahmins in the town of Ekachakra.
At Ekachakra, Bhima kills the demon Baka (Bakasura), who demanded a human victim and food from the townspeople.
Several places, in Bihar and in West Bengal, claim to be Ekachakra in local tradition; no identification is settled.
Himalaya and the Northern Journeys: Pandu retires with Kunti and Madri to the Shatashringa ('hundred-peaked') mountain in the Himalaya, where the Pandavas are born.
During the exile, Arjuna performs austerities in the Himalaya, fights Shiva disguised as a hunter (Kirata), and receives the Pashupata weapon.
Arjuna then visits Indra's heaven, where he gains divine weapons and spends about five years, according to the Vana Parva.
On their pilgrimage the Pandavas reach the Gandhamadana mountain and the hermitage of Badari, where Bhima meets Hanuman while seeking the Saugandhika flowers for Draupadi.
In the Mahaprasthanika Parva, the Pandavas and Draupadi travel east, south and west (seeing the drowned Dwaraka) and then north into the Himalaya toward Mount Meru.
On the final Himalayan journey, Draupadi falls first, then Sahadeva, Nakula, Arjuna and Bhima; only Yudhishthira and the dog reach Indra's chariot.
Order of falling on the final journey: 1 Draupadi | 2 Sahadeva | 3 Nakula | 4 Arjuna | 5 Bhima | survives Yudhishthira (with the dog).
Badari is traditionally identified with Badrinath in Uttarakhand, India.
Rivers of the Epic: The Ganga is both a river and a goddess in the epic; as the goddess Ganga she is Bhishma's mother, and Hastinapura stands on her bank.
The Yamuna flows past Indraprastha and is where Vyasa was born on an island; Satyavati ferried travellers across it.
Karna's basket floats from the Ashva river to the Charmanvati, the Yamuna and the Ganga before he is found near Champa.
The Sarasvati river flows near the Kamyaka forest and Kurukshetra; in the Shalya Parva Balarama makes a pilgrimage along its sacred fords during the war.
The Drishadvati river, with the Sarasvati, bounds the sacred land of Kurukshetra in the epic's description.
The Hiranvati river flows near the Pandava camp at Kurukshetra.
In the Ashramavasika Parva, Vyasa makes the warriors killed in the war rise from the Ganga for one night to meet their families.
The Sarasvati is often identified with the Ghaggar-Hakra river system, a long-debated identification; the epic describes it as disappearing into the desert.
Other Kingdoms and Allied Realms: Magadha is the eastern kingdom of Jarasandha, whose capital is Girivraja; Bhima kills Jarasandha in a wrestling duel there, with Krishna and Arjuna present. Girivraja is traditionally identified with Rajgir in Bihar, India.
Anga is the eastern kingdom Duryodhana gives to Karna at the princes' tournament; its capital Champa is traditionally identified with a site near Bhagalpur in Bihar, India.
Gandhara is the north-western kingdom of Gandhari and Shakuni, traditionally identified with the region around the Peshawar valley in present-day Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan.
Madra is the north-western kingdom of Madri and Shalya, with its capital at Shakala, traditionally identified with Sialkot in present-day Pakistan.
Kashi is the kingdom of Amba, Ambika and Ambalika, with its capital at Varanasi.
Chedi is the kingdom of Shishupala, whom Krishna kills at Yudhishthira's Rajasuya.
Sindhu (Sindhu-Sauvira) is the kingdom of Jayadratha, husband of Dushala.
Mathura is the Yadava city where Krishna kills Kamsa (told mainly in the Harivamsha) before the Yadavas move to Dwaraka.
Manipura is the kingdom of Chitrangada and her son Babhruvahana; its location is disputed, and its common identification with modern Manipur is a tradition rather than an established fact.
Archaeology and Identification Debates: Many sites traditionally linked to the Mahabharata (Hastinapur, Purana Qila in Delhi, Kurukshetra, Ahichchhatra, Kampil, Mathura, Bairat) have yielded Painted Grey Ware, a pottery culture dated roughly to the late 2nd and early-to-mid 1st millennium BCE.

B. B. Lal's mid-20th-century project on 'Mahabharata sites' proposed links between Painted Grey Ware settlements and the epic's Kuru-Panchala geography; critics note that the pottery shows settlement at those places, not that the epic's events happened.
No archaeological find has been accepted by scholars as confirming any specific event, person or battle of the Mahabharata.
Proposed dates for a historical Kurukshetra war range widely, from traditional reckonings near 3102 BCE to scholarly suggestions in the early 1st millennium BCE; none is established.
The marine explorations off Dwarka reported structures and artefacts whose age and connection to the epic's Dwaraka are disputed.

Local traditions across India and beyond claim many places associated with the Pandavas, such as caves, lakes and temples said to have been visited during the exile; these are living traditions rather than historical identifications.

Dharma — Meaning and Scope: Dharma, from the Sanskrit root dhri ('to hold, support'), means the order that sustains the world and society, and by extension duty, law, righteousness and right conduct; the Mahabharata is often called a meditation on dharma.

The Mahabharata treats dharma at several levels: cosmic order, the duties of one's social class and life-stage (varnashrama-dharma), the duties of kings (rajadharma), emergency rules (apaddharma) and the dharma of liberation (mokshadharma).

Dharma is personified in the epic as the god Dharma (identified with Yama), father of Yudhishthira and source of Vidura's incarnation; he tests Yudhishthira as the Yaksha, as the dog and through the illusion of hell.
Gandhari repeatedly tells Duryodhana 'where there is dharma, there is victory' (yato dharmas tato jayah); the phrase is now the motto of the Supreme Court of India.
Yudhishthira, answering the Yaksha in the Vana Parva, says in substance that the truth of dharma is hidden as if in a cave and that the path walked by the great is the path to follow.
The epic's closing verses (the Bharata Savitri) state that wealth and pleasure flow from dharma and that dharma should never be abandoned for desire, fear, greed or even life itself.

The Mahabharata claims comprehensiveness on the aims of life: what is found here on dharma, artha, kama and moksha may be found elsewhere, but what is not here is found nowhere (Adi Parva and Svargarohana Parva).
Dharma-Sukshma — The Subtlety of Dharma: Dharma-sukshma ('dharma is subtle') expresses the Mahabharata's recognition that right action is often hard to discern and that duties conflict.

In the dice hall (Sabha Parva), Draupadi asked whether Yudhishthira, having already lost himself, had any right to stake her; Bhishma replied that dharma is subtle and he could not resolve the question, a classic instance of dharma-sukshma.

Yudhishthira's half-truth to Drona, that 'Ashwatthama' (an elephant of that name) was dead, shows dharma-sukshma: the text says his chariot, which had always floated four finger-breadths above the ground, then touched the earth.

In the Karna Parva, Krishna tells Arjuna of the ascetic Kaushika, who truthfully told robbers where fleeing villagers hid and went to hell for causing their deaths, to argue that truthfulness must be judged by its effects on the welfare of beings.

In the Karna Parva, Krishna also tells of the hunter Balaka, who killed a blind beast that had been about to destroy all creatures and so went to heaven, illustrating that outward acts must be judged in context.

Krishna's stratagems in the war (Shikhandi before Bhishma, the false news of Ashwatthama's death, Bhima's blow below the navel, Karna killed while freeing his chariot wheel) are the epic's sharpest tests of dharma-sukshma, and the epic itself debates them.
Bimal Krishna Matilal's essays (e.g. in Moral Dilemmas in the Mahabharata, 1989) and Gurcharan Das's The Difficulty of Being Good (2009) are modern studies centred on dharma-sukshma.
Dharma-sukshma is distinct from moral relativism: the epic insists dharma is real but that discerning it requires judgment, context and attention to consequences.
Karma — Action, Consequence and Rebirth: Karma in the Mahabharata means action and its consequences, which bind beings to rebirth and shape their fortunes across lifetimes.
The Anushasana Parva story of Gautami, the hunter, the snake, Death and Time argues that a being's own past karma, rather than the immediate agent, is the decisive cause of death.
The Bhagavad Gita (Bhishma Parva) teaches nishkama karma, action without attachment to its fruits, as a way to act without bondage.
Gandhari's curse of Krishna, Krishna's death by Jara's arrow and Yudhishthira's brief vision of hell all show the epic's insistence that even great or divine figures meet consequences of their acts.
Karma in the epic coexists uneasily with destiny (daiva) and time (kala); the text offers several models of causation rather than one system.
The Mausala Parva has the Yadava quarrel revive the war's unresolved deeds (the night massacre, the killing of Bhurishravas), dramatising karma as consequences that return.
Svadharma and Kshatriya-Dharma: Svadharma means one's own particular duty according to birth, role and stage of life; the Bhagavad Gita says it is better to do one's own dharma imperfectly than another's well (Gita 3.35, echoed in 18.47).

Kshatriya-dharma, the warrior's duty, includes protecting the people, never refusing a challenge to battle, not turning back in war, giving gifts and sacrificing; dying in battle is held to lead to heaven.
Kshatriya-dharma explains Duryodhana's place in heaven in the Svargarohana Parva: Narada says he won it by dying fearlessly in battle at Kurukshetra.
Yudhishthira's wish to renounce after the war is criticised by his brothers and Draupadi as a betrayal of his kshatriya svadharma.

Drona, Kripa and Ashwatthama were brahmins by birth who lived as warriors; the epic, and characters in it, sometimes criticise this mixing of roles, and Ashwatthama's night massacre is seen as its darkest result.
Karna's svadharma is ambiguous: raised as a suta (charioteer's son) but born a kshatriya to Kunti, he is repeatedly denied warrior status, a central theme in sympathetic modern readings.
The hunter-butcher Dharmavyadha in the Vana Parva teaches a brahmin that faithfully practising one's own hereditary occupation can be a path of dharma, even in a violent trade.
Yudhishthira's rule of never refusing a challenge, a kshatriya norm, is one reason he accepted the dice game (Sabha Parva).
Rules of Righteous War and Their Breache: Before the battle, the two sides agreed rules of righteous war (dharmayuddha), set out at the start of the Bhishma Parva: fighting only equals with equal weapons, not attacking those who were fleeing, unarmed, surrendering, distracted or engaged with another, and not attacking charioteers, animals or non-combatants such as drummers and conch-blowers.

Major breaches of the rules of war in the epic: the killing of Abhimanyu by several warriors together (day 13) | Arjuna cutting off the arm of Bhurishravas while he fought Satyaki (day 14) | Satyaki killing Bhurishravas while he sat in meditation (day 14) | the deception that led to Drona's death (day 15) | Arjuna killing Karna while his wheel was stuck (day 17) | Bhima striking Duryodhana's thigh below the navel (day 18) | Ashwatthama's night massacre of sleepers (after day 18)
Shikhandi being placed before Bhishma (day 10) exploited Bhishma's vow not to fight one who had been a woman; it is often listed among the war's morally questionable stratagems.
Balarama was enraged by Bhima's blow below the navel against Duryodhana; Krishna defended it by citing Bhima's vow and Duryodhana's own crimes (Shalya Parva).
The post-war books present the breaches as moral debts: Gandhari's reproaches, Yudhishthira's vision of hell and the Yadava quarrel at Prabhasa all recall them.
Modern discussions of just war theory often cite the Mahabharata's rules of war and their breaches as an early, self-critical treatment of conduct in war (jus in bello).
Rajadharma and Kingship — Legitimacy of: Rajadharma holds that the king exists to protect; a king who fails to protect forfeits legitimacy, and the stories of Vena (deposed and killed by sages) and Prithu (the ideal king) frame this idea.

The Kuru succession was contested because Dhritarashtra, the elder, was excluded from the throne for blindness and the younger Pandu ruled; Dhritarashtra later ruled after Pandu's retirement to the forest and death, and whether he held the throne as king in his own right or as a caretaker for Pandu's line is itself one of the disputed points.

Duryodhana claimed the throne as son of the reigning king Dhritarashtra, while Yudhishthira claimed it as eldest of his generation and son of Pandu, the crowned king; the epic never fully resolves the legal question.

The Pandavas were born through divine fathers by Pandu's request (a form of niyoga), and by the legal norms the epic uses they counted as Pandu's sons; Duryodhana's side at times questioned their legitimacy.

Karna, as Kunti's first-born, would have been the eldest Pandava and arguably the senior heir; Krishna offered him the throne in the Udyoga Parva, and he refused out of loyalty to Duryodhana and the family that raised him.
The Kuru lineage includes precedents for passing over elder sons: Yayati chose his youngest son Puru, and Devapi, elder brother of Shantanu, was passed over because of a skin disease.
Bhishma's vow of celibacy and renunciation of the throne for his father Shantanu's marriage to Satyavati set in motion the succession problems of later generations.
Yudhishthira's legitimacy after the war rests on victory, consecration, Bhishma's instruction and the Ashvamedha, which ritually asserted sovereignty and expiated the war.
Moksha and the Aims of Life (Purushartha: The four aims of human life (purusharthas) are dharma (righteousness), artha (wealth and power), kama (pleasure and desire) and moksha (liberation).

In a Shanti Parva discussion, Yudhishthira asks which aim is best: Vidura praises dharma, Arjuna praises artha, the twins praise dharma joined with artha, and Bhima praises kama; Yudhishthira concludes in favour of freedom from all of them (moksha).
Moksha, liberation from the cycle of rebirth (samsara), is the subject of the Mokshadharma section of the Shanti Parva and of parts of the Bhagavad Gita and the Anugita.
The Mahabharata holds activist duty and world-renouncing liberation in tension; Yudhishthira's post-war longing for the forest dramatises this conflict.
The Bhagavad Gita's resolution, acting without attachment and offering action to God, is one of several the epic offers; the Mokshadharma also presents more renunciatory paths.
Satya — Truth: Satya (truth, truthfulness) is among the highest virtues in the Mahabharata; Yudhishthira is renowned as one who never lies, which makes his half-lie about Ashwatthama so significant.
Yudhishthira's half-lie to Drona is recalled in the Svargarohana Parva, where Indra says Yudhishthira was shown an illusion of hell because he had deceived Drona.
The epic qualifies absolute truthfulness: Krishna argues in the Karna Parva, through the story of the ascetic Kaushika, that speech that causes harm to the innocent is not true dharma.
Bhishma's lifelong adherence to his vow (a form of truth to one's word) is both admired and shown to have tragic consequences for the Kuru line.
The epic often pairs satya with dharma, presenting truth as the foundation of dharma, while also acknowledging occasions where speaking truth would serve adharma.
Ahimsa — Non-Harm: Ahimsa (non-harm, non-violence) is praised throughout the Mahabharata; the phrase 'ahimsa paramo dharmah' ('non-harm is the highest dharma') occurs in the epic, notably in the Anushasana Parva.
The popular extension 'dharma himsa tathaiva cha' ('and so is violence in the service of dharma'), often attributed to the Mahabharata, is not found in the epic and is a modern addition.

The epic's praise of ahimsa stands in tension with kshatriya-dharma, which requires kings and warriors to use force; Arjuna's dilemma in the Gita and Yudhishthira's post-war remorse express this tension.
The merchant Tuladhara's teaching to the ascetic Jajali (Shanti Parva) and the golden mongoose episode (Ashvamedhika Parva) are prominent ahimsa-oriented passages.
Dharmavyadha, the butcher-sage of the Vana Parva, notes that complete non-harm is impossible since even farming and walking harm living beings, a realistic view of ahimsa.
Mahatma Gandhi read the Mahabharata and the Gita allegorically and argued that the epic shows the futility of war; this is a modern interpretation, not the only possible reading.
Daiva and Purushakara — Fate and Human E: Daiva (fate, destiny, the divine dispensation) and purushakara (human effort) are debated throughout the Mahabharata without a single final answer.
Dhritarashtra repeatedly blames fate for the destruction of his sons, a fatalism the epic often presents as an excuse for his own weakness and indulgence of Duryodhana.

In the Vana Parva, Draupadi argues against Yudhishthira's patience, criticising the Creator as unjust and urging human effort; Yudhishthira replies that dharma should be followed for its own sake, not for reward.
The Anushasana Parva dialogue on daiva and purushakara uses the simile of seed and field to argue that destiny bears fruit only through human effort.

Kala (Time) is presented as an overwhelming force: in the Gita Krishna declares himself Time, the destroyer of worlds (Gita 11.32), and in the Mausala Parva Vyasa tells Arjuna that time is the root of all things.

The post-war books repeatedly invoke time and destiny to console the grieving (Vidura and Vyasa to Dhritarashtra, Vyasa to Arjuna), while the didactic sections still insist on responsibility and effort.
Vows (Pratijna) and Their Consequences: Vows (pratijna) drive much of the Mahabharata's plot; a kshatriya's word, once given, was considered binding even when it led to disaster.

Bhishma's vow (Adi Parva): lifelong celibacy and renunciation of the throne so that Shantanu could marry Satyavati; it earned him the name Bhishma ('the terrible [vow]') and the boon of choosing his death.
Bhima's vows (Sabha Parva): to break Duryodhana's thigh and to drink Dushasana's blood; he fulfilled both in the war (Karna and Shalya Parvas).

Arjuna's vow (Drona Parva): to kill Jayadratha before sunset the day after Abhimanyu's death or enter fire himself; Arjuna also had a vow to kill anyone who told him to give up the Gandiva, which nearly led him to kill Yudhishthira in the Karna Parva until Krishna showed a way out.

Krishna's undertaking not to bear arms in the war was strained when he twice advanced on Bhishma (in the Bhishma Parva once raising his discus and once with only his charioteer's whip; popular retellings and art often show him lifting a chariot wheel); popular retellings add that Bhishma had vowed to make Krishna take up arms.

Draupadi's vow to leave her hair unbound until avenged, and to wash it in Dushasana's blood, is prominent in later drama (e.g. Bhatta Narayana's Venisamhara) and popular retellings; the Critical Edition has no such explicit blood-washing vow, though in the Udyoga Parva Draupadi shows Krishna her hair, once seized by Dushasana, and demands that it be remembered.
Ashwatthama's vow to the dying Duryodhana to destroy the Panchalas led to the night massacre.
Amba's vow to destroy Bhishma, fulfilled through her rebirth as Shikhandi, links vows across lives.

Major vows and fulfilment: Bhishma's celibacy – kept for life | Bhima's thigh and blood vows – fulfilled in the war | Arjuna's Jayadratha vow – fulfilled on day 14 | Ashwatthama's vow – fulfilled in the night massacre | Amba's vow – fulfilled through Shikhandi on day 10
Curses (Shapa) in the Epic: Curses (shapa) function as instruments of fate and consequence in the Mahabharata, often given in anger by sages or grieving women and binding even on gods.

Curses shaping the post-war books: Gandhari cursed Krishna (Yadava ruin in the 36th year) | the sages Vishvamitra, Kanva and Narada cursed the Yadavas through Samba (the iron club) | Krishna cursed Ashwatthama (3000 years of wandering) | Yudhishthira cursed women (to be unable to keep secrets)

Earlier curses with consequences in the war: the Vasus cursed by Vashishtha to be born as humans, one of whom was Bhishma | Pandu cursed by the sage Kindama to die on union with a wife | Karna cursed by Parashurama to forget his weapon in need and by a brahmin to have his chariot wheel sink | Arjuna cursed by Urvashi to live a year as a eunuch, used in the Virata year | the sage Maitreya cursing Duryodhana that Bhima would break his thigh
In the epic's account, Vidura was born of a servant woman because the sage Mandavya cursed Dharma (Yama) for punishing him excessively.
Parikshit was cursed by Shringi, a sage's son, to die of a snakebite within seven days, which leads to Janamejaya's snake sacrifice (Adi Parva frame).
The curse said to come from the Earth goddess (Bhudevi) against Karna appears in popular and regional retellings rather than the Critical Edition narrative.
Grief, Futility and Reconciliation: The post-war books turn the epic from victory to grief: Yudhishthira says the victory feels like defeat, and the Stri Parva shows the war through the eyes of widows.

The poet-critic Anandavardhana (9th century, Dhvanyaloka) argued that the Mahabharata's dominant rasa (aesthetic mood) is shanta (peace, quietude), leading to disenchantment with the world, rather than the heroic mood.
Reconciliation scenes, such as Vyasa's one-night raising of the dead and the final vision in heaven where former enemies sit together, offer resolution without erasing the cost.

The deaths of almost the entire older generation (Bhishma, Drona, Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, Kunti, Vidura) and of Krishna end an age; the epic places the war at the junction of the Dvapara and Kali ages.

The Critical Edition (BORI, Pune): The Critical Edition of the Mahabharata was prepared by the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) in Pune; work began in 1919 and the constituted text was completed in 1966.
Critical Edition milestones: project begun 1919 | first volume (Adi Parva) published 1933 | constituted text completed 1966
V. S. Sukthankar was general editor of the Critical Edition until his death in 1943; he was followed by S. K. Belvalkar and then P. L. Vaidya.
The Critical Edition collated a very large number of manuscripts from across South Asia in many scripts; the figure commonly reported is about 1,259 manuscripts.

The Critical Edition aims to reconstruct the earliest recoverable common archetype of the manuscript tradition, not an 'original' text by Vyasa; passages found in only some manuscripts are relegated to footnotes or appendices.

The Critical Edition's reconstructed text is considerably shorter than the vulgate; the epic's self-description as a 'hundred-thousand-verse' collection (shatasahasri samhita) applies more nearly to expanded versions, especially with the Harivamsha appended.
The Harivamsha, the appendix (khila) on Krishna's life and lineage, was published in a separate critical edition by BORI (1969–1971).

Critics of the Critical Edition, including some modern scholars and traditionalists, argue that an archetype reconstructed from divergent recensions may never have existed as a single text, and that excluded passages were living parts of the tradition.
Vulgate, Recensions and Passages Flagged: The 'vulgate' usually means the Northern-recension text with the 17th-century commentary of Nilakantha Chaturdhara (Bharata Bhava Dipa), basis of the Bombay and Calcutta printed editions and of K. M. Ganguli's English translation.

Manuscripts of the Mahabharata fall broadly into a Northern recension and a Southern recension (the latter represented by the Kumbakonam edition, 1906–1910), each with sub-versions by script and region.
The Southern recension is generally longer than the Northern, adding episodes and expansions; neither is simply 'the original'.
The story of Ganesha writing the epic as Vyasa dictated it is found in some manuscripts but is excluded from the Critical Edition's constituted text.
In the Critical Edition's dice-hall scene, Draupadi's garments multiply without an explicit prayer to Krishna; the explicit appeal to Krishna appears in the vulgate and popular retellings.

Popular post-war details not found in the Critical Edition narrative include Ashwatthama's chiranjivi status, the fish-swallowed iron becoming Jara's arrowhead, and Jara as Vali reborn; these come from Puranic or later traditions.
Chapter and verse numbers differ between the Critical Edition and the vulgate; for example, the Vishnu Sahasranama is commonly cited as 13.135 in the Critical Edition and 13.149 in the vulgate.
Episodes such as Barbarika (associated with the Khatu Shyam tradition) are absent from the Sanskrit Mahabharata and come from later texts such as the Skanda Purana and from folk tradition.
Major Translations: K. M. Ganguli's complete English prose translation (published 1883–1896 by P. C. Roy) follows the vulgate text and remains widely available online.
M. N. Dutt published another complete English translation between about 1895 and 1905, also based on vulgate-type texts.

J. A. B. van Buitenen began an English translation of the Critical Edition (University of Chicago Press), completing Books 1–5 in three volumes (1973–1978) before his death; James L. Fitzgerald continued with Book 11 and part of Book 12 (2004).
Bibek Debroy completed an unabridged English translation of the Critical Edition in ten volumes (Penguin, 2010–2014).
The Clay Sanskrit Library published parallel Sanskrit-English volumes of several books of the Mahabharata in the 2000s.

Popular abridgements include C. Rajagopalachari's retelling (1951) and many retellings in Indian languages; abridgements often blend Critical Edition, vulgate and popular episodes without marking the difference.
Classical Sanskrit and Regional Indian R: Plays attributed to Bhasa, published by T. Ganapati Sastri from Kerala manuscripts in the early 1910s, include Urubhanga (The Broken Thigh), which presents Duryodhana sympathetically in his final hours, and Karnabhara (Karna's Burden); their date and authorship are debated.
Bhatta Narayana's Sanskrit drama Venisamhara (c. 7th–8th century) centres on Draupadi's braid and Bhima's vengeance.
Bharavi's Kiratarjuniya (6th century) and Magha's Shishupalavadha (7th century) are classical Sanskrit court epics (mahakavya) based on Mahabharata episodes.
Tamil retellings include Perundevanar's Bharatavenba (c. 9th century) and Villiputturar's Villi Bharatam (c. 14th century), which shapes Tamil popular and ritual traditions.

Kannada retellings include Pampa's Vikramarjuna Vijaya (10th century, also called Pampa Bharata), which makes Arjuna the hero and honours Karna, and Kumaravyasa's Karnata Bharata Kathamanjari (c. 15th century).
The Telugu Mahabharatam (Andhra Mahabharatam) was composed by the 'poet trinity' (Kavitraya): Nannaya (11th century), Tikkana (13th century) and Errana (14th century).

Other regional versions include Sarala Das's Odia Mahabharata (15th century), Kashiram Das's Bengali Mahabharata (c. 16th–17th century) and Thunchaththu Ezhuthachan's Malayalam Mahabharatam Kilippattu (16th century); these often add local episodes.
Regional dates for medieval poets are approximate and contested; they should be treated as conventional scholarly estimates.
Folk, Ritual and Temple Traditions: In Tamil Nadu, the goddess Draupadi Amman is worshipped in a cult with fire-walking festivals and Terukkuttu street theatre; Alf Hiltebeitel's The Cult of Draupadi (1988–1991) is the major study.

Tamil tradition holds that Aravan (Iravan in Sanskrit), son of Arjuna and the Naga princess Ulupi, offered himself as a sacrifice before the war and was married for one night to Krishna in female form (Mohini); this is celebrated at the Koovagam festival, important to the transgender (aravani/thirunangai) community.
In the Sanskrit Mahabharata, Iravan dies on the eighth day of battle fighting the rakshasa Alambusha; the pre-war self-sacrifice is a Tamil and regional addition.

Duryodhana is honoured at a temple at Poruvazhy (Malanada) in Kerala, and villages in parts of Uttarakhand are reported to venerate Duryodhana and Karna; these local traditions invert the epic's moral alignment.
The Pandav Lila ritual dramas of the Garhwal Himalaya enact episodes including the Pandavas' final journey, which is locally tied to the Himalayan landscape.
Many local places across India and Nepal claim association with the Pandavas' exile or final journey; such identifications are traditional and not historically verifiable.
Southeast Asian Versions — Java, Bali an: Old Javanese prose renderings (parwa) of books of the Mahabharata were made around the late 10th century, associated with the court of King Dharmawangsa Teguh of East Java.
The Old Javanese Kakawin Bharatayuddha, composed by Mpu Sedah and Mpu Panuluh in 1157 CE under King Jayabhaya of Kediri, retells the war in courtly verse.
Mpu Kanwa's Kakawin Arjunawiwaha (11th century, under King Airlangga) retells Arjuna's penance and his reward from the gods.

Javanese and Balinese wayang (shadow puppet and dance drama) traditions adapt the Mahabharata extensively, adding indigenous clown-servant characters (punakawan) such as Semar, Gareng, Petruk and Bagong, who have no counterpart in the Sanskrit text.

In Javanese wayang, Draupadi (Drupadi) is usually the wife of Yudhishthira (Puntadewa) alone rather than of all five brothers, and Srikandi (Shikhandi) is portrayed as a woman warrior married to Arjuna; these are major departures from the Sanskrit epic.
Southeast Asian versions should be treated as independent creative traditions, not as witnesses to an earlier Indian text.
Jain, Buddhist and Persian Tellings: Jain retellings of the Pandava and Krishna stories include Jinasena's Harivamsha Purana (783 CE), Hemachandra's Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra (12th century) and Devaprabha Suri's Pandavacharita (13th century).

In Jain tellings, Krishna is one of the nine Vasudevas of the Jain universal history; because of the violence of his life he is said to go to hell after death but is destined to become a future Tirthankara.
In Jain tellings, the Pandavas eventually become Jain monks and attain liberation, often associated with Mount Shatrunjaya, replacing the Hindu Mahaprasthanika and Svargarohana endings.

Jain versions of Krishna's end commonly have Dwaraka destroyed by fire through the wrath of an ascetic named Dvaipayana insulted by drunken Yadava youths, and Krishna killed by Jarakumara, his own half-brother; details vary between Jain authors.

Some Buddhist Jataka stories contain motifs parallel to the Mahabharata (for example, a Ghata Jataka on the fall of Vasudeva's clan and a reference to a woman with five husbands in the Kunala Jataka); their relationship to the Sanskrit epic is debated.
The Mughal emperor Akbar commissioned a Persian translation of the Mahabharata, the Razmnama ('Book of War'), in the 1580s, with illustrated manuscripts by court painters.
Modern Literary, Stage and Screen Retell: Modern Mahabharata retellings with publication dates: Rashmirathi (Dinkar, Hindi) 1952 | Andha Yug (Dharamvir Bharati, Hindi) c. 1954 | Mrityunjay (Shivaji Sawant, Marathi) 1967 | Yuganta (Irawati Karve, Marathi) 1967 | Parva (S. L. Bhyrappa, Kannada) 1979 | Randamoozham (M. T. Vasudevan Nair, Malayalam) 1984 | Yajnaseni (Pratibha Ray, Odia) 1984 | The Palace of Illusions (Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni, English) 2008

Dharamvir Bharati's Andha Yug ('The Age of Blindness') is set on the last day of the war and its aftermath, with Ashwatthama, Gandhari's curse of Krishna and Krishna's death; it is read as a meditation on post-war moral blindness after the Second World War and Partition.
S. L. Bhyrappa's Kannada novel Parva retells the epic in realistic terms, removing supernatural elements and treating the characters as historical humans.
M. T. Vasudevan Nair's Randamoozham retells the epic from Bhima's point of view, the 'second turn' of a brother who is never first.
Irawati Karve's Yuganta is a set of anthropologically informed essays on the epic's characters, notable for its unsentimental readings of Bhishma, Kunti, Gandhari, Draupadi and Karna.
Peter Brook's Mahabharata, adapted with Jean-Claude Carrière, was staged in 1985 and filmed in 1989.
B. R. Chopra's Hindi television serial Mahabharat (1988–1990) shaped popular understanding of the epic across India and includes many popular rather than Critical Edition episodes.
Karna — Sympathetic Readings: Sympathetic modern readings present Karna as a tragic hero denied his rightful status by caste prejudice and fate: abandoned at birth by Kunti, insulted as a charioteer's son at the tournament, and cursed by teachers.
Karna is celebrated for generosity (as 'Daanveer', the hero of giving), notably for giving away his natural armour and earrings to Indra disguised as a brahmin.
Karna's loyalty to Duryodhana, who made him king of Anga, and his refusal of Krishna's and Kunti's offers before the war, are central to his sympathetic portrayal.
Works central to Karna sympathy include Bhasa's Karnabhara, Ramdhari Singh Dinkar's Hindi poem Rashmirathi (1952) and Shivaji Sawant's Marathi novel Mrityunjay (1967).

Critical readings counter that Karna took part in the humiliation of Draupadi in the dice hall, urged Draupadi's disrobing and joined the group killing of Abhimanyu, so the epic portrays him as morally mixed.
The post-war revelation that Karna was the Pandavas' elder brother (Stri Parva) and Yudhishthira's grief turn the epic itself toward a retrospective sympathy for him.
Draupadi and Feminist Readings: Feminist readings highlight Draupadi's legal question in the dice hall, whether a husband who had lost himself could stake his wife, as a challenge the assembled elders could not answer.
Draupadi's speeches in the Vana Parva, criticising Yudhishthira's passivity and questioning divine justice, are read as among the epic's strongest arguments for human agency.
Draupadi's fall first on the final journey, blamed by Yudhishthira on her partiality to Arjuna, is often criticised as an unjust verdict on a woman who suffered most for the Pandavas.
Pratibha Ray's Odia novel Yajnaseni (1984) and Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni's The Palace of Illusions (2008) retell the epic from Draupadi's point of view.
Mahasweta Devi's Bengali short story 'Draupadi' (1978), translated by Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (1981), reimagines Draupadi as Dopdi Mejhen, a tribal woman resisting state violence.

Other women's voices discussed in feminist readings include Gandhari (who chose to blindfold herself), Kunti, Amba/Shikhandi, Madhavi (in the Udyoga Parva), Sulabha (who debates King Janaka) and the widows of the Stri Parva.
Feminist scholars disagree on whether the epic critiques patriarchy or merely displays it; readings range from Draupadi as a feminist icon to Draupadi as an instrument of male honour.
Ethics of War and Violence: The Mahabharata is widely read as a deeply ambivalent war epic: it justifies the Pandavas' war as dharmic yet shows its victory as nearly indistinguishable from defeat.

Readers debate whether Krishna's stratagems (Shikhandi, the Ashwatthama deception, the blow below the navel, Karna's death) are justified necessity, divine design beyond human ethics, or moral failures the epic deliberately exposes.
Ashwatthama's night massacre is often read as the logical end of escalating breaches of the rules of war by both sides, rather than an isolated atrocity.
The Stri Parva laments, Gandhari's curse and the golden mongoose are frequently cited as the epic's internal critique of war and royal violence.

Gandhi's allegorical reading treated the war as the inner battle between good and evil; others, including many nationalists such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak, read the Gita and epic as endorsing righteous action, including force.
Modern scholars compare the epic's rules of war with just war traditions; the comparison is illuminating but anachronistic if taken as identical concepts.
Scholarly Theories of Composition: Most scholars hold that the Mahabharata grew over several centuries; a common estimate places the main period of composition between roughly the 4th century BCE and the 4th century CE.

Alf Hiltebeitel argued that the Mahabharata was composed as a written work over a relatively short span, between the mid-2nd century BCE and the turn of the Common Era; this is a minority but influential position.

The epic hints at its own growth: it calls itself 'Jaya' in its opening invocation, speaks of a 'Bharata' of 24,000 verses without the subsidiary tales, and of a full collection of 100,000 verses; the modern three-stage model (Jaya, then Bharata, then Mahabharata) is a scholarly inference from such statements, not something the text lays out.
Stated sizes of the epic in its own Adi Parva: Bharata core 24000 verses | full Mahabharata 100000 verses (traditional claims, not measured counts)

Nineteenth-century 'inversion' theories, notably by Adolf Holtzmann, claimed that the Kauravas were originally the heroes and the story was later rewritten in the Pandavas' favour; these theories are now generally rejected.
Georges Dumézil (Mythe et épopée, 1968), building on Stig Wikander (1947), read the Pandavas as reflecting Indo-European mythic functions; this comparative reading remains influential but debated.

V. S. Sukthankar's 'Bhrguization' thesis (1936) held that brahmins of the Bhrigu clan reworked and expanded the epic; Madeleine Biardeau and Alf Hiltebeitel emphasised the epic's coherent religious and mythic design.

A 6th-century copper-plate inscription from Khoh (Madhya Pradesh), commonly dated to 533–534 CE, refers to the Mahabharata as the 'collection of 100,000 verses', indicating the expanded epic existed by then.
Historicity and Dating of the War — Mult: Whether the Kurukshetra war happened is unproven; views range from a historical core in a conflict among Iron Age Kuru-Panchala clans to a largely mythic and literary creation.
Traditional Indian reckoning places the war at the junction of the Dvapara and Kali ages and dates the start of the Kali Yuga to 3102 BCE, a date used in the astronomer Aryabhata's work (499 CE).
The Aihole inscription of the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II (634 CE) dates itself 3,735 years after the Bharata war, consistent with the 3102 BCE tradition.
Another tradition, cited by Varahamihira (6th century) from Vriddha Garga and by Kalhana's Rajatarangini (12th century), places Yudhishthira about 653 years into the Kali Yuga, around 2449 BCE.

Puranic genealogies state an interval from Parikshit's birth to the coronation of Mahapadma Nanda of 1,015 or 1,050 years (manuscripts vary, some reading 1,500); scholars using this have proposed dates from around the 15th to the 9th century BCE; F. E. Pargiter proposed about 950 BCE, and B. B. Lal, using shorter average reigns, about 836 BCE.

Proposed dates for the war (all contested): Kali Yuga tradition 3102 BCE | Varahamihira/Kalhana tradition c. 2449 BCE | Puranic-genealogy estimates c. 1400–950 BCE | B. B. Lal's genealogy-plus-archaeology estimate c. 836 BCE

Archaeologist B. B. Lal's excavations at Hastinapura (1950–1952) found Painted Grey Ware levels (roughly early first millennium BCE) and evidence of a flood, which he linked with the Puranic report that the capital moved to Kaushambi after a Ganga flood; the link is suggestive, not proof.

Astronomical arguments based on planetary positions mentioned in the epic have produced widely divergent dates, for example 3067 BCE (B. N. Narahari Achar) and 5561 BCE (P. V. Vartak); most scholars regard the epic's astronomical references as internally inconsistent and unsuitable for precise dating.

Marine archaeology off Bet Dwarka and Dwarka in Gujarat (notably under S. R. Rao from the 1980s) found submerged structures that some link to the Dwaraka of the epic; dating and interpretation of these finds remain disputed.

The epic's numbers (eighteen akshauhinis, over 1.6 billion dead) and its divine interventions show that, whatever historical memory it preserves, the text is not a chronicle; precise dates should be presented as hypotheses.
